IN Queen Anne's reign, Lord Bateman married three wives, all of whom were his servants.- A beggar-woman meeting him one day in the street, made him a very low curtsey. BROUGHAM, in the House of Lords, said ho re- membered a case wherein Lord Eldon referred it in succession to three Chief Courts below, to decide what a particular document was. The Court of King's Bench decided it was a lease in fee; the Common Pleas,. that it was a lease in tail-. the Ex- chequer, that it was a lease for years. Whereupon Lord Eldon, when it came back to him, decided firr himself that it was no lease at all. "PAPA, what is a tornado ?" asked a youthful seeker after information. Glancing nervously around the room to see if the. coast was clear, he said, "You have ofter heard your mother blowing me up for bringing company home without pre- viously notifying her." "Yes, sir." "Well, that is as much like a ornado as anything I know of. But you needn't tell your mother that I said so, however." The service of a sign painter were secured, and When he fuaished his work he Put on his" imprint " by placing his initials, "'F. A. H.," down on the left hand corner of the sign. When the widow come to criticise the work she queried—" What does W. A. H.' stand for?" "Why, Wanted, A Husband," replied the painter. "Oh, yes— I see?" she mused. "It was very thoughful of you, and here are five shillings." General Booth, who isnow touring through New Zealand, revisits Melbourne on 13th November, and will be engaged there until the 18th. On the 1 9th he is going to bombard the famous city of the gold- fields—Ballarat, which, like Eastbourne, refuses to allow the Army to march through its streets. From the 21st to the 24th he will be in the South Austra- -lianmetropolis, Adelaide, and 'on the 25th he takes steamer for India.

Mr. Herbert Vivian, the volcanic young gentle-, man who used to ride the storm and direct the "Whirlwind," has ceased to edit "Life," the ir.:- quent changes in the editorship of which amply il- lustrate " Life's many changes.' Master Vivian will shortly "breakout in a fresh place " with an indivi- dualistic newspaper to be called the "Scorpion.' " Phcebus, what a name with whiel to sound the trump ot future fame 1"

On the subject of the payment of members Sir Michael Hicks-Bench reiterates and emphasises the Tory position of absolute opposition enuniciated by, Mr. Goschen the other day at Cambridge. If "would entail an enormous burden on the coun- try," and "when they got their work well done for nothing, why should they pay people for it ?" lie shies altogether the real arguments, and gives us one More proof of the folly of the sta cement that, so far as labour is concerned, the Liberals and Tories are six of one to half a dozen of the other.

Cheese-making is one of the subjects included in the technical instruction scheme of the Lancashire County Council, and,judging from a statement made at a conference at Preston the other day, it is a pro- cess of which the (Thiry farmers of the County Pala- tine have a gooddeal to learn. In many Lancashire dairies, it. was asserted, cheeses are now made "between the slopstone, the fireplace, and the drain, and are cured in the bedrooms." The sooner, there- fore, a little instruction in cheese-making is im- parted the better.

By Saturday's Australian mail we have news of the Rev. C. A, Berry, the well-known Congrega- tional preacher of Wolverhampton. He arrived in Melbourne on 16 September, and the Melbourne Berald of the following day says :—" When Mr. Berry set out on his travels he had, the permission of his medical advisers. to conduct one service in the Congregational ,Church, Collins-st., Melbourne kr,f which the Rev. Dr. Bevan,fornaerly of Highbury, is pastor). It is not likely, however, owing to the state of his health, that the Collins-st., sanctuary will ring with the eloquent voice of the brilliant preacher."

"Wha wudna dee for Charlie ?" The countless mil- lions who are longing to throw off the Hanoverian yoke, or else to drop their heads on Tower Hill for the sake of the Young Pretender,will please to com- municate at once with the "Legitimist Jacobite League." We mention this because things don't look as rosy as they might for the Howie of Stuart just now. The League had a meeting at St. Ives; on Tuesday night, and a Whiggish mayor and a Han- overian School Board chairman actually carried, " amid'great enthusiasm," a resolution in favour of the maintenance of Queen Victoria on the throne. nut what about Queen Anne?

If the" Indian Mirror "is to be trusted Mrs. Besant has a grand time before her in India. or three months, Says our contemporary, her eloquence will electrify the people. " Dr. Pentecost came to evangelise Indians and Anglo-Indians. Ris work has fallen flat. It will be a different thing with Mrs. Besant's mission. Indians will flock to her lectures,. it is easy enough to assume; but Anglo- Indians, too will flock to hear, and if most of these. go to hear her out of mere curiosity, some few will doubtless remain with her convinced, all their doubts dissipated in thin air. There will he a great spiritual stirin this country the next few months.' -- Mrs. Besant's daughter, Miss Mabel Besant, is said to be about to publish her first literary effort, a story dealing with the subject of hypnotism. Miss Besant is a lovely girl, tall and slender, with pale, , -clear complexion and short, dark curly hair. She attained her majority a few weeks ago, the event being celebrated by a supper given by the United Democratic Club, of which Mrs. and . Miss Besant are both members. Miss Mabel Besant, who lives with her mother at Blavatsky Lodge, helps the , latter with her work among the match girls at Bow, for whom Mrs. Besant and some other Theosophists started a club about a year ago. , .The country house season has yielded at least On good story, and in these times of general depression of spirits this even is something to be thankful for. A short, but dignified Personage arriving on a Visit to An_ intimate friend, was :much astonished by the singular conduct of the footman, who met him at the door. The familiarity—amounting to posi- tive; rudeness—of the powdered flunkey at last evoked a sharp admonition, when; to his horror, the latter commenced, hustlinfr--y, 'him' about, and fairly chasing him into the drawing-room, landed him there with a valedictory kick. However, 06 de- nouement of the incident remains to be told; for a boisterous younger brother of the host it was who, having attired himself in a footman's livery,had de- vised and carried out this startling practical joke.

The tables have been turned on the land-grabber at Caterham. Instead of prosecuting trespassers, he has been prosecuted himself. The name of the grabber in question was Charles Aspray. He was prosecuted at the instance of the Godstone High- way Board for obstructing a footpath running across his fields, which footpath was shown to have been in use as a public right of 'way for over 60 years, though for 25 years past Asprey ha been doing all he knows to rob his neighbours of their rights. No doubt to his great astonishment he has been found guilty and now awaits sentence. We take the liberty of hoping that the sentence will be an exemplary one, and also that other highway authorities will take a hint from the action of the Godstone Board.

The most interesting and important speeches at the autumn meeting of the council of the Libera- tion Society on Monday were those by Mr. hung- worth and and Mr. P. W. Clayden, who proposed and seconded the resolution of the day, bearing on Welsh disestablishment. Mr. Illingworth pointed to the united front of the whole Liberal party on the question, and expressed the general feeling when he said that he could see little difference between the Welsh Church and the Irish. Mr. Clayden, in a speech which dealt with the subject in its widest aspects, made several very happy hits. "The shadow" he said "of the general election was before them, but it was a shadow which rested on the faces of their opponents while the sunrise was upon their own."

A story told of Sir Augustus Harris's .new tenor, M. Cossira, is worth repeating. The son of a fisher- man, and himself brought up to the sea, he a few years ago drew an unlucky number in the conscrip- tion, and was absorbed into the ranks of the 18th Chasseurs,where he soon became famous as a troller of soldiers' songs. In the Ordinary coarse he would have served his time, and perhaps have gone back to fishing, but accident placed him instead on the stage of the Paris Grand Opera, and later on at the Covent Garden Italian Opera. The " Gazetten de France" relates bow it happened. One summer day President Grevy attended a review at Long- champs,one brigade consisting of the 18th Chasseurs and the 46th of the line. The manceuvres were relieved by an interval for refreshment, during which the linesmen gathered round, and loudly ap- plauded the songs of one of their number. "Pooh exclaimed a Chasseur, " we have in the 18th a fellow who can sing a great deal better than that." He was, of course, challenged to produce him, whereupon M. Cossira came forward and regaled his comrades with the patriotic hymn of Alsace- Lorraine•As luck would have it, Brigadier-General hearing,adnedre' struck by the d him to report voice eor thefw as youngwithi n warrior, or bimself at headquarters the next morning. In the result Private Cos&ira carried a letter from the General to M. Ambroise Thomas, of the Conserva- toire, and France soon had a soldier less.

After seven more days sail- ing with moderate weather we ARRIVEID AT ADELAIDE the first place of call in Australia (all on one side, as the sailors say, like a crab,for some of our cargo had shifted during the gale). There we heard that two vessels had been lost during the gale—one being passed bottom upwards. We congratulated our- selves on our safe arrival, and having lost so much time on our way we had only one day's supply of coal in our bunkers; and had rough weather con- tinued much longer we should have been in an awkward fix. We only stayed here a few hours (long enough to discharge and coal) sailing away on Saturday night, and experiencing rough weather on Sunday and Sunday night, during which time we saw a vessel upside down,which had stranded on the rocks outside Melbourne Harbour. It was no easy raatter getting our pilot on board; he was just thrown into the arms of one of the sailors, who held him like grim death. The entrance to the bay is about one mile across, with a good. deep , channel in the centre, and sandy banks on each side. It is about 40 miles from Melbourne city. In a few hours we were anchored in the middle of the bay amongst other vessels that had experienced similar , rough weather. And now I bring my letter, to a close by saying that the Captain received two testi- monials signed by the passengers, thanking him and his crew for their skill and kindness during the voyage. The newspaper had an exciting account of the gale during which they said our second mate lost his leg and that we lost two lifeboats, which was not true. Raving arrived safely I will con- clude (and send you an account of Melbourne .further on) with thankfulness at being permitted 1 to arrive safely.

div.head: VOYAGE TO AIJBTRALIA.
div.p: A VOYAGE TO AIJBTRALIA.
BY W. lINSWORTIL tft (CONCLUDED). AL Now to return to our home on the sea—by this Pme the coal was on board, and we lifted our an- chor and

• SET OUT FOR THE SOUTHERN OCEAN The sailors told us we were now going to "see a sea" though up to the present (except in the Bay of _ Biscay), we had had fine weather. Every prepara- tion was made for it all was 'made fast that was loose. The well decks were cauled and pitched end made secure, so that the waves would pass over without coming below,but, to the surprise of every- body, we rounded the cape and got well out to sea in comparatively fine weather; and while we were in this happy state—l will diverge a little to call your attention to the moving creatures in the firma- ment we came across in this neighbourhood—the Cape pigeon,mollehawk,and the albatross, followed the vessel, to all appearance,day after day,and were constantly on the wing, with a flight different en- tirely to that of the English birds. They simply spread out their wings and float about in the air; especially the albatross. This bird, with. a body the size of a large duck, would spread out its great wings—which the sailors said would measure from tip to tip about 16 feet—and sail round and round the vessel, without apparently moving a single feather. 1 have seen them float through the air for miles and all the movement if it wanted to lower itself, would be simply to bend its wings, or if. to! raise itself spread them straight out and soar away' a mile or two in front of us and then come back,but the speed they go at is tremendous. We were travel- ling 10 miles an hour, but these birds would pass us like lightning, and would only stop at the stern of the boat when something in the shape of meat was thrown overboard. Then they would come down with a flap of the wings (which was a signal for all • smaller birds to keep out of the way), and off again, • and no matter how hard the wind blows, they go as easy against it as with it. The mollehawk and Cape pigeon have a somewhat similar flight, but not so steady, they being much smaller than the albatross. These also come along side the vessel, and the distance they fly during their stay with us must be great, as they would fly round and round from morning until night. No matter how early you got up they were there,and would not rest the, ;whole day,except to drop in the water for food. I was disappointed in finding the albatross had such a Small body, but if ycin would like to know more you will have to come and see for yourself, for, artho' I have said so-much, I fear I shall not be able to leave the same impression on your minds as they • have left on mine. There-is-another subject which 1 should like to say something about, but I. fear it is too high, for me, that is • ,• - t

-THE HEAVENLY BODIES. But the sun-rise.and-sun-set at sea is•a grand sight. There is one thing that bothers me, and that is if the world is round how-is it that the sun only made its appearance about 6-30 a.m., and left us at 6 p.m. in sninrner, and dark almost as soon as it is set? There. can be no excuse for saying the sun is fur- ther away from us, for it goes right over our head.; then again, there is a cluster of stars that are only seen in the southern :Hemisphere, such as the Southern-Cross, and yet we see -Jupiter and Venus out in the same Vicinity, but Ivill feave the mat- ter with the knowing ones,-who are not particular to a, few millions of miles, and proceed. My boy Torn says some Of his chums at home asked him to get out and have a swing when he crossed the line, and he wishes me to say that the ship would not stop. Seven days after leaving- the Cape, we were in about tha same latitude as England, and being winter it was very cold with occasional hail-storms. When the wind blew it was bitter cold ; now comes the necessity for warm clothing; and here comes one of our mistakes. We had made very little pre- paration for it, being told there was no necessity, and being advised to take only light thin clothing. This we found was a mistake, and I would advise all coming this way at that time of the.year to bring *dim dOthingwith them, in fact, I should say, Come just as you would dress in England. My great surprise when I landed at Melbourne was to find people walking about with their overcoats on, as we had been told, their winter was like our sum- mer. But the people say here that. their winter has changed considerably-this last 10 years. I sup- 'pose at Cr ristmas it will be that hot' that we shall he glad to shut ourselves up to.keep the heat out— This will be rather a change for us, having been accustomed to shut ourselves up to keep the cold put.

div.head: THE' GREATEST EVENT ON OUR JOURNEY.
div.p: THE' GREATEST EVENT ON OUR JOURNEY.

On July 30 we met with very rough weather, the sea rising steadily until Sunday, August 3rd, when it was something tremendous,. and it was with great difficulty the vessel -could be kept in front of the waves. The engines were going full speed, and the sea lashing about in all directions. At night it reached the height of its fury (the height of the waves being estimated at from 60 to 70 feet), and three of our sails were blown away. It Ow becathe evident something must be done, either turn round and face it or pour oil on,the water. The latter was adopted, and either that or the sea going down made things a little more agree- able. I am inclined to think that the old proverb as to pouring oil on troubled waters had its effect. During the height of the tempest, one of our pas- Sengers died (about Which I shall have something to say further on). During the night a wooden box or coffin was made,and next day a funeral service was held in the saloon,committing the body to the deep. This is a solemn occasion, and, although funerals induce a natural repugnance,one of this kind makes us feel a kind of a sneakingre,gard for mother earth. The sea was running very high at the time, and any attempt at ceremony was out of the question, as it took mourners all their time to stand on their feet, and the engine had to be kept at full speed. The body was .put over the side during that part of the serviee--- We commit "&c.—and although it was weighted by heavy bars, my impression was that it would not hold together 10 minutes after it left. the side of the ship. Talk about launching life boats in a sea like this! I will leave you to draw your own conclusions. During the Wednesday (6th) a heavy sea struck the vessel on both sides and came down on the well deck hatches with a regular swamp, breaking it into splinters. You will better under- stand the force of what I say when I tell you that this deck was supported by iron girders, and not only did it break the deck in but the girders also. This being a covering over the well-deck, the water did no further damage—but it certainly made things very uncomfortable below. One of the engineers estimated that the weight of the wave would be about 60 tons. By this time, I presume you will think we were having a lively time of it. Well, we vvere—for every now and then the galley or cook house—would have a turn; the pans and kettle would be rocked loose and go rolling from side to side and such a row. You have heard the row a dog makes running down the street with a tin can tied to its tail. Well, fancy 50 of them, and then you can tell the row we had. Cooking at this stage was, of course, out Of the question,and we had to catch what we could. One gentleman sitting at the saloon table was thrown right out of his chair, others were pitched right out of their berths into the middle of their cabin. I must not forget the engines, for when the propeller got out of the water (when the waves lifted up the stern of the ship) it would go spinning round like mad; .the vessel would plunge down the wave like a toboggin slide and would rear it- self up on the wave in front or rather the waves that bad run past us. It was then you could -see the wildness of the situation to advantage as you stood on the bridge. All credit is due to the captain, who did not leave the bridge for 24 hours. We had 7 days of this sort of weather, and were not sorry when it began to subside a little, for it had begun to be unpleasant below, as all had been battened down, even to the ventilators. In conversation with the chief engineer, who had been round Cape Horn, and the Western Coast trade for many years he said those waves were the highest he had ever seen. I said "These are what. you call mountains high,"and he said "Yes." They certainly were very high, and looked very dreadful, but to talk about " mobntaina high "reminds one of the tale of "Our cat and another." Now-to return to

div.head: ISLE OF MAN INTERNATIONAL
div.p: THE ISLE OF MAN INTERNATIONAL
EXHIBITION.

Mr. Henry W. Pearson, of Liverpool, hasjust been appointed General Manager of the forthcoming In- ternational Exhibition, to be held at Douglas, Isle of Man next season. Mr. Pearson had charge of the, very successfnl Industrial Exhibition, which was. held last winter in Glasgow. and previous to that, of the Liverpool Polytechhic Exhibition. The Douglas Exhibition will be of a general, comprehen- sive and national character, special provision being made for exhibits from England, Ireland, Scotland. and Wales. The Island industries will also receive proper attention. To make the Exhibtion ,more complete, space is to be allotted to a number of Continental exhibitors. An International Fine Art Gallery will form one of the principal features. Science and-Industry will also be well repres nted. The Exhibition will be lighted throughout with electricity,and witlithe ornamental pleasure grounds and lake will cover about twentyacres, which have been secured at Belle Vue, Douglas. It is expected to open about the middle of June; next Year.
LA.bY CARLISLE ON WOMEN'S WORK.

A meeting was held under the auspices of the local Women's Liberal Association, at the Assembly Rooms, Hardman-st. Liverpool,on Monday evening, when the Countess Of Carlisle delivered an eloquent address on Liberalisrc. Mrs. Egerton Stewart Brown occupied the chair. There was a large attendance, including a number of the members of the Warring- ton Women's Liberal Association. The President described the object of the Women's Liberal Associa- tion, and made an earnest appeal to all voters to do their best to return Liberal members at the forth- coming municipal elections.—The Countess of Car- li,le pleaded the women's cause. She said she was new to platform work, but each time she made an effort she seemed to feel more and more how muck had been neglected in the past. They were told that men were not prepared to admit them as equals un- til they had given proofs of their fitness for it. She contended that the better educated women were the more fitteFl,to carry out their maternal duties. Wo- men.werbsaiul to be delicate, but men were often delicate toe. Women must have their freedom, and try to understand political knowledge. They wanted to do their share in the world's work, and to stand side' by side With their sistei's in the industrial. classes, and to make men understand how precious was the soul of women. On the drink question,she said if the Liverpool women did their duty they could get half the licences in Liverpool stopped. She' concluded by earnestly advocating Home Rule for Ireland.

div.head: COURT LEET OF -HALTON.
div.p: THE COURT LEET OF -HALTON.
HISTORICAL SKETCH.

Speaking as High steward of Haß,on Court Leet, last week, Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, said he was reckoning the other day that was the 730th time the court had met. They had papers showing the great antiquity of the court, and one document contained the names of those who had signed the presentment in the year 1220. It was almost im- possible to believe that any institution could go on for so many year, but it was a fzet, and the papers were ncw deposited in the Record Office at Lon- don. In olden times these courts were of very great importance, and were instituted in the days of William the Conqueror. The whole of England was then scheiuled in what WAS called Doomsday Book, and the country was divided amongst the King's followers. The county of Chester was divided intoa number of honours; these were again sub-divided into manors; and so the honour and manor of Halton were formed, and afterwards be- came an appanage of the Crown. It'was not exactly a Crown Manor, but it belonged to the Sovereign of the country by virtue of being the Duke of Lancas-- ter, so that really the Queen was Lady Paramount of the Manor. The revenues of the Duchy of Lancaster were now administered not for her benefit, but as part of the revenues of the country. En the days when these courts had power there were no justices of the peace—they were created some centuries later—and these courts were the places where the business of the Manor was done. Judges of Assize coming at intervals. The land was divided by law amongst three classes of people: First a all there were the slaves, probably the descendants of the ancient Britons, and they would remember the description of this class given in Sir Walter Scott's "Ivanhoe." Then there were those who had no land at all, and lived in cbttages—not labourers in our sense of the term,because they got no wages, and were without land. There were those who held land by Copy of Court Roll. as that Manor of Halton was now. The lord admitted tenants on the land, who had rights to hold under him as long as they did certain work for him and as long as they did military service and fought for him; and he protected them. They could easily imagine what the position of a small man was with the great Lords of the Manors. The middle classes did not exist,and the people were glad to claim the protection of the Lords of the Manor. In process of time, instead of giving labour, and fighting,the people made money payments,and,sub- ject to certain duties performed in those courts, the cottagers got lots of land allotted to them, as well as a number of fields and small enclosures about the country. They had not full liberty, however, till a very late date ;indeed they could not leave their native township unless they had permission from their lord. In those courts some ridiculous present- I ments were made. Men were summoned for not ringing their pigs; and all sorts of petty quarrels and squabbles, and everything else were decided in these courts. Now they were a relic of the past; but he hoped he was too good a Conservative ever to discontinue Halton Court Leet whilst he lived. He suggested the courts would die out, and pity it was that they should ; but he was desired by the Duchy of Lancaster to keep llalton Court Leet, i which he had great pleasure n doing. There was :not much business in the Manor of Halton, as most of the land had been enfranchised, but still there were a good many in Widnes and Halton who held land by 'copy of court roll. The roll was made by the lord, who at the death of a parent' alloWed the son to succeed the father on payment of a small heriot. This system prevailed in many countries in • Europe to-day. They had now gone into a different system. He was exceedingly glad to see so many at ,court that day, and thanked them for their attendance.—Mr. Pritchard asked if the court had any power over the roads of the-district.—Mr. Davies said the power of the Court had never been abotished,but they had THE SICKLY PEOPLE, fallen into desuetude through various Actmicheing I consider it the height of folly for a doctor to re- P commend anyone in a consumption to take a voy state of the footpath leading from the Union-road age passed.—Mr. Pritchard drew attention to the bad , of this kind for the good of his health, especially as I to Halton. It was used by nine tenths of the peo- third class passenger. The food,in the first place, is pie of the township, and he wished to know if the too rough; and again the knocking about he gets is Court Leet had power to order something to be enough to kill ivy delicate person. The sleeping ac- done.—Mr. Davies said the Court had the power,but commodation ir totally unfit for them, and seamen they must first present the responsible person. They I are not men of much sympathy. We had two cases could not present the township.—Mr. Wright said of this kind. One died and the other was reduced to the footpath had been voluntarily repaired.—Mr. a mere skeleton. It is true wine, brandy, beef tea, Astbury said he had seen the road r6paired by the arrowripot, &c.,were supplied to them,together with township men, and Mr. Davies said in that case the ? Highway Board should be appealed to. other delicacies,but what are these to a sickly

div.head: DARING IMPOSTOR, THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT
div.p: A DARING IMPOSTOR, THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT
ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER -XXI. CONFIDENCE.
In the pa:fiance- -of- lig ---oWn profession, Mott Reybold felt sure that he "held a winning hand."

He knew that Irene Lefferts bad much famll3 pride, and that she would stop at no sacrifice tc save from publicity the evil-doing of her brother. He further knew, or believed, that Irene hac, transferred to Allen Lee,the love she once had fol him, or, at least, that her interest was so great ir- the young man who had saved her life, that sin would accept of any terms he might propose,, ic order to keep her proteg4 from the penitentiary. R,eybold's forethought and power of combination proved that he had talents of no eommon order— talents which might have won honourable success, had they been used in an honourable way. When he went to his quarters, after his stirring interview with Irene Lefferts; he fairly hugged him- self at the thought that he was the master of the situation.

As he was about to go up the stairs that led to his apartments, he met his partner, Jack Hydo, coming down. "Hello, deah boy 1" was Hyde's greeting. "Have you found a fortune, or has the news reached you 014 some forgotten uncle has made you his sole heir.?"
"Neither one nor the other. But, why do you ask 2"

"Because, old chappie, you do look so deuced well pleased with yourself that I cawn't but believe, don't cher know, that something delightful has hap- pened to you," drawled Hyde. "No, nothing that I did not expect, I assure you. But, I say, who's upstairs?" "Only that detective cad, who goes by the ex- traordinary name' of Cash. I'd like to- change him for his weight in gold; I would, ba. Jove ;" and Hyd€ laughed in his soft way, as if he thought he had said something funny. . " Ah, Cash is waiting for me," said Reybold, and lie shot past his partner and bounded upstairs two steps at a time. . In the room which was devoted to card-play- ing at night Reybold found a short, stout man, with smooth face and a head as near bald as it well could be, and still have a sign of hair, awaiting him.

"Well, Cash, what news ? " asked Reyhold, taking a chair near his visitor and setting the key for the conv6rsation by speaking in a low tone. " Things is workin' all right, I guess," said Cash. with a dumb laugh and a knov.ling wink.
"And Frank "Frank, yes; well, I've just left Frank."
"And how is he ?"
"Drunk as a fiddler. You see, I carry out orders, Mr. Reybold, and I'll keep Frank soaked and under key till you give the word to let up,' said Cash.

In justice to the many good and honest men wha take pride in being detectives, it should be said that Cash was not a regular officer, nor connected with any organised "bureau." He belonged to the class known as "private detectives," some of whom are quite as ready to sell their time and cunning for the perpetration or defence of crime as they are to give their Se •vices for a consideration to the most laudable object. "I want Frank kept out of the way; but, mind you, Cash, you must see that he does not drink so as to endanger bis life." "Of course not; Mr. Reybold ; but I can't much see of what use his life is to him or any one else,' said Cash, with a h ghly virtuous manner. It must be enough for you to know that his life is of the greatest value to me at this time; but, while this is the case, it is all-important that he should be kept out of sight till I am ready to use him. Do you understand 7" "You can bet your sweet life, I tumble to that little racket every time." And Cash winked both eyes very fast, as if he thought it essential to the understanding of his words. "Have you seen Mingo since 7" ' "No ; but I saw his wife in the street this morning. I tell you, Mr. Reybold, that woman 'F. a terror • from Terrorsville—a keen one from away back; and I wonder that a man that has to get in such tine work as Pete keeps her around." Reybold coughed approval, but made no other response. Taking some money from his pocket- book, he handed it to Cash, with the remark: "You must keep me posted; and let me tell you. if you see me through-this matter in good shape. I'll be so fixed that I can help you; and those whc know me say I have a good memory for those whc stand by me." "If that's so," said Cash, rising and shaking out the crown of his soft felt hat, which he had been fitting on his knee, "then you won't forget me—no, not till the day you die; and I hope that interestin event is a great many years off." "I hope so, too. Good day," said Reybold. _ _ _ _ . _

- Cash repeated "Good day," and 'made a motion as if he thought about shaking hands; but he went off without any further formality. Incapable of anything like honour .or fidelity himself, Reybold. was ,not the man to place any reliance in his friends or his tools, except so far as he could control the former, and superintend the latter; and it must be confessed that with sucii friends and such tools as he 'had, he was quite right. Cash counted the money when he got out of sight, and evidently pleased to find it was twenty dollars —being in small bills it looked like much more—he went to a liquor saloon and treated himself. Lighting a cigar, he sauntered off frith that air of combined opulence and leisure that always comes tc some men when they have a little more ready money than usual in their pockets. He stepped into a number of the very lowest bars up alley-ways and down in suffocating basements. and in each place he drank, and conversed in the most familiar way with the wretched creatures standing behind the counters. At length Cash found himself in front of Mingo Pere's establishment. It was anything but inviting when seen by, the light of the opposite lamp at night; but with its sunken door, its mossy and ragged roof—like a curious Wig—its scaly and bat- tered windows, the place had a repulsively disrepu- table appearance by daylight. Mingo himself answered Cash's rap, and it needed no second glance to show that he had been drinking, or else he was recovering from a recent debauch.

Cash and Mingo met like old friends, and they adjourned, after making sure that the door was as securely fastened as its rotten state would admit, to the little room where the ex-convict and Reybold were accustomed to hold their cozisultse tion s.
Here they drank ag•;, , but Cash showed he wat no more affected by his recent libations than if he had been drinking water instead of the abominable stuff sold in the dives.

"Well, Mingo," Cash began, with the confidential manner of an old associate, "you iid that job up fine, and I hope you got paid for it as it deserves." "What job's .hat," growled Mingo. "Why, the jewellery racket." , "I don't know no jewellery racket. "Oh, come, Mingo; none of that to me." , _
"I'm givin' you riawthn' but the, straight tip. Hope I may be struck dead if I aint been doin' square."

Oh of course you have. Everything is, right and square in the profesh. Well, I don't blame you for layin' for Lee. Confound a feller, say I, that'll go back on a pal as he did on you, aricrgo for to put on airs—just as • if- he thought that a forger was any better than the man that cracks cribs" said Cash. Yes, cuss him, he's gone up, and he'll stay up," hissed Mingo. "I could have made big money out of that job, but I worked for less just to get even with 367. When he gets out of (plod agin, mebbe he'll be more willin' to mix in with his ole chums."

I say, Mingo." •"Say on." "If you work for glory, instead of nioney, then you're not the man I tak(! you' for." .“ I. do work for money, but ,when I can ring in a liitle revenge, then 111 tak_e _less money," _said Mingo. - These men spoke about "ork-":, just as if their infamous practices were„,sdine respectable mechani- cal calling. ' , " Still you was hiTed ; and I don't 'mind tellin ou the same man hires me. He's playin' for a big stake, and don't:you forget it,,Mingd," "I don't f9rget it." - "Then don't you think you and me'd be fp;IS if we didnX ring in so as to get our share of the boodle?" "Yes, I do; and I'll have it, by—" 'lt was evident Mingo was about to swear, but the oath stopped before reaching his swollen lips, his attention being attracted by a suppressed cough that came from a little corner closet. fr'
He leaped to his feet, sprang in the direction di the noise, and flung open the closet door. Then the oath did. come, as, stooping, he seized his Wife by the throat and pulled her out.
11.11141PTER .r 'FIRE!"
When Mingo tore his wife, Minnie, from the closet, she sent up a shriek of alarm, and by a powerful effort, freed herself—flom-his_grasp, and made a spring for the single door opening into thE MOM.

With the cunning of a thief and the- strength of a brute, he anticipated the movement, and leaping before her, he planted his back against the door, and reached out his long arms with his fingers curved like the claws of a tiger. The frightened woman came to a sudden halt, and -panted like a hunted hare, as she stood looking intc his blood-shot eyes. "What was you a-doin' in there?" he asked, at he kept one hand extended, and with the othei pointed Co the closet in which he found her con. cealed.

" I—l was in the room when I heard you ane Cash coming in," she gasped; and sne lookee pleadingly to her husband's companion, as if im. ploring his protection and interference. ". Ha, ha 1" hissed Mingo, "and so you ran in therE to be out of the way, coz you was skeered ; is that it ? "
"Ye—yes; that's it," she said, her face ashy witl terror; and she backed towards the closet again as if to avoid the devil of murder which she• sass In his eyes.
He opened his mouth till the yellow teeth fairl3 flashed through his stubby beard, and then he said with a laugh that only a fiend could imitate success. fully:
"-Oh, you are so innocent Oh, you are such b white cooing dove, cuss you 1" Mingo took a stridt towards her, and closed his fingers till they snappec again. , _ _

Oh, see here, Mingo 1" called out Cash, as he arose from his chair, and laid his hand soothingly or the man's shoul4er. "What do you want me to see 7" snapped Mingo and he glared at Cash as if he were going to stranglt him, which, being the stronger man, he might easib have done.
"Women 's earns things," said Cash, shrinking back. "They want to find out everything; and I think, sometimes, there ain't no use a tryin' to stor 'em.'

"Right, cash; right every time. This woman's been tryin' to find out everything, cuss her? I've told her all a wife should know, but that don't content her; so she hides and goes to listenin• an' listenin', an' when she aint a listenin' she's a growlin' an' a whinin', till I aint got no more

patience." Again he rushed at her like a furious bull, and again, with a cry of dread, she avoided him by sinking to the floor. Her very weakness and timidity added to thE coward's anger, and he took another stride and stood over her, as if he were gloating in his owr brute strength and power for harm. "Don't, Mingo! Don't 1" protested Cash. "Wait till you've got over yer anger, an' then correct Ulf woman as she should be corrected—if you thinh She needs it." For reply Mingo hurled Cash to one side and kicked at his wife. "Let me out, Pete 1 Let me out, and I'll neve] do it again 1" cried Minnie, in the pleading voice of a frightened child. "No, she won't never do it again," joined in Cash. " I'll see that she don't never do it again.' Mingo addressed this to his companion; ther glaring down at the crouching. woman, and again extending his huge hands, he continued: "I 'll tea' yer eyes out so that you can't watch; and I'll pup yer tongue out so that you can't blab." He bent lower over her, foaming at the mouth His blood-shot eyes were ablaze, and the veins swelled into ridges on his short, red throat. Minn;E was now shrinking before the corner cupboard, with her thin, white hands pleadingly up-raised. As a tiger might seize a fawn, he suddenly pounced down and fastened the fingers of both hands in hef throat.
She cried out, but the sound was suddenly checked. He lifted her from the floor, as if there weie no weight on his hands, and shook her for an instant.

"Stop, Mingo; stop, or there'll be murder!" shouted Cash, as he flung 'himself on the ruffian's arms and broke his grasp. The interference came too late. The poor woman's face grew purple and her form limp, and there was blood on her face as she fell in a heap to the floor. Mingo reached down his hands, as if he were abouc to seize her again, but Cash once more held him back.
"Great Scott, man 1 you've killed her! " cried the sham detective, and he averted his face from .the
body on the floor.

"1 —l'm glad I did," said Mingo, gasping, and dropping into a chair. "She's been a balkin' of me ever since I got out last time, and she didn't pay nc heed to my warnin's." But the ruffian's anger had gone down, and the hands, recently so rigid and full of murder, trembled. He sat where he could see his wife lying on the floor, face down, and giving no sign of life. The possible effect of this act on himself, rathez than any regret for it, sobered him. He kept his eYes fixed on the prostrate form, as if he were fascinated, and, with his coarse lips compressed, he breathed very hard. "I guess I'd better be gittin' out of this," said Cash, moving towards the door, and carefully avoid- ing the body in his path. "'Taint just the thing for an outsider to interfere between a husband and his wife. It always ends in trouble." • Still breathing hard, Mingo leaped to his feet, and said, in a cringing, pleading voice: , "Wait, Cash; wait, an' let's see how bad she's hurt." Cash's courage and firmness, such as they were, asserted themselves when he saw the other's alarm: "No, Mingo," he said, "that's your job, an' you must attend to it yersel'." He went over, and laying his hand on the door knob and giving it a turn, he added: "I aint seed nothing. You needn't be afeerd of me, if the worst comes to the worst." Seeing that Mingo made no response, he went out and softly closed the door behind him. Still Mingo sat there, his eyes fixed, with an expression of ever increasing horror, cn the motionless heap on the floor. The awful deed had sobered him, and the hot blood in his veins was turning into ice every moment. He knew but one remedy for all his mental and physical ills, and to this he now turned. There was a black bottle on the little rickety pine table by his side, and placing this to his lips, he held it there till the last drop of the fiery stuff was drained. "She's dead, but it's her own fault. She oughtn't to 'ye played me that way. I warned her again and again, but she would not let up." This he said aloud, as he steadied himself by the back of his chair, and leaned towards the heap on the floor. He took a forward step as if he were going to examine it, but, in an instant, he staggered back, with both hands pressed to his face. "Ha! She's done for; an', if this is found out, I'll be done for, too." This he muttered aloud, as he groped his way to th-?, door, for the approach of night and a storm made it suddenly dark. • • - - With one backward glance he left the room, and carefully locked the door on the outside. The im- pulse to save himself from the consequences of his crime s;irred him but, excepting in the vaguest way, he had no feiling of horror at the deed, for his con Science was dead Except when some thief was in hiding in the tumble down house, or some of the outlaw gang came there at night to plan a robbery, or to conceal the plunder they had stolen, Mingo Pete and the ill-starred Minnie were the only occu- pants of the place. It would seem that every bit of plaster and every stick of timber in the wretched a:J.Rie had become debased like its inhabitants.

-2:Tingo went into an adjoining room, where, 'after Pulling down the paper shades on the broken wind- ows, Lie IA a lamp. There was a bed in this room, and,; drawing from under it a box, he took therefrom a large number of articles of jewellery; these he quickly and dexterously secreted about his person. This done, he crowded a change of clothes into a earppt-bag that looked to be already full. With the i•apidity and skill of one accustomed to such .Work, he put on a false beard and wig, and with the aid of a stick of Indian ink and a little cra.ckd Ln wael look'ng-glass, he made a number of lines about his eyes and nose that completely changed his appear- n .
had but just completed these preparations for t ight, when he was startled by a vigorous rap- pi-p..94 at the' docir, -
J . - . athing.hard and panting, like one after a long run rom danger, he bent his head in thdldireetion of i•lie sound, as if to make sure that his ears did no eodve him.

A half minute of painful silence, and he was begi Thing to believe that the sound was due to his own imagination, when again the rapping was ,repe ted, this time with more vigour than before. go lo:kesed the lamp, raised the window and

putting out his head, he.saw a tall, dark figure in the sunken doorway. "Who's that ?" he asked. "Me," came the reply. "Who's me ?" "Don't you know ?" "If I did I would'nt ax. W'at's yer name?' "Farley." "The blazes I" was Mingo's comment, and draw- ing back his head and lowering the window, he hastened down to the door, which he opened._

, . --.-‘4-Yuu seenrto-be-a:11---attleep--herei" growled- Rey- bold, evidently in no good humour. . __"Well, rm up I" fespended Jingo, in the same tones. • . , , .., , !`„Where's Minnie? She always hears me." '• '

".Slie's asleep; she aint a feelin' well," said Minge, making as if he would prevent the other from entering. "Let usgo upstnirs, 3lingo. I want to have a long talk with yon," said Reybold. "Now ?"."7Yes, now; that's what I'm here for." " Can't you wait 2" ".No." " Can't-you have me meet you somewhere else an' talk ? "
"What's wrong with this place 7" "Oh, Farley, there aint nothin' wrong with this place, as I know of, only Minnie—she's been a tumblin' to our racket an' a listenin'."
"If I had such a wife I'd get rid of her mighty quick," said Reybold, angrily. "Yes, I know, some men would; but I'm the tenderest-hearted feller in the world. I'm as gentle as a kid—" •

"As two kids," sneered Reybold. "Yes, as a flock of kids. I don't want no family fusses, an' so I lets Minnie have her way." "You are an angel." "I guess I am. Bat I say, Farle7, why can't I meet you somewhere else in an hour or two?" "You seem anxious to get me away." "Well, no; not edzackly that; but the fac' is I've got another little matter to 'tend to right off, an' it's pressin' me like a grip. So, if you'll say the word an' name the place, I'll be on hand," said Mingo, still standing before Reybold, as if to pre- vent his ascending the stairs. Reybold gave a long, low whistle; then suddenly checking himself, he asked: "Do you know where Cash lives ?" "Where Cash lives? Yes, know it like a book." "Where's the plsce 2" Over on Ninth-street, a- little way off from Third Avenue." "Au aristocratic place." "Yes, Farley, an awful swell place—of the kind.; "Can you call at my quarters to-night 2' " When?" "At ten." "Yes, or at eleven, or at twelve." "Come at ten. I'll be watching for you." "What's up?" "I want you to guide me to Cash's."
"I can do that." "And I can depend on you to be on hand 2"

"I say yes; an' you'll agree that in all our little deals I've anus kept my word with you," said Mingo. Reybold did not heed this bid for a compliment. "I'll look for you," was all he said, as he made his way towards the gaslight in the street, and Mingo closed the door behind him.

A's-cautiously as if he feared the woman lying on the floor overhead might be, aroused into life by his footfall, Mingo made his way.. back to the room wbere he'had. left the light burning. If he had entered the house to commit a burglary, he could not, have moved with more silence arid stealth.
He evidently had a fixed plan in his mind, for he worked quickly and without hesitation.
He to-ok the straw :mattress from the bed and tore out the musty contents, and! over this and the bed clothes he poured the c.ontents_of a kerosene can. • • _• - _ _ _ _
This 'done, he placed one of the bed slats across a little table, and putting the lamp, on one end of the slat, he balanced it with an empty wash-bowl at•the other. . •

The lamp was directly over the straw, so that, if it remained there lit; as Ming ;proposed it should, the time would soon coma when the exhaustion. of the oil would destroy the ,b'alance, and the lamp would fall to the floor and set fire to the hone. The incendiary's plan was as simple as it proved to be effective. -

Satisfied that he had taken every precaution to guard against the discovery of his crime, Mingo picked up the carpet-bag -a.nd left the room; taking care that the blinds Were drawn inside and the door locked behind him.
He made his way to the street, and having looked the front door, he dropped the key into a sewer, and then looked up at the house. There was no light, no sign of life visible from the front.

He was still a strong, active man, so that he did not feel the burden of the bag or the weight in his rockets. He started off at a quick pace, keeping in the shadows of the narrow, unfrequented streets that lead to the north.

He had not been gone from the house ten minutes, when he heard the quick fall of hoofs and the thrilling vibrations of bells, while the gamins playing in the streets sent up the exultant cry of " Fire 1 Fire! Fire 1" as if they gloried in destruc- tior

Th' EiOng's registered for trans- mission abrooad, formn perts, an' runs thus:

FUNNIER THAN A PLAY. Friend Jones had got some cash, So he went to cut a dash And the pretty girls te mash, down at Brighton; With his eyeglass and a stick, He was really ".up to Dick," And he wore a rather" loudish " suit—a light un. From a newly tarnished seat My friend Jones had such c treat, For he ogled passing " totties " half the day; , . And, to his delight at last, A young lady as she passed Smiled upon him in a killing sort of way.

CHORUS: Jones tried to rise to see her on her way, And his face assumed a look of blank dismay; For before my friend could go They'd to cut away—you know, The seat of his—lfm—t'was funnier than a play. Chancing one day to peruse In the Matrimonial News That a husband was requested by a widow Who was thirty, tall, and blonde And of children very fond, With a yearly income of four hundred quid, oh, My dear friend Jones he wrote (As John Smith) a tender note, And arranged to meet the same some miles away. He described the suit he'd wear, And he trusted she'd be there • And would carry in he hand a big bouquet.

CHORUS: And poor Jones was very punctual that day, But, imagine, please, his horror and dismay, When before his eyes he saw, His respected ma-in-law! The conclusion was much funnier than a play. , But the greatest sell of all, Was when Jones went to a ball— 'Twas a masked one, and he made up as a pirate, His wife went there as well, But on no account would tell What she went as, and he felt a trifle irate. - At the ball, a little nun, • Took his fancy, so for fun, lie just spoon'd her—for at spooning he's au fait ; Yes, he danced with her, and sat, And he fetehed her this and that, And be " yarned " to her till early the next day.
CHORUS:

Then he said; "My little dear, unmask, I pray"; •And the little dear obliged—to his dismay. 'Twas a joke, upon my life,• For the lady was his wife, And what followed was as funny as a play. It's just possible aw may, stick another verse in abeawt him bathin', an' geddin' th' wrong van. Avir fancy th' Moral Vigilance Committee wod pass this song as bein' harmless—thad is, containin' nowt fis'le bring a cheeky blush to th' shame ov modesty, or a modest blush to the cheek of shame, or a blush o' shame to th' cheek o! modesty; aw've fergetten th' exact wordin'. One or 'two o' my rich acquaintances, or relayshuns, may blush for th cheek.o' th' author, though!

div.head: DEAIH OF A BIBLICAL SCHOLAR.
div.p: DEAIH OF A BIBLICAL SCHOLAR.

Scholars all over the world will learn with pro- found regret of the death, at Hendon. Vicarage, on Monday, of Dr. Scrivener. He was one of those learned and industrious,but not self-obtrusive men, to whom promotion comes late in life. He had been an assistant master in Sherborne School, then curate of Sandford Orcas in Somersetshire, after- wards headmaster of Falmouth School and incumb- ent of Penwerris and then for fourteen years rec- tor of Gerrans, before he was made Prebendary of Exeter, and the Duke of Portland gave him the Rectory of Hendon. It was in these earlier years his chief fame as a Biblical critic was won. His "Notes on the authorised Version of the New Testament and his collation of twenty manuscripts of the Gospels first brought him into notice. his intro- duction to New Testament Criticism and his Greek Testament have become text-books on the moder- ate orthodox side. All his critical works are dis- tinguished by thoroughness and candour, and are held in high respect even by those who do not agree with his conclusions. He was a distinguished member of the New Testament Company of Revisers and edited a Greek Testament indicating the changes the Revisers made in the common text. A Civil List pension of £lOO a year was given him in 1872 in recognition of his services to. Biblical critic- ism and in aid of the publication of his works. A paralytic attack in-1884 did not wholly lay him aside from his work in the promotion of New Testa- ment learning, and he has died in harness, /eaving a name that scholars will long hold in reverence. He was in his 79th year.

div.p: KTTiKENNy ELEGTION.

Mr. Patrick M'Dermott, the Nationalist nominee, was on Thursday returned for North Kilkenny unopposed, the Parnellites having failed to nominate a candidate. Speaking at Kilkenny, liMr. Michael Davitt announced his intention to stand for an Irish constituency at the general election. He said that election was a proof of WI utter hopelessness of the strlggle now being waged WA/sr:Redmond and his followers: He appealed to the common-sense of the people to insist on an end being put to this unhappy strife.
WARRINGTON TOWS' COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday- evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Burgess, Platt-, Wright, Suttoh, Greenall, Holmes; Conncillors Flood,Ashton,Cannelf, Fleming, Muir, Shaw Green, Hepherd, Heaton, Greening, J. Fairclough, F. A. Roberts, Dixon, ilutchin,on, Browne, Monks, R. T. Fairclough, Bolton; Messrs. Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor). Chorley (borough treasurer.) WATCH COMMITTEE. •

This Committee recbmmexcled that the tender of Messrs. Maskery and Company for the repair of the prison van at £l6 7s. 6d. be accepted. There was also a recommendation that a license be granted to Mrs Sheridan for the performance of stage plays in the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road, for 12 months. A certifi- cate from the Home Secretary as to the efficiency arid discipline of the police force was likewise recorded on the minutes.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the MAYOR. •
NEW BUILDINGS.-STREET LIGHTING.-THE WIDENING ,OF
BRIDGE-ST.

The Street Improvement aal Lighting Committee re- commended•that the plans of the following buildings, Sze., be approved :—Proposed streets off Padgate-larie for Mr. J. Antrobus ' • alterations and additions to shops in Bewsey-street for Mr. James Skelland ; workshops off Bostock-street for Mrs. Mackie; and six houses in Lovely lane for Mr. John Lloyd, The Committee also recom- mended the erection of several new lamps. Alderman PLATT, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the Committee were now making a larger use of the 30-candle lights in the • public streets, which was a move in the right direction,as single-burner lamps for main streets was about out of date. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DixoN asked if there had been an applica- tion with regard to a light being 'placed's° that the clock at the post office might be seen. Councillor SHAW GREEN suggested the advisability of placing an additional lamp in Lodge-lane, and Council- lor GREENING supported the suggestion. Alderman BURGESS asked if the Committee intended to proceed farther with.the widening of Bridge-st... Alderman WRIGHT said that the attention of the Com- mittee would be given to the matter of another lamp in Lodge-lane. Alderman PLATT, in replying, remarked that the sur- veyor had received a letter with regard to the light near the post office, but there had riot been a meeting of the Ccimmittee since it was received. As to the -widening of Bridge-street the Committee had not as yet given any serious thought to the further widening of Bridge-street, but he agreed it was a matter of extreme urgency, and that the sooner it was done ,the better. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed. THE SANITARY commirrEE.—ACCEPTANCE 'OE TENDERS.—

div.head: ALLEGED NUISANCE AT LONGFORD
div.p: ALLEGED NUISANCE AT LONGFORD

The aboVe Committee submitted the following resolu- tions :—That the contract entered into with Mr. Willia,m. Sharratt, of Manchester, for the supply of carbolic pow- der at £6 per ton, be renewed fora further term of three years; that the tender of Mrs. Alice Hatton to supply 20 gallons of neatsfoot oil at 3s. per gallon be accepted ; that the tender of Messrs. J. H. Parkinson and Son to sup- ply 20 sets of brooms at 50s. per set, 40 dozen brooms at 20s. pr dozen, and 12 dozen pail brushes at 16s. 6d. per dozen be accepted. Alderman BURGESS and Alderman SUTTON' seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor Drxorr said it had been complained to him that the cffensive smell from Longford depot had very much increased. and especial 4, on the night of the 19th or 20th.•_ _ _

--T-I;aiayon said he was aciviied Councillor Dixon was out of order, as there was nothing on the minutes with regard to Longford. • Councillor DIXON: What are we to do then ? I gave notice of a mOtion, and I was told it was out of order. Alderman Ilinoess said he had no objection to Coun- cillor Dixon making his statement. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk rules it is out of. order. Councillor DixoN : Iyave notice,.
The Tows CLERK said-Councillor Dixon gave notice of a motion which was entirely out of order, and he. wrote and told him so,

Alderman BURGESS said they had had a complaint, coming indirectly from a gentleman of very .considerable importance,with regard to the stench coming from Long- ford depot. That was on Saturday morning last, but on inquiry being made nothing was going on at the works, and there had not been a fire in the furnaces from eight o'clock on Friday night. The smell was not from the works, but there was another works close by that was offending, and they were held responsible for the mis- deeds of that other works. The Longford depot was as clean and fresh a place as could be. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The minutes were coniffmed. THE HOWLEY BROOK.—THE STATE OF THE STREETS.

The minutes of the raving and Sewerage Committee contained the following resolutions :—That a main sewer be constructed in Forster-st: ' • that the tender of Messrs. J. Gibson and Son to erect cement stores and sheds at the store yard, Howley, at £203, be accepted; that an order for 50 tons of macadam, at 83. 3d. per ton, delivered at Whitecross Wharf, be given to the Warring- ton Slate Company, Limited. In consequence of diffi- culties created by some of the owners with respect to the construction of a sewer in Howley, it was resolved that the resolutions of the Council of the 7th July last referring to the construction of the sewer in Howley, with the exception of the resolution accepting the tender of Mr. William Williams, be rescinded. It was further resolved that a public sewer be constructed in Howley- lane along the centre of such lane according to the plan prepared by the Borough Surveyor, and that so much of Howley Brook as is co-extensive with the new sewer be filled up. Alderman WRIGHT moved the confirmation of the minutes, and mentioned that the Committee intended to make improvements in the condition of the macadam streets, which were much needed in many places. With regard to Howley Brook the arrangements they had tried to make with the property owners had fallen through, owing to the stubbornnessof certain people, who, he felt sure, were standing in their own light. They had, how- ever, decided to lay down the sewer as near the centre of the road as possible, without 'touching anyone's pro- perty. Councillor FLEMING called attention to the defective condition of Crossley-st., and the thoroughfare at School Brow. _ -

_ The MAYOR thought it would be an advantage to the people living at Friars Green if there was a tiled footpath put down there instead of cobbles. Alderman WRIGHT, in answer, to Councillor Browne, said the intended sewer at Howley would be three feet in diameter, and would run from the river to about the end of Mill-lane. The other matters mentioned should have the attention of the Committee. The minutes were then confirmed.

SCHOOL •ITTENDANCE. The School Attendance Committee stated that from the report of the Inspector it appeared that 51 eases had been before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 48 cases, and 3 boys sent to industrial schools. Thirty-five cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. At a later meeting of the Committee the inspector reported that 22 cases had been before the magistrates, fines inflicted in 19 cases, and two boys sent to the Clio. The Council was recommended t:;) contribute the sum of 6s. per week until July, 1892, towards the maintenance ef a boy, named John Bennett, ordered by the magis- trates to be sent to the Ship" Clio." The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Coun- cillor FLEMING.

London ; placard : Procession in War- rington at coronation of Queen Victoria' from Mr. J. S. Sherratt ; kestrel, shot in Arplev, from Mr. D. Jones: The Curator reported the receipt of 102 pictures,on loan, from Miss Gaskell, of Weymouth. It was resolved that George Knott be appointed porter, at 18s. a week wages. The Technical Instruction Sub-Committee re- ported that Messrs. Muir and Jenkins had been appointed delegates to the annual meeting of the Union of Lanca- shire and Cheshire Institutes. Councillor ShAw GREEN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes,alluded tb the great increase of 102 per cent. in the number of books issued in the lending depart- ment, which; he said, proved the wisdom of the Council in freeing the library. (Hear' hear.) The minutes were confirmed. THE CEMETERY.

From the report of the registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee, it appeared that the 'interments during the past four weeks were—adults, 36, minors 59, stillborn and premature 12. Corresponding period last year—adults 36, minors 55, stillborn and premature 9. The receipts for the past four weeks were £75 Bs. 7d., corresponding period last year £7l 7s. 10d. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTHE.-THE pPENING
OF THE NEW BATHS.

Prom the report of the bathkeeper to the above Com- mittee, it appeared that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £l9 35., and the corresponding period last year, £lB ss. Bd. The Committee also recom- mended that the foundation stone of the new baths be said on the 29th October, and that his worship the Mayor be requested to lay the same. Councillor BOLTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he hoped the working classes would show that they-appreciated the new baths and those who had furnished the bathsfwithena, (Hear, hear.) Councillor MUIR said the Chairman of the Committee had been asked to lay the foundation stone, but :he very handsomely assigned that duty to the Mayor.

Alderman BURGESS said that was without precedent, and he asked if the Local Government Board had not intimated that a local inquiry would be necessary before the baths could be proceeded with. He thought they were somewhat indiscreet. The laying of the stone would have been very much better left until the inquiry had been held. _

Councillor Dr. CANNELL was very much surprised at Alderman Burgess being so inconsistent. He surely did not think that they, as a Committee, would do anything that was wrong. Were they to get the baths done, or what were they to do? He would not be a member of the Cmmittee if they were to be played with like this. The MAYOR didn't think thtre need be any feeling about the matter.

_ Councillor HEATON said Alderman Burgess was not in posQession of all the facts of the case. He was sorry Alderman Burgess should think no Committee had a right to go to London except members of the Sanitary Committee. _ _ _

~.......—. Alderman BURGESS asked if the Local Government Board ha cj sanctioned the Committee's proposals? The MAron did not think they they were in a position to state all that took place at the Local Government Board offices, but he was perfectly certain that if there was any expense to be borne afterwards he should be quite willing to bear it. Alderman SUTTON said he should like the Mayor to lay the foundation stone, but he could not help thinking that there had been a great deal of undue haste in this matter. It would have been netter if they had waited until the proper time had passed before they proceeded to lay the foundation stone to the new baths. - _ _

Councillor BOLTON said there would be a Local Government Board inquiry, but it would be a formal matter, and would cost only about £5. There was no doubt about what they were asking for being granted. The minutes were then agreed to. MARKETS COMMITTEE.

The total income of the Markets Committee for the month had been £340 13s. 7d.., as compared with the corresp3nding. Period last year £283 4s. 3d. ; increase £5795. 4d. The minutes were confirmed:on the:motion of Alder- •nrin GREENALL. GAS COMMITTEE. —LESS DISCOUNT TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.

- The Gas Committee reported thrt the average illumin- ating !lower of-the gas for the past four Weeks was equal to 1871 candles at both works. The Committee had also passed he following resolutions That the resolution of the 2nd August, 1889, relating to the right of way over land in Chrinies'-yard granted to Mr. Edward Con- nor be rescinded, and that Mr. Conner be allowed to use. and occupy part of Chrimes'-yard, and a cottage adjoiu-. big, at.-7 per annum, subject to six months' notice," also, "That 'owing to the increased cost of labour and materials, the maximum discount allowed to consumers from and after the 25th October instant shall not exceed_ 10d. per'l,ooo cubic feet. ' Alderman HOLMES moved the confirmation of the minutes : and'referring to the question of discount, ob- served that there were some of their large manufacturers who had been haVing gas at less than cost price. These firms were Whitecross, Dallam Forge, and Walkers' Brewery. •Councillor Fleming said he could not buy anything at less than cost price,and yet they were selling gas at less than cost price. If some people could be put on those terms he did not see why they should not have the same advantages. COuncillor MUIR : Am Ito understand that a reduc- tion of the discount includes all consumers? (Several voices : " No, no.") The MAYOR: Only the three large firms. Councillor DIXON said he had been requested to call the attention of the Chairman of the Committee to the bad lighting in the told-st. Wesleyan Chapel. (Laughter. - Alderman HOLMES said the amount of the discount had depended upon the quantity of gas consumed, and the three films named used the largest quantity. If the discount was reduced, the gas would pay. The minutes were then agreed to.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.

TERRIBLE DISASTER IN THE CHANNEL. FIFTEEN LIVES LOST. The steamer Boston, of London, from Cardiff, with coal, collided at about four o'clock on Monday morning, three miles from the Eddystone Lighthouse, with the barque Charlwood (Captain Hiscock), from Antwerp for Valparaiso with a general cargo. Captaiß Hiscock, his wife and son, the governess and servant, all the officers, four seamen, and two apprentices-15 in all— were drowned. The captain's daughter, four seamen, and two apprentices were saved, and conveyed to Fal- mouth aboard the Boston. The Charlwood was a Liverpool barque, of about 1,000 tons. Two of those saved are now in the hospital suffering from the effects of long immersion. One of them states that he pushed a floating plank to the captain's daughter, by which means she held on until picked up.

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the above Committee comprised a re- port of Mr. James Bolton, accountant, on the system of accounts of the Water Works department, which was read and ordered to be entered on the minutes. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Committee.
Councillor DIXON said he had the other day occasion to go to a firm, and was informed the works were stand- ing because the supply of water had been stopped, and

The MAYOR (interrupting) : We have not got actual posse.ssion yet. The conveyance will be signed. on Fri- day; and then you can-call us to account for any 'negli- gence. Councillor FLOOD: Will. the report referred to in the Minutes be placed in the hands of the Council? , The MAYOR: It is only, a report on the method of hook-keeping. You can see the report with the greatest pleasure. Mr. Bolton and Mr. Shaw Green recommend a new system of keeping accounts. The minutes were then agreed to.

VOTE OE THANKS TO THE MAYOR. Alderman Horams moved "That the best thanks of this Council be presented to Richard Walker Francomb, Esq.,, Alderman of this borough, for the satisfactory =riper in which he has discharged the responsible dales devolving upon him as Mayor and chief magistrate of this borough, during this, his second year of office, and for the unvarying courtesy and, *partiality displayed by him when presiding over the deliberations of the Council, and in his intercourse with its members." He said the Mayor. had discharged his duties remarkably well, and in ainanner which was highly satisfactory to the whole of the Members and to the town. (Hear, hear.) He had, therefore, much pleasure in moving the resolution.

- Alderman WRIGHT seconded the motion, and remarked that Alderman Holmes had not said one word more than the Mayor richly deserved. It was under great pressure that the Mayor was induced to take the office last year. Councillor GREENING also, as a junior member of the Council, paid his tribute of respect to the Mayor. Councillor HUTCHINSON supported the resolution. Alderman BURGESS wished to add his testimony to the manner in which the Mayor had discharged his duties. He could add somethinp to what had been said. He thought, they might fairly suggest that Alderman Fran- comb's serVices should be continued for another year, and then he would have an opportunity of carrying on to the end the erection of the baths, of which he would lay the foundation stone next Thursday. (Laughter). Councillor BOLTON, Councillor HEATON, and Alderman SurroN also spoke of the efficient manner in which the Mayor had performed the dUties of his office. •The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously.

The MAYOR, in reply, said he had the satisfaction of knowing that throughoutlis two years of office he had done his best. No doubt he had exhibited many short- comings, but at the same time they must put that down to his inability • for he had had only one object in view, and that had been to do his duty. As far as the members of the Council were concerned, he wished to thank every- one individually, for it was impossible for any Mayor to have received greater kindness than he had done. (Hear, hear.) He should also like to thank the officials. A town like Warrington, which had such a band of good officials, must be in a very favourable condition. During last year, when they were having Bills passed, the officials had to work almost night and day; but he never heard a single grumble, and every official, from theihighest to the lowest, was anxious to do what he could for the good of the town (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: TEE CORK CONTEST.
div.p: TEE CORK CONTEST.
FACTION FIGHTS.

.The•canyassing at Cork on Saturday was attended by a disorderly scene. Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., complained that he had been followed into the voters' houses by Canon O'Mahony and other priests, who denounced him as one of "Kitty O'Shea's men," and called upon the people to hunt him from their dwellings. Mr. O'Cc nnor said that for about an hour'he was - Made the target of showers of mud, which covered his head and face. Dis- orderly scenes also took place on Sunday. Mr. John Dillon and other Nationalist M.P.'s spoke at °Dundalk on Sunday. ; There were some rather lively scenes at Cork on Tues- day. For hours the streets were thronged with people whose proceedings made it evident that each of the Nationalist divisions was powerfully represented. The police succeeded in keeping the opposing elements in fairly good order for the greater part of the day, but In the evening they came to close quarters,and a number of free fights occurred. The Nationalists and Parnellites prosecuted their canvasses diligently throughout Wed- nesday. At night there was a sharp encounter between a Nationalist and a Parnellite crowd. 1 32 people were treated at the hospitals during Wed- nesday night for injuries caused in the election fights by Oinks, stones, and blows. , Mr. Dillon was unable to leave the house on Thursday, owing to a swelling of the leg, following a blow received On Wednesday. On Thursday evening a violent encounter took place between Parnellites and Nationalists, and members of Parliament representing each side were mixed up. Mr. O'Connor returned from the melee with a weapon which he said he had captured frorn the Nationalists, and which he described as an assegai. At a still later hour another violent encounter took place. The police used their truncheons freely, and among the injured were Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., and Mr. William Redmond, M.P. , , The Sheriff has decided to fix Tuesday next as nomina- iton day and to take the Poll on the following Friday.

The arrival of Emin Pasha and Dr. Stuldmann in the neighbourhood of Wadelai is announced.
