div.head: oUTRA.GE IN DUBLIN. EXPLOSION OF A BOMB.
div.p: oUTRA.GE IN DUBLIN. EXPLOSION OF A BOMB.

Shortly after eight o'clock, on Monday night, a bomb or hand grenade was thrown through the window of the editor's room of the "National Press" offices in Dublin. The windows were broken, and much damage was done to the furniture, but no one was injured. It is supposed that the missile was thrown from a house opposite the buildinc, of the "National Press." Nearly the whole of the windows of the building on the side overlooking Middle Abbey-st. were broken, as well as those of a house opposite. There was intense excitement in the neighbourhood as the news of the outrage spread, and in a few minutes the street was blocked with people. It was a remarkable thing that no personal injury was sus- tained, for the report of the exploding missile was tre- mendous, and the shattering of glass which followed might have seriously hurt the passers-by, who, however, were few at the time. It is suspected that the outrage has its origin in the bad feeling of the Parnellites.

div.head: COUNCILLOR. DIXON ON THE INTER-
div.p: COUNCILLOR. DIXON ON THE INTER-
CEPTING DEPOTS.

On Wednesday evening at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Debating Society, Mr. Ford pre- siding, Mr. Councillor Dixon read a paper the sub- ject of which was announced as "The sanitary affairs of the borough." but which was confined to the question of intercepting depots. There were only five corporations, he said,that he knew of who were dealing with excreta, those of Rochdale, Man- chester, Birmingham, Stafford, and Warrington. He described the processes adopted by the four first-named,comparing them with that used at War- rington. There were some things in connection with the manufacture at the Warrington intercept- ing depots so repulsive, that if it had not been for the sake of the , boys and girls whose food must taste more or less of the gas and the foul air that passed from the depots, he did not think he should have bothered himself with going into the Town Council or troubled himself about the process. The Corporation did not introduce anything to cause a nuisance. it arose from the air getting contamin- ated with the effluvia. The Sanitary Committee asserted that the air passed through some chemical and this purified it,but he did not believe this. He maintained that the only way to purify the air, was by having a stack and a good furnace and passing the air through fire.—Mr. Diggle thought Mr. Dixon was "off his horse alto- gether"—(laughter)—and heldisputed several of his statements. It was not the fresh material but the putrid material that caused the nuisance.—Mr. Pickavance characterised the statement that there was no smell from the depots, as a lie, and described his experiences of the smell.—Mr. John Gandy said the depots were an abominable and unmitigated nuisance, and it was a foul lie to deny that they were a nuisance. There was another nuisance at the Rubber Works, which he perceived fifty times more frequently.—Messrs. J. Horton and Summers and the Chairman, continued the discussion, and Mr. Diggle having again spoken, Mr. Dixon replied. He remarked that there was one law for the Corpora- tion and another for manufacturers. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE
div.p: UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE

The annual meetings of the United Kingdom Alliance were held in Manchester on Tuesday. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., presided at the meeting of the Council in the morning, and spoke gleefully of the" abnormal progress" the movement had made during the year. The same hopeful tone charac- terized most of the speeches. A number of resolu- tions were discussed and adopted. An increae of revenue was asked in view of the general election, and of " the special efforts to frustrate the labours of the Alliance now being put forth by the various organizations for the defence of the liquor traffic." It was resolved that the support ot the Alliance should in no case be given to any Parliamentary candidate who would not promise to vote for a measure conferring the vote upon the people.
MR.'JOHN MORLEY ON THE LICENSING QUESTION.

Mi. John Morley, M.P„ presided on Tuesday even- ing at the annual public meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance in the Free Trade Hall, Manches- ter. He said there might be some aspects of the question on which he might not be of the same mind as all of them, but he understood that the Alliance had always made it a rule cordially to wel- come and support all men who were ready to travel the nextstage of the journey with them,even if they felt compelled to get out of the coach when that stage was successfully accomplished. A dozen years ago, before he was a member of the House of Com- mons, he gcve a public expression to his recognition of the operations of the Alliance and of their moral energy which could only be compared to that which led to the abolition of slavery,and which he believed would, when it was completed,be as beneficial in its results. The next stage of their journey—the prac- tical object immediately before them—was tha establishment by legislation of the principle that the People living in a locality shall have the same full, complete, and unrestricted powers of deter- mining the number or the existence of public- houses within their borders as were now possessed by the justices,and as were now possesssed and every day exercised by the owners of individual estates. The action of the magistrates at the recent brews. ter sessions throughout the country had been, he did not hesitate to say, timid, faltering, uncertain, and thoroughly unsatisfactory. The meeting was addressed by Sir Wilfred Lawson, M.P., Canon Wil- berforce, Mr. W. S. Caine, and others.

It is stated that there has been a fresh display of insubordination in one of the Guards' battalions, the affair being the result of dissatisfaction with the quality of the food supplied. The London steamers Godalming and James Joicey collided in the Thames on Wednesday morning, and the last-named vessel had to be run ashore to prevent her from sinking, the Golalming returning to London damaged.

OPENING OF THE NEW BATHS AT WARRINGTON. On Thursday afternoon the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Francomb) laid the fe•undation stone of the proposed new baths, or rather extensions of the present baths, in Legh-st. Amongst those present were the Mayor and Mayoress, Alderman Chandley (chairman of the Baths Committee), Aldermen Greenall and Wright, Councillors H. Roberts, Plumpton, Muir, Heaton, J. Fairclough, Bolton, Cannell, Hepherd, Hutchinson, Garner; Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), and Mrs. Whittle, Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Messrs. J. S. Garland, S. Kenyon, &c. Full particulars of the new baths have already been given in these columns. They will include a new swimming bath with a water space of 75ft. by 43ft., as well as shower, soap, and vapour baths. The baths will be furnished with all the most modern appliances. They will probably cost nearly £5,000. Alderman CIIANDLEY said there would be de- posited under the foundation stone copies of the IVarrington newsr.apers, a Corporation year book, and some silver and bronze coins of this year's coin- age. He remarked that one of the great charac- teristics of this age was a great thirst and demand for increased sanitary recreation. (Hear, hear.) It was now something like 20 years since the present baths passed into the hands of the Corporation. In that day the baths were considered sufficient for the then smallness of the population but since then times had changed and population had increa4ed,and now what they considered only a fair improvement would have been considered in that day most luxu- rious. He then referred to the history of the baths question in the Town Council, and added that they were all heartily glad it had fallen to the lot of the present Mayor to signalise his second :year of office by laying the foundation stone of that proposed addition to the baths. (Applause.) He then called upon the Mayor to lay the stone. The MAYOR then formally laid the stone. He remarked that most of them were aware that the public of War- rington had been very dissatisfied with the bathing faci- lities the Corporation had been able to offer them for many years, although they did not know the amount of difficulties the Corporation had to deal with. They had a very difficult question in regard to the water supply, but last year the Corporation purchased the Water Works, and that would give them an excellent supply of water. He believed they would be able to be very gene- rous with the water because the sewers would require a lot of flushing, and consequently they would be able to get fresh water in the baths every day if required. (Hear, hear.) The f Mayor then briefly alluded to the action of the Town Council in regard to the baths, and said that the deputation of the Baths Committee which- went to other towns were struck by the splendid acconi- modation there afforded, as compared with Warrington Baths. That stirred them up, and they'got their borough surveyor at work drawing up plans. It would be utterly impossible • for any gentleman to work harder or to do more to 'Please the Committee and the people at large than Mr. Longdin had done. (Hear, hear.) He had shown an endless amount of energy and a great amount of ability, and he (the Mayor) believed that when the baths were finished they would he second to none in Lancashire. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. S.KENYON, in the course of a short address, said those baths would be a very great advantage to the in- habitants of Warrington. Bathing was a very enjoy- able, a very useful, and a very healthy exercise. He was pleased that in those baths they were providing for the accommodation of ladies, for he thought every girl and boy should learn to swim. (Hear, hear.) The lay- ing of the foundation stone of those baths would not be the least of the things the Mayor had done during the two years he had had the privilege and honour to dis- charge so well the duties of the Mayoralty. (Hear, hear and applause.) Councillor H. ROBERTS heartily congratulated the Mayor upon the closing act of his official career as Mayor ot that borough. He regretted that through an oversight of his own he was not present at the last Council meeting to offer to the Mayor his thanks along with the rest of the members of the Corporation for the assiduous way iniwhich he had conscientiously discharged his duties as Mayor of the town during the past two 1 years. (Hear, hear.) There had been during the years of past Mayors great events, but he submitted that, taking into consideration the acquisition of the Warring- ton Waterworks on the one hand and the carrying out of that public baths extension on another, there were, no events which would be in their results 'a more last- ing bmefit to the community at large than the two acts to which he had just referred. (Hear, hear) He believed I that public baths were a positive necessity, and that as a part of its education every child ought to be taught to swim. He hoped that with the extended facilities their public schools would take up that matter, and, as far as they possibly could, would attach the teaching of swim- min.' to every class in their charge. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Alderman CIIANDLEY asked if anyone 'else wished to make any remarks, and Mr. Diggle caused some laugh- ter by coming forward from the ring of spectators. He remarked that he had had to do with water all his life, ' and hs was going to tell how he learned to swim, but the closure was then applied, and Mr. Diggle subsided. Cheers for the Mayor and Mayoress and the Chairman of the Baths Committee brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: WEDDING PARTY BURIED.
div.p: A WEDDING PARTY BURIED.
LOSS OF THIRTY LIVES,

TUNIS, TURSDLY.—Considerable excitement was caused here this afternoon owing to an accident which it is quite possible will be attended with iatal results.. It ap- pears that a wall adjoining the premises of the tramway company, which had only been completed within the last few days, became undermined owing to the torren- tial rains, and that this afternoon it suddenly collapsed, burying about 30 natives who were taking part in a wedding ceremony in two houses upon which the wall abutted. Gangs of men are actively engaged in re- moving the debris. Turns, WEDNEqIM.Y.—The loss of life due to the col- lapse of a wall of the tramway company's premises and the consequent destruction of two houses has proved to be very serious. Eighteen bodies have been recovered, from the debris, and rescue parties are still at work. A number of persons are, without doubt, still buried in the ruins. According to general belief, fully twelve persons are thus buried, and it is certain none of these can be recovered alive.

The funeral of the wedding guests who perished in Tuesday's accident took place on Wednesday, in the pres- ence of a large concourse of people. Previous to the inter- ment 16 corpses were identified. Other persons were killed belonging to families which live at a considerable distance from Tunis.

Probate has been granted of the will of the late Eirl Powis, the personal estate being valued at £162,452 13s. 10d.
PROBLEMS FOR WORKING-MEN.
A NEW SOCIETY AT EARLESTOWN.7:-7:

The Rev. T. Collins, Primitive Methcdist minister, Earlestown, has only been resident in the town a few months, but he evidently intends to make him— self useful in the interest of the working-men, by endeavouring to elevate them socially and morally. He holds certain views in regard to working-men, and has an idea that if men can be got together to talk over matters affecting themselves,their country, and their immediate surroundings, they would be able to develope the work that ministers and workers of Christian churches generally could never assume. He accordingly called a meeting, inviting anyone and everyone, without sect or creed,to meet in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, on Saturday night. In response to his invitation, a good number of workmen put in an appearance, and Mr. Collins was voted to preside. In order to set his views be- fore the meeting, he said, he had been looking round quietly, and had concluded that they lived among a first-class skilled artisan population,and to him it was very clear, that there was sufficient mental vigour to take an interest in things, speak- ing from the broad standpoint of a country or com- munity. There was a large class of young men who ought by some means to be brought to take interest in a great variety of things they did not, to him, appear to take any interest in. And,after carefully looking over this matter, he concluded that if any- thing was to be done, the men must be got toge- ther, and do it themselves. Whatever they did he should be prepared to co-operate with them, as he was satisfied that they could take nothing in hand but what he could follow, either with the object of cultivating it or in order to be prepared to show , no less reason for dissenting from it. He then an- nounced that he had written to the various clergy- men in the district, and read the replies he had re- ceived, of which the following are extracts : Rev. Canon Whitley wrote—" As I have to avoid the night air, especially on Saturday evening, I shall not be able to attend. I rejoice to hear of any well and soberly conducted plans for elevating the classes, and especially the men of Earlestown." Rev. H. Monk,of St. Peter's, Newton, wrote—" Foras- much as my colleague and I are undertaking this winter much more work than hitherto of a spiritual nature (which is our proper vocation), I regret that my time. will be too fully occupied to permit me to take part in the interesting secular work you propose to inaugurate. Trusting that those who have leisure thus to promote the welfare of Earlestown men (so far as the formation of a debating society can promote it) may succeed in their endeavour." The Rev. James Allatt wrote—" I say "No thank you," to the most attractive proposals made to me for Saturday night, as the majority of only ordinary men must do, who have to meet the same audience two, three, or four times every week, and really want not only something to say, but to say something." Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of St. John's—" My hands are more than full at present." , Rev. E. J. Hack, wrote' All wisely directed efforts to advance the interests and happiness of the men of Earles- town have my good wishes. Should your desires run in practical grooves, I should like to be able to give you a helping hand." Rev. T. Wynne-Jones, Wesleyan minister, wrote—" I gladly again assure you of ray sympathy and readiness to co-operate in the undertaking. . . . I have no programme to suggest, but if the undertaking is to suc- ceed, questions affecting the problems of everyday life, economic problems, &c. ,must be freely discussed. Sing- ing should also be prominent. Working-men should understand the real attitude of Jesus Christ towards the pressing problems of the present." ' The Rev. J. Cottam, Baptist minister, wrote "I shalt. be pleased to help forward any measure you may adopt at your meeting to-night, in the direction proposed in your note, as far as time and opportunity will allow." Mr. Thomas Molyneaux, wrote "What you propose, has long been in my mind,but for the reasons mentioned it has had to lie there for more favourable opportunities, which I trust may now be found in you." After the reading of the letters. Mr. Mullins proposed and Mr. W. Davies seconded" That a Society be formed for the discussion and consideration of all questions, local and Imperial, that affect men generally. either ' politically, socially, or morally, the Society to be unsect- arian." This was unaniinously carried, and the meeting proceeded to the election of a temporary committee, in order to organise the society and get it into working order. The following were elected :—Revs. T. Collins T. Wynne-Jones, J. Cottam, E. J. Hack, Messrs. L. T. Foulkes, W. Davies, J. Hall, J. Taylor, J. G. Mullins D. Williams, R. Higgins, D. Forrester, and G. A. Long- worth. Mr. G. F. Clarke was appointed secretary pro tem. It was then decided to meet in the same place next Saturday night at eight o'clock, when the subjeet :for discussion will be " Are our Commissioners doing their duty or not ?" Mr. J. G. Mullins to Jpen the disz • cussion.

COMPENSATION FOR PERSONAL INJURY.

In the Queen's tench, lAndon, on Thursday, Jame Sampson, publican, was awarded £2OO damages for per- sonal injury against Fuller, Smith, and Fuller, brewers; A. dra.yman was lowering a barrel of beer into plaintiff's cellar, when the post to which the rope was attached broke, and the barrel fell against the plaintiff, and the court now held that the defendants were responsible for the repair of the post.

MR. MORLEY AND JOHN BRIGHT.

Mr. John Morley, speaking after the unveiling of a statue of Mr. John Bright, on Saturday, at Rochdale, referred to the influence Mr. Bright had exercised in re- ference to Free Trade, the Parliamentary Franchise, and other matters. The distinguished man who had been at the bead of the Government for the last five years said that the doctrines of the old Manchester school were now repudiated; but looking to thedoctrines on which states- men of both parties conducted affairs, upon which Mr. Bright laid down rules, he could not admit that the doctrines of the Manchester school had lost their hold upon the policy of the country, which must be a policy of peace non-intervention, and Free Trade. In regard to the Irish question, he stated how his old colleagues regretted to cloud the last years of Mr. Bright's career by separating from him, but they did so because the fears which Mr. Bright once expressed that all remedial measures were too late had come about. •
THE SHIP CANAL AND RIVER POLLUTION.
The Chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Lord Egerton af Tatton) has addressed the following letter to the local authorities of the watersheds of the Irwell and Mersey :
"The Manchester Ship Canal Company, Boardroom, 31, Spring Gardens, Manchester, 26th October, 1891.

"Sir,—ln view of the approaching completion ot the Ship Canal, I wish to draw your attention to the state of the rivers Irwell and Mersey and their tributaries, , not only owing to the pollution by sewage (which I trust may be dealt with vigorously, as was foreshadowed at thefirat meeting by the Joint Committee of the two counties, under the presidency of the Right Hon. J. T. Hibbert), but also owing to the large quantity of solid refuse froufvvorks and factories which is seriously delay- ing the work of the Ship Canal Company by the depos- its which are formed in the bed of the river, especially in the newly dredged portions. "I would earnestly impress upon your Authority the necessity of enforcing the law against all who put solid refuse or cinders into the tributary streams,or place them in such positions that they must necessarily be carried away by the first flood or fresh of the stream, or of discouraging such practices. " While the question of the treatment of the pollution by sewage must be delayed by the necessary works to allow of the disposal of such matter, there is no such difficulty in dealing with the question of solid manufac- Ituring refuse or cinders. An enormous additional cost has been imposed on the Ship Canal Company in its endeavours to bring this 'great enterprise to an early completion by the floods of the last twelve months, bringing down a volume of cin- ders and solids far beyond their calculations, and I trust, therefore, I may appeal to your Authority not to allow the completion of the canal to be seriously retarded by the wilful carelessness of manufacturers and others act- ing in defiance of the law, and to ask your hearty co- operation in the abatement of the nuisance complained - of, without the necessity of any legal proceedings being taken.—l bave the honour to be, sir, your very obedient servant, (Signed) " Eonwrow OF TarroN, Chairman."

A Paris telegram of Wednesday reports a shocking double murder, the victims being a father and daughter named Andrivot, and the assisiu a retired schoolmaster named Louis Rernard, with whom M. Andrivot had ' had a lawsuit pending for several years. It was rumoured on the Glasgow Exchange on Wed- nesday that the Scotch Railway agreement is of a more extensive character than was at first supposed. The result was a very substantial advance in thevalue of tke leading Scotch railway shares.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN, as W9* Trouncing Mr. Chamberlain. pointed out last week, haa

been' going from bad to worse. He is as furious as a woman scorned, because, al- though he has left the Liberal party, that party manages to get on just as well without him as if he hai never existed. He cannot forgive MT. GLADSTONE for succeeding where he himself has. failed; and of late he has done all he could to mis- represent the leader of the Liberal party. So glaring has this misrepresentation become— utterly at variance is it with what Mr. CHAMBER.. LAIN has previously said—that Mr. Joubr MORLEY took upon himself the task of trouncing the mem- ber for West Birmingham, at a meeting in Man- chester, on Monday night, and he did it so thoroughly that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is likely to be "sore all over" for some time to come. Mr. Moe- LET reminded his audience that the politician who now gives the Conservative party credit "for almost all the social legislation of the time" was the same who, in 1884, "electrified the House of Commons and infuriated the Tory opposition by talking of those who had robbed the people of their land, who had robbed the people of their schools, who had robbed the people of their endowments.' Furthsr, his preaching of the doctrine of ransom had caused him to be spoken of by Lord SALISBURY as a modern Jack Cade. To-day he is in alliance with Lord SALISBURY, and yet, in face of such an alliance, he has held his head out to be hit by sneering at the heterogeneous character of the Liberal party. Mr. MORLEY therefore strikes, but he strikes with a weapon from Mr. CHAMBER- Lines armoury—a quotation from the speech which the author of "The Radical Programme made, at Warrington, when he was starring it ita 1885. It is as follows:

" I don't think there are any of us who will be tempted to desert our own cause and our own party in order to make a new alliance with that hetero- genous comoination which styles itself the Consti- tutional party, and which includes within its ranks Flee Traders and Protectionists, Ulster Orangemen, and English Roman Catholics, licensed victuallers, and Established Churchmen, Tory Democrats, and fossil reactionists,all uniting their discordant voices in order to form a mutual protection society for assuring to each of its members place and privilege and power.

How curious that the one man who was tempted and who yielded to the temptation was Mr. CHAMBERLAIN himself! And yet, after joining the heterogeneous combination, and thus rendering it still more heterogeneous, he cannot tolerate the Liberal party because they too are heterogeneous. But it is often so with the fallen ; they imagine that sin in others of which they know they are themselves guilty. Pursuing his policy of quoting Mr. Chamberlain against Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Morley was enabled to show that his former colleague was in other re- spects equally contradictory. In his Sunderland speech, the other day, Mr. Chamberlain declared that, when he was in office, he had to withdraw his Shipping Bill because he got very little sympathy from Mr. Gladstone. This is the statement of 1891; but here is the account of the withdrawal of the bill which he gave at Hull, in 1885; when the matter was fresh in his mind : " I thought that all men, whatever the political faith to which they might give their adhesion, were at least at one in desiring the welfare and se- lcurity of the man to whom we owe so much Pin as we do—the British sailor. Well, I was disaPteu.• received no assistance from the Tor) partv. When it was found that the shipowners in Parliament and the representatives of the shipping interest were party were un- ! about to oppose this Bill, the Tory able to resist the temptation of putting the Govern- ment in a minority. Speaking generally, I learnt whole would go very soon that the Tory party as a against the Bill and would do all they could to render its passing impossible. The leader of the party, the Marquis of Salisbury,took up the cause of shipowners, and accused me of having brought for- ward fantastic charges against the shipowners, and did all in his power to stimulate the opposition to the proposals I had made. The opp n ositio i was con- tinuous and persistent, and t became necessary to drop the Bill.' If Mr. Chamberlain was right in 1885 when he said it was Lord Salisbury's opposition which caused him to drop the Bill, he cannot be right to- day in attributing it to Mr. Gladstone's lack of

sympathy. Whichever way he turns, he is con- victed of flat contradiction and gross misrepre- sention. It is the same with his view on the British occupation of Egypt ; he was a party as a member of Mr. Gladstone's Government to the policy of evacuation as soon as it could be carried out with safety, yet to-day he has no language too strong for those who still advocate that policy. Summing up the case in this respect against Mr. Chamber- lain Mr. Morley said : "It comes to this,that a statesman may sit at the council table with men, he may share their com- mon anxieties and their common responsibilities, he may arrive with them atter deliberations at a common conclusion as to what is the best thing to be done, and yet he is to be free years after, for some paltry purpose of the moment, he is to be free to hold up those very colleagues with whom he has sat at the council table, for whose conclusions he is absolutely responsible, to hold them on the ground of those very transactions up to obloquy and to contempt. (Shame.) Gentlemen thatis a hitting below the belt. (Loud and prolonged sheering.) That is hitting below the belt, for which 1 will venture to say you won't find a paral- lel in the worst times of our political history. (Renewed cheers.)"

We have nothing to add to this; it if asevere but it is a just condemnation. Mr. Chamberlain, like thelate Mr. Parnell,has allowed himself to be ruled by passion. Whatever Mr. Gladstone may have done in foreign affairs, he has made no such "awful mess," of it as the member for West Birmingham has made of his affairs as an English politician.

IN view of the Municipal "How to Vete." Elections which take place on Monday next "The Friend of the Working-man" beats Boyle Roche's bird, for he is not only in two places at the same time, but here, there, and everywhere. The cry all round is "Goan 's your friend—not Short"; and the elector who tries to take in all that he hears and reads on the subject of the merits and achieve- ments of the respective candidates may be excused if he finds himself at the end of it all just a trifle bewildered. Still he has got to make up his mind, and it is his duty as a citizen to give his vote for the candidate who will best serve his interests as a citizen. To this end we would direct attention to two questions which are occupying the mind of the country; one relates to - temperance and the other to labour. If the applicant speaks with a certain sound on these issues, it will be found, as a rule, that he may be relied upon in less import- ant matters. In Warrington, plain questions have been put by the Temperance Federation on the one band, and the Trades Council on the other; and the Doubtful Voter, who turns so

many elections, cannot do better, in our opinion, than examine the answers which have been given by the respective candidates during the past week. It is sometimes said that there is little or no difference between the Liberals and the Tories in these matters; but it will be found, when the test is thus applied, that there is a great deal of difference, and that, when the account is struck, the balance is very much to the credit of the Liberals.

To take the subject of Temperance first: The questions put were, "I.—Will you, if elected, vote against any person connected with the Liquor Trade having a seat upon the Watch Committee? 2.—Are you in favour of the Chief Constable being instructed to systematically enforce the Licensing Laws, with a view to reducing the drunkenness which prevails in Warrington?" With regard to the first it will be seen that an issue is raised which affects to a certain extent the honour and good faith of the Town Council. It goes without say- I ing that "the trade" and its victims occup a 1 great deal of the time of the police, and it is I equally obvious that brewers and publicans ought to be the last persons to be selected in the forma- tion of a Watch Committee. Yet will it be be- lieved that there are two Conservative candidates only who venture to pledge themselves to vote against any Councillor connected with the liquor trade sitting on the Watch Committee ? As will be seen from the details which we give in our eleo- tion news, four of the nine Conservatives have sent no reply; three have shirked the issue, while two stand alone in answering in the affimative. What a contrast this to the Liberal candidates who have all given" Yes" as an answer! With regard to the second question—which relates to the systematic enforcement of the Licensing Laws, the same bur Conservatives fail to reply, one gives an eqnivocal answer, and four only reply in the affirtniftive. Again we would say—contrast this with the attitude of the Liberal candidates whose answer to the question is " Yes "—and that with- out a single exception.

It is pretty much the same with regard to the three questions put by the Trades Council. The first and third relate to the Corporation contracts being given to employers who pay standard wages, and to the insertion of a fair-wages clause in these contracts. The second question bears on the pro- posal to give holidays to "poor paid servants "of the Corporation, paying wages for the same as in

the case of "the better paid servants:' It will be remembered that, last October, when the fair- wages issue was raised in the Town Council, the Tories left the Council Chamber in a body, and thus prevented a discussion. in July last the matter was not only discussed but voted upon with the result that the motion on the subject was carried byls votes to 11, the 11 who opposed be- ing all Tories! Could working-men have stronger evidence as to which party is for them and which is against them? But, reverting to the questions put during the past week, we gather from the re- commendations of the Town Council that the Liberal candidates have to a man replied in the affirmative. In Howley Ward, Councillor BOLTOISI has also replied in the affirmative, although he was amongst those who walked out and styled the motion ridiculous, as first proposed. Further than that, he did not vote for the motion when the opportunity was given him in July last, and the Trades Unionists are therefore fully justified in saying "Mr. BOLTON'S past conduct does not warrant our support." In Town Hall Ward, St. Austin's Ward, and Latchford Ward, the Liberal candidates stand alone in having given favourable replies, whilst in the other wards they are bracketed with the Tories, some of whom are now ready to support that which they opposed in July last. Under these circumstances, the electors should have no difficulty in deciding what to do; they cannot but perceive that alike on the Temp- ranee question and the Labour question the Liberals are on the one side and the Tories are on another; and, that, if they have at heart the highest interests of the borough, their plain duty is to give their votes to the Liberal candidates Amblonday next.

TOMMY BURNS. Tommy Burns, the well-known champion swim- mer and diver, will perform another diving feat to- day near Warrington. It is his intention to dive from the girders of Walton Arches at two o'clock into the Mersey, a dive of close on 100 ft. at low water.

Several letters on the election are unavoidable and reluctantly withheld; but the writers will see that the points raised have not been overlooked. We also hold over until our next issue some details as:to the new Wesleyan school at Sankey Bridges.

The Strand Division of London has again re- turned a Smith and a Tory; but it is something to have reduced the Tory majority by 520 since last election. Such a reduction of the Tory majo- rity at Warrington would mean the return of a Liberal. As a prospect that is not at all amiss.

How is it the Tories have allowed the Nationa- list candidate a walk-over at Kilkenny? There is no difficulty in understanding why the Parnel- lites should this time fight shy of tip) place; but for the Tories to turn tail, at the very height of their boasting about "the success of Mr. Balfour' s policy "—what can it mean? . Does it mean that their talk about his success is just so much blather and blarney? It looks like it.

Here pleasant story of the late Mr. W. H. Smith. It is told in the November number of " Blackwood's " magazine :—During last session two members were discussing some point in a side • lobby during a division—the leader of the House happening to pass at the moment. "Here is the headmaster," said one of them," let us refer it to him." "Ah ! don't call me that" was Mr. Smith's rejoinder; "I am only one of the big boys."

The Democrats of the United States have hit upon the novel idea of trying to get financial help (for election purposes) from English and German manufacturers, by promising a repeal of the 311'Kinley Act, which has proved so injurious to foreign trade. The scheme may be tried; but it is doubtful whether it will be successful, even if the money be forthcoming. Brother Jonathan is likely to get his back up, if he sees evidence of foreign interference.

The law officers of the Government are not in very high repute. They were proved to be quite wrong as to the vested interests of brewers; and now there is some doubt as to the legal position of the Salvationists. Speaking at Eastbourne, on Tuesday night, Admiral Field, M.P., Conservative, and borough member, said he had the best reason for stating that Sir Edward Clarke's views respec- ing the Salvationist lawlessness were not shared by the Government. Sir Edward can scarcely feel comfortable after this revelation.

The Alliance meeting at Manchester, on Tues- day night, was a great success. Mr. John Mor- ley's clear enunciation of, and adhesion to, the principle of Local Option roused the large audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm. He frankly con- fessed that, until the decision in the Sharpe v. Wakefield ease, he was not aware of the strength of the Alliance position from a legal point of view. lie accepts the decision tts final, and, once placed on the Parliamentary engine, he is prepared now to put on steam and go ahead.

People are dying of famine in Russia, and this, as in the case of the Irish Famine, not so much because there is a lack of disposition to afford relief as because of the difficulties of communica- tion and organisation. Russian officials, too, are notoriously corrupt, and it is feared that some of the contributions will fail to reach the sufferers. Can this be the reason why no Relief Fund has been opened in England? Why not have an Eng- lish fund, and rut it in the hands of English agents in Russia? Something should be done to save the perishing.

It is stated that Mr. Herbert Roberts and Mr. E. K. Muspratt have withdrawn their names as candidates for selection by the Liberal Party to take the place of Mr. John Roberts at the general election. The only name before the Selection Committee now, therefore, is that of Mr. J. Herbert Lewis, J.P., chairman of the Flints!) ire County Council. Mr. Muspratt ought to be in Parliament. He is well known and highly esteemed in Widnes and Liverpool, and, as Presi- dent of the Financial Reform Association, he is rendering service which is of national importance.

Shelley in his farneous poetical epistle to Maria Gisborne jocularly suggests that, on meeting in the next world,they may "Toss up who died first of drinking tea." But according to Sir Andrew Clark there is such a thing as good tea and wicked tea. He is obliging enough to give his recipe which is as follows :—" If you want to have,either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which wil not injure and which will refresh, get Black China tea, putting in the right measure, the old-fash- ioned teaspoonful for each person, and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good."

How long will the magistrates of Warrington continue to join Mr. Diggle in the farce of " Police Court applications re Intercepting DepOts ? " Having once decided that they have no authority in the matter, it is bringing the Court into contempt to repeat a performance which is less suited to a bar than a bar-parlour. Mr. Diggle being a " gentleman " must kill time somehow, and "Satan finds" &c; but have the magistrates no better means of employing their time? Have they no sense of the ridiculous?

There V 7 203 complaint at the meeting of the Haydock Local Board, on Monday, that there was a falling off in attendance at school, parents being apparently under the impression that, with less or no fees to pay, it did not matter much about their children going regularly to school. Something of the same kind was remarked upon by the Dares- bury magistrates on Tuesday. At both places there was an intimation that the law as to compul- sory attendance would in future be strictly en- forced. And so it should be, especially where the school fee has been abolished.

Alterations at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, are to be made which may be an improvement from the publican's, but not from the public, point of view. The matter was before Messrs. Francomb, Harrison and Sutton, at the Police Court, on Monday; and the following was the suggestive reply of the Chief Constable :—" I don't know that it would have any effect if I had any objection. All I can say is, that I had rather there had been no more vaults in Bridge-street, and particularly the door into Ship-yard. As your worships will be aware, Ship-yard is already famous for rows and disturbances. At the same time, Ido not know that I can offer any objection." •

"Rows and disturbances" in Ship-yard; so by way of ensuring peace and harmony for the future it is proposed to open a door in the yard from a public-house! How kind and considerate! How admirably calculated t.." secure the end in view! Why should the Chief Constable's objection have any effect? Don't these magistrates know what they are about? And are they not all honourable men?
Drink and be mad then ; 'tis your country bids— Gloriously drunk Obey the important call; Her cause demands the assistance of your throats— Ye all can swallow and she asks no more.

Alderman Burgess is right; it does "look rather foolish " laying the foundation stone for new baths at Warrington,before the Local Govern- ment Board have sanctioned the scheme. Accord- ing to Councillor Bolton, the idea seems to have been hit on to tickle the vanity of the Mayor ; for he said it was to be " almemento of his year of office." His Worship showed himself anxious to have the memento lugged in, for he said if there was any expense incurred—as a consequence pre- sumably of this too hasty proceeding—he would be "quite willing to bear it.' And yet,as Alderman Burgess says, it is, altogether, " rather foolish."

Mr. R. A. Naylor's conscience seems to be troubl- ing him. Speaking at the Warrington Ragged School, on Monday evening, he said :—" Church- men and Dissenters, Conservatives, Liberals, and red-hot Radicals used to meet on Temperance platforms, without trying to tear each others eyes. Now, unfortunately, whether owing to politics, or sectarianism, temperance people seemed to be at

WESLEYAN TEA PARTY AT RUNCORN.—A congrega- tional tea party in connection with the Rnncor n Wesleyan circuit, was held in Brunswick schools on Monday evening. About 250 persons sat down to tea, and afterwards a well attended meeting was held. The Rev. W. Arrowsmith presided and delivered an address. Speeches were also made by the Rev. James Hanby, Messrs. John Simpson, T. Sinister, B. Kniveton, and Robert Norman, and the proceedings were charact- erised by much earnestness and enthusiasm. UMBRELLAS RECOVERRD.—J. and W. DUTTON, SAUkey-St., Warrington.—Advt. A STOCIEHAM FARMER AND lIIS GUN.

Joseph Baguley, farmer, Stockham, was summoned to answer the complaint of Mr. William Speechley, an officer of Inland Revenue, who charged him with using a gun without a license.—Mr. Moore supervisor, of Inland Revenue, prosecuted and the defendant pleaded guilty. P.S. Costello said about 20 minutes to six on the morn- ing of the fourth September he saw the defendant shoot a rabbit on land in his own occupation at Stockham. The defendant said he had no license.—Mr. Moore said defendant had not taken a license out for the last three years. He said he thought that a license was not neces- sary to shoot on his own land, and such an idea showed the necessity of bringing the case before the Bench, as there might be other cases of the same kind.—The de- fendant was fined 10s. and costs.

At the fortnightly meetirwof the above order, a paper was read by Mr. Thomas Clarke, on "Sunday Closing." The subject was well handled and showed much research. The writer demonstrated the great advantage it would be even to the publicans themselves. He made a strong point of the extra labour involved for the barman and waiters to work on the Sur.day. He estimated that there would be about 200 employed in Runcorn on the I.Ard's day, and that the expenditure would be about £2OO on drink each Sunday. He thought that we had Sunday Closing almost within our grasp, and urged the members to make it a vital question. There was a large attendance of members, the following taking part in the discussion: Messrs. Thomas Whyte, David Smith, John Walton, Daniel Bisbrown, Thomas Holt, Thomas Heesom, and Edward Bay. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Clarke for his valuable paper. A WIDNES LABOURER'S SATURDAY NIGHT SPRBE.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Ellen Mitchell, Sankey-st., and Mary J. Doyle, Wellington-st., were charged with stealing a purse, containing 295., the pro- perty of John Byrne, Moss Bank-road.—Prosecutor said he met the prisoners on Saturday night in Waterloo-rd. Mitchell asked him to pay for drinks, which he did. After they had been together some time he missed the purse, and charged Mitchell with stealing it. He told her that if she would give him the money he would pay for more drink, and would say nothing about it. Mitchell then told the prisoner Doyle to give him the purse,where- upon Doyle handed him the purse, which only contained 15s. Eke said that was all she had, and he would get no Tweddle apprehended Mitchell on Saturday night, and when in the police station she produced a purse containing 16s.—P.C. Berry apprehended Doyle.— Prisoners, who pleaded not guilty, were committei to the Sessions for trial.

FASHIONAELE MARRIAGE AT WIDNES.

A large audience assembled in Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel on Thursday afternoon to witness the marriage ceremony of Mr. W. C. Clarke, eldest son of Mr. W. Clarke, of Beaconsfield, Ditton,and Miss Annie Carey ,of the Hollies, Hough Green. The bride, who who was attired in a dress of white brocaded cottilli, with silk lace front, was attended by Miss Carey, Miss Evelyn Carey, Miss Bella Carey, and Miss B. Clarke as bridesmaids. The Misses Carey were dressed in grey cloth trimmed with white surah silk and hats to match and Miss B. Clarke was attired in a dress of white crepe, with hat to match. Master H. Clarke, wh3 wore a suit of navy velvet, acted as page. Mr. W. B. Fletcher was best man and the other groomsmen were Messrs. George and Randle Carey. The Rev. G. S. Meek was the officiating minister. The presents were numerous and costly ; amongst them being a gold watch presented to the bridegroom by his father's employ-es. A WARNING TO WIDNES PAWNBROKERS. At Widnes Police Court. on Monday, Sarah McCann, aged 10 years, of 29 Pleasant-st., pleaded guilty to steal- in.' a pair of boots, worth 45. ed. the property of Edward Kelly, of 8 Ann-st. East. The prisoner had stolen the boots whilst employed in cleaning at Kelly's house, and had pawned them for 3s. at James Carroll's shop.—The assistant, Joseph Carroll, informed the Bench that the girl said the boots were her mother's.—Mr. Timmis : Is there not some rule amongst pa vonbrokers not to take things in pledge from young children ?—Witness: We don't take pledges from strange children.—Mr. Timmis : You are not half as strict as you ought to be.—Mr. Tim- mis, in binding the girl over to be of good behaviour for three months, said that the pawnbroker was greatly to blame, as it was his duty not to take pledges from chil- dren under 12 years of age. He advised Carroll to be more careful in futuie, or he would get himself into trouble. It was a great incentive to steal when pledges were taken fl'orn such young children.—Mr. Deacon agreed with the Chairman, and said he thought it was a very bad ease. GAB FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter,: Bridge-et., Wittrington.—Advt. GREEN-WAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS. RUNCORN.

Durin-g—la-st winter a number of magic lantern enter- tainments were given in these schools with the object of improving the attendance of the scholars, at both the r day and evening schools. A considerable sum was realised, part of which was used to defray the purchase money of a first-class magic lantern, the remainder being devoted to the prize fund. The first of the series of lectures for the present season was delivered on Friday evening last week, by Mr. E. Sneyd Kynnersley, Her Majesty's Inspector of Schools. The boys schoolroom was crowded with an attentive and appreciative audi- ence. Dr. McDougall, F.R.C.S.E., presided, and extended a hearty welcome to Mr. Kynnersley, who then proceeded with his lecture on Canada. After a brief preliminary sketch of the discovery and progress of the Colony the lecturer described a journey from Quebec across the Continent of America •to the Rocky Mountains, particular attention being paid to the big cities and their buildings. He was very severe upon the general ugliness of ecclesiastical architecture,and he said as a rule the most handsome building in a city was the Post Office. The lives and habits of the Colonists and of the native Indians were pourtrayed, the,lecturer inters- persing his remarks with an amount of dry humour that proved highly amusing. The lecture was profusely illnstrated by means of the oxy-hydrogen lantern, manipulated by Mr. T. Bowyer.—The Rev. Canon Wood proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Kynnersley for his very interesting lecture. It was very interesting to see an official without his warpaint. (Applause.) It was quite comforting to think that Government officials were really the same as other men, and they owed Mr. Kynnersley their gratitude not only for the capital lecture and interesting views but also for coming amongst them in the exceedingly pleasant and agreeable way in which he had that night. (Applause.)—The Rev' Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion, remarking that the lecture had been a great treat.—The motion was carried by acclamiation. On the proposition of Mr. W. Shaw, seconded by Mr. A. Salkeld, a similar compliment was paid to Dr. McDougall for presiding. lIMBRELLASIRECOVERED.-4. and W.Purrox, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt.

RUNCORN POLICE Ninvs.

On Thursday, before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas, Charles Rawson, of Back Mersey-st., was charged with keeping a house of ill-fame, and he was sentenced to a month's hard labour.—Joseph Mee- was fined ss. and costs for being drunk.
A. Sr. HELENS PUBLICAN DROWNED.

On Thursday night, David Chenney, 39 years of age, landlord of the Bee Hive Inn, Moss Nook, Sut- ton, was drowned in an old clay pit,near his house. The deceased man had gone to the pit for some geese which he owned and while walking along the side of the water be slipped and fell in. A man named Rigby attempted to rescue him, but failei to do so, and the body was not recovered for over an hour. PRESENTATION TO A STATIONMASTER.

Mr. Brewne, who for several years has been stationmaster at Culcheth station, on the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, has been removed to Rotherham, and is succeeded at Culcheth by Mr. Newton, of Glossop. Before leav- ing Culcheth, Mr. Browne was the recipient of a tea and coffee service, presented by the employes at the station and friends in the village, as a mark of the respect and high esteem in which he was held by them.

CRUSHED TO DEATH IN A ST. HELENS COLLIERY. A shocking fatality occurred at Sutton Heath Colliery, St. Helens, on Thursday night. William Gee, 19 years of age, of Cairo Square, Thatto Heath, was working with several other men in one of the "down brows "of the mine when one of the props, supporting the roof gave way. A large stone weighing about a ton came down and alighted on Gee who was crushed to death. Two men named Jaques and Barton had narrow escapes, and ono of them sustained slight injury.
MANCHESTER AND LIVER- POOL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

Lord Egerton of Tatton, speaking on Monday at the annual meeting of the Royal Manchester, Liver- pool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, expressed his belief that technical education is necessary in order to place English agriculture generally on a level with that of other countries. Lord Derby opposed a resolution, moved by Mr. John liaison, to change the title to that of the Royal Lancashire Agricultural Society. The pro- posal was rejected by a considerable majority. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. CHLAD :BURNED TO DEA.TH.

Joseph Fairhurst, two years old, son of Joseph Fairhurst, collier, of 61, Ashcroft-st., St. Helens, died on Sunday night from injuries received early in the morning. The child was playing before the fire, and during the temporary absence of the mother his nightdress got ignited. He was badly burned about the body, arms, and legs, and notwith- standing the attentions of Dr. Donnellan, expired as stated. Mr. Brighouse coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, on the body of the deceased. A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned.

div.p: BOY GAMBLURS AT WIDNIIS.

William Carr, a buy 15 years of age, whose home is in daniey-st., was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of gambling with cards. P.C. Bamforth proved that on the 19th inst., in Dock-st., the defendant was playing "Banker" with seven other boys. A fine of 2s. ed. was imposed.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The usual weekly meeting of the above society was held on Monday evening at the Wesleyan schoolroom, Mr. F. 0. Moston being in the chair. The subject, which was "The Resurrection," had been adjourned from the previous Monday. Messrs. Bereton, Simpson, Brigg, Taylor,H. S. Brown, and Allen spoke. Mr. E. Moston was the ossayist. TILE VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY.

The adjourned discussion on this subject was resumed at the Widnes Debating Society, on Wednesday night, under the presidency of Dr. iffieeffe. During the dis- cussion letters were read from several persons in North- with and Crewe, stating that provisions were much cheaper in those places than at Widnes. A large majo- rity voted in favour of the construction of the bridge.

div.head: FRENCH CLASS AT WIDNES.
div.p: FRENCH CLASS AT WIDNES.

In connection with the French class formed by the Widnes Technical Instruction Committee, a lecture on " How to learn French" was delivered in Simms Cross, school on Tuesday evening. Toe lecturer was Monsieur Meunier, of Liverpoolswho has been appointed teacher to tlie class. A number of names of persons de- sirous of joining the class were taken by Mr. S. Ilayle, the secretary.
RUNCORN GOSPISI. UNION.

Special services were held in Hope Hall, in connection with this body, on Sunday. In the morning the Evan- gelist preached, in the afternoon the Rev. .7. Martin de- livered a sermon, and in the evening Mr. Ralph Peacock officiated. Collections were made in aid of the mission. A service of song entitled, "The man who spoiled the music" was rendered by the choir, on Saturday night, under the leadership of Mr. J. Moorfield. Mr. J. J. Speakman presided, and the narrative was read by Mr. George Lacey. WIDNES FRBII LIBRARY COMMITTRII.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. Accounts amount- ing to £lB 17s. 9d., were passed for payment. The Librarian (Miss Procter), reported that 4,247 books had been issued during the month, and the total attendance in the reading room had been 12,831. The resignation of Miss Walker. assistant librarian, was read and ac- cepted. It was stated that Miss Walker was shortly to be married.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of the Board was held in the Board room on Tueaday evening when there were present Mr. .1. Pritchard, Chairman, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. A. Sal- keld, Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, and Mr. G. Moss (clerk). Dr. McDougall pro- posed that Mr. Thomas Handley be elected a member of the Board in place of Mr. Howitt, resigned. Mr. S. Tay- lor seconded the motion,and it was carried unanimously. This was the whole of the business.

MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN. The young people connected with these missions are organising a bazaar which goes by the title of Beehive, and with the object of raising funds towards their pro- ject they gave an entertainment in the mission room on Monday evening. There was a good audience, and Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, presided. A programme of songs, recitations, tsc., were gone through in capital style, and the song "Ten little nigger boys" given in character by ten young boys, was especially enjoyed.
ROBBERY EY BOYS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, John A. Tumbl- ing, Cross-st. ; Thomas Pierce, Farrant-et.; John Whit- field, Cross-it., and John Heywood, Grove-st.,boys, were charged with stealing from a shed on the premises of J. Mitchell, grocer, Widnes-road,a quantity of cakes, dried fruit, &c. The defendants admitted their guilt, and as it was their first offence they were bound over to appear when called upon, and were warned that they would be severely punished for any future offence.

RUNCORN CHURCH ARMY. In connection with this religious organisation, harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday, when the Vicar. the Rev. Canon Ward, preached in the morning, and the Rev. G. D. Wray, Vicar of Halton, in the even- ing. There was a good congregation at each service. On Monday eveninz a public meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. Cunningham, and addresses were given by Captains Goodwin and Hardy and the Rev. G. H. Kingston. The fruit and vegetables were sold in aid of the funds.

div.head: ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, WIDNES.
div.p: ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, WIDNES.

With the object of raising funds to liquidate the debt on the new altar recently erected in this church, a con- cert was given in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening, and a large and appreciative audience assembled. A capital programme was presented, and the ladies and gentlemen who took part acquitted themselves with credit and were frequently loudly applauded. The vocalists were soprano, Mrs. Doyle; contralto, Miss Dwyer ; tenor, Mr. C. Finn and Mr. ienkinson ; baritones, Mr. C. Kent and Mr. D. Murphy; humorists, Mr. F. Hayes and Mr. C. J. O'Neil. Mr. Christopher was the accompanist. The St. Mary's band also played several selections. Advantage was taken of the gathering to present the Rev. Father Quirke with a gold watch and chain, which had been subscribed for by the congregation and members of St. Mary's, as a token of the respect and esteem in which the rev. facher is held, and their appreciation of the untiring zeal he displayed amongst them. Mr. O'Keeffe, who presided, made the presentation, end eulogised Father Quirke's character and ability.—Father Quirke acknowledged the gift in a brief but suitable speech, and the musical programme was proceeded with. UNJUST SCALES AND WEIGHTS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Jonah Evans, manager of the Co-operative Stores in Ditton-road, was summoned by Inspector Kilpatrick, for selling bread otherwise than by weight. It was proved that the so- ciety's carter delivered the loaves in Pitt-st., without weighing them. The Inspector afterwards found they were soz. 5 drachms light.-Mr. F.J. Poole said the com- mittee of the society had issued instructions that no bread should be sold unless weighed, and that any of- sender would be at once discharged. It was not to the interest of the society to sell bread under weight. The defendant was fined £1 and costs 123. He was then charged that the scales in the cart were three drachms out of balance against the purchaser. A fine of and costs 12s. was also imposed in this case.-Wm. Miles, coal dealer, Salisbury-st., was charged with having two 561 b. weights which were 12 and 8 drachms light respec- tively. The defendant pleaded that pieces had been chipped off the weights through the men throwing them about. A fine of £1 and 123. costs was imposed-Win. Furber, greengrocer, West-st., was fined 103. and costs for having in his possession the following unjust weights :-71b. 2 drachms, 41b. 4 drachms, 21b. drachms, 11b. 1 drachm light.-Joseph Longton, farmer, Ditchfield Farm, Hough Green, was summoned tor hav- ing four 561 b. weights which were respectively 140 z., 4 drachms. 30z., 10 drachms, 8 drachms, and 3oz. 4 drms. light. He was further charged with having a pair of scales which were 12oz, out of balance against the pur- chaser : and on which defendant admitted to Inspector Kilpatrick that he had on the previous day weighed 48 sacks of wheat. Mr. Peters contended that farmers were not traders under the Act, and said the wheat was simply weighed for their own satilfaction, and the scales were never used for any other purpose. A fine of £1 and costs was imposed in each case. Inspector Kil- patrick asked that the scales should be forfeited, as they had been in use 50 years, and would cost more to repair them than they were worth. The Bench ordered the scales to be forfeited.-Elizabeth Moss,Holly Bank Farm, Dutton, was charged with having the following unjust weights in her possession :-561b. soz. 10 drachms, 561 b. soz. 4 drachms, 561 b. 4oz. 8 drachms, 561 b. lea. 7 drms., EBlb. 30z. 6 drachms, 1441).1 drachms, and 21b. lidrms. light. div.head: PROVIDENT ASSOCIATION OF LONDON.
div.p: THE PROVIDENT ASSOCIATION OF LONDON.

On Wednesday night a ballot meeting in conne.c- tion with the Provident Association of London, was held in the St. Helens Town Ilall, when there was a very large attendance. CouncillorJ. B. Kenyon, district superintendent, Earlestown, after which the first local ballot was held and the number drawn was 104,200. div.head: PLAYING WITH GUNPOWDER.
div.p: PLAYING WITH GUNPOWDER.

On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, three lads, named John Platt, Robert Byatt, and William Platt, all living at Blackbrook, were summoned for damaging eight stone "sleepers,' the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. On the sth September the lads bought some gun- powder and went to the Parr branch of the com- pany's line. At that branch the old-fashioned stone "sleepers," which have holes bored in, are stored, and the lads fired the gunpowder in the holes and damaged the stones. The damage amounted to one guinea. A fine of is. was inflicted in each case, and the lads were ordered to pay 10s. 6d. costs and 7s. damage, altogether 18s. 6d., or seven days. KITCHEN U ANGERS.—Garland Builders Ironmonger, War- ngten.— Advt.
Mn. BRUNNER, M.P.. AND THH POLLUTION OF RIVERS.

The " Manchester Examiner and Times," in an article on "The pollution of our Rivers "says : "At the moment when the subject is being grap- pled with in earnest, it is gratifying and helpful to note the attitude of the manufacturers, who, through their representatives at the inquiry, stated they were against pollution, and sought only equal treatment ; and to call to mind that it was one a our largest chemical manufacturers Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who introduced and succeeded in carrying, amongst other amendments to the Local Government Act, 1888, the clause under which the Joint Committee has been constituted ; and who has since said with regard to it that he trusted and believed it would "change the face of the country to auch an extent as to make it a far more beauti- ful and pleasant country to live in." a statement which we heartily endorse, and believe to be possible of fulfilment." . _

BHOCKING DEATH AT HAYDOCK LODGE ASymc On Tuesday, Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Ilaydock Lodge Private Asylum relative to the death of John Ward, an inmate of the asylum, who died on Friday last. Dr. Street, the medical superintendent of the asylum, stated that the deceased was admitted on the 7th August last, and was fifty-six years of age. Ile made a post-mortem examination of deceased, and found that the stomach was half full of partially digested food, and in the windpipe there was a small quantity of soft food, just below the vocal chords. This, in Dr. Street's opinion, caused spasm of the glottis and suffocation.—Thomas Dunlop, charge attendant at. the asylum, said that as the deceased refused his food, he had to be fed with a spoon. Just before' deceased expired Dunlop ha I been feeding him with some soft food. Ile iroticed a sudden change come over deceased, and thought he was choking, and sent for Dr. Moore, the assistant medical superin- tendent, but deceased died just as the doctor arrived.—After hearing the evidence of Dr. Moore, the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." div.head: SOLICITOR'S CLIIRK IN THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: A SOLICITOR'S CLIIRK IN THE POLICE COURT.

A respectably-dressed man, giving the nWine- of IVilliamson, of Liverpool, was charged at St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, with begging on Monday afternoon. Constable Nicholson deposed that he saw the prisoner begging in solicitors' and other offices. Prisoner informed the magistrates that for 50 years he had been a conveyancing and common law clerk in solicitors' offices. He was nearly 70 years of age, and he had latterly been employed in Liverpool. He was on his way to Manchester, and he expected to find some copying employment in the solicitors' cffices in St.Helens in connection with the elections. It was true that as he could not obtain employment he asked the clerks for a little assistance to help him on his journey towatds Manchester. It was their custom to do so, but he strongly denied that he was a beggar. Ile had never been in prison in his life before, and for six years he was chief clerk to the late Mr. Justice Williams.—The constable,in answer to the Chief Constable, stated that the prisoner was the worse for drink when apprehended. —The Bench discharged the prisoner with a caution, and asked him to leave the town. The man Williamson, again appeared in the dock, on Wednesday, on a similar charge. A constable proved that he had gone into the office of Mr. Webster, solicitor, Church-st., and began begging. Williamson who had any amount of - volubility, said he knew Mr. Webster and he went in there on the assumption that he would get a glass of sherry or port. (Laughter.) As he was an old lawyer's clerk he thought he might get some engrossing to do there. He was sent to goal for seven days.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY —Before Major Hazlehurst and Dr. Steele.

It was alleged that the defendant was in the Mersey Vaults and the complainant entered,when, without provocation, she struck her three blows on the face, making her nose bleed profusely and blacking her eye.
