div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. HUGH HUGHES, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. HUGH HUGHES, OF RUNCORN.

Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, was well filled on Wednesday night with a company gathered to- gether to do honour to Mr. Hugh Hughes, ex-captain of the Runcorn Football Club. For nine years, Hughie, as his very numerous admirers love to call him, had been captain of the first team, and by his judicious training .of his men, and the espri de corps with which he inspired them, combined with his skilful generalship on the field of play, he had the gratification of seeing Runcorn Club rise to the highest pinnacle of football fame. For many years he was a valued member of the Cheshire County team, and during the last two seasons lie held the honourable and onerous position of captain of that organisation. Under these circumstances his corn- rade.s and the followers of the club could not permit him to retire without a formal recognition of his worth and character, and the principal feature of the gathering on Wednesday was the presentation to him of an illumi- nated address and a handsome and valuable gold watch and chain. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presided, and in opening the proceedings, he said be was proud as presi- dent of the club to be present to conduct the meeting, a gathering such as in his opinion had never been held in Runcorn before. It was one where they were all asso- ciated to do honour to one of their comrades—(ap- plause)—and he thought the numerous faces he saw be- fore him augured well for their comrades who were in advance of their fellows, that they were hound someday to have the same recognition. (Applause.) It was a pleasure to him (Mr. Speakman) to be associated with the Runcorn Football team. (Applause.) It was a still greater pleasure to see the unanimity that caused them in nearly every contest to win the victory— (applause)— and he hoped the Runcorn foot hall would long continue rolling. (Applause.) When it was their choice to fix someone else in his place, as president, it will not make the slightest difference to him—he should resign his position and still retain his interest amongst them. (Loud applause.)— The programme was then proceeded with and in the in- terval the presentation took place, and the Chairman remarked that in Captain Hughes they had had a good general and a good leader—(Applause)—and he was proud of him as lie was proud of all of them. (Hear, hear.) As lie had mentioned before, wherever Captain Hughes was on a Saturday he was always found at the Sabbath School and in the chapel choir,of which he was an honourable member. He could see from the faces round about him that they still looked up to Captain Hughes, and he hoped that they would try to emulate at all times the good example he had been able to set them and follow in his footsteps. (Applause.) Might God spare him long to be an ornament to his native town. (Applause.)—Mr. J. E. Langshaw (secretary) then read the following testimonial. " This testimonial is pre- sented by the townspeople of Runcorn and his comrades of the club to Mr. Hugh Hughes, along with a gold watch and chain, bearing his monogram and an inscrip- tion, in recognition of very valuable services rendered to Runcorn Football Club. In the year 1882 Mr. Hughes was elected captain of the first team and was unani- mously re-elected for a period of eight years. During this time Mr. Hughes by his gentlemanly conduct, excellent wisdom and skill gained the confidence of his comrades and the good will of the officers and during the season 1889-90 saw his club cne of the foremost in England. We wish in this testimonial to 'thank Mr. Hughes for his untiring energy,and very will- ing service rendered to the club at all times, and pray that he may have long life, health, and happiness. , Signed on behalf of his comrades, and of the substribers, Philip Speakman, president. Runeorn, 28th October, 1891." (Loud applause.) Amid deafening applause,Mrs. Speakman then gracefully handed the watch and chain to Captain Hughes, who in reply said he did not know how to find words to express his thanks. He did not know what he had done to deserve this. What he had done for Runcorn Club had been very little. He had al- ways had a good team, and if a captain had not such a team, he would not be able to win many matches. (Ap- plause.) They had a great many old players to thank for raising the club up to its present position, of whom he might mention Messrs. Bate, Joule, Lightburn, and Speakman. (Applause.) He could not tell them how pleared he was to read in the newspaper a few days ago, of the manner in which Harry Speakman was playing In the new world, and he hoped lie might long have health and strength to show the Colonials how they played football in Runcorn. (Applause.) After an al- lusion to the progress of the club, Mr. Hughes said if there was one way in which the Runcorn members could show their appreciation of what little he had done,it was in still keeping up the good form that the club had at- tained, and he hoped they would long be at the top of of the tree, as they had been for the last year or two. (Loud applause.)—Mr. J. W. Light- burn proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Speakman for her presence that night and for presenting the testi- monial.—Mr. Clegg seconded the motion, and added the same of Mr. Spealctrian to whom he said the club owed a debt of gratitude. (Applause.) The motion was carried by acclamation.—ln reply Mr. Speakman referred to Mrs. Speakman's connection with nurse fund and the gratification the club aflorded her in raising so large a sum for that object. They had, he said, no conception of the amount of good that fund was doing for suffering humanity in Runcorn. (Applause.) They had a nurse second to none in the Kingdom, and she was doing her work right valiantly, and he was glad indeed that Mrs. Speakman was a member of the Nurse Committee. As to himself he hoped that the good feeling that now existed between himself and the club would long pre- vail. (Applause.)—On the motion of Mr. W. Carroll, a vote of thanks was accorded to the donors. In the course of the evening a capital programme of music was gone through by the following local vocalists—Messrs. C. Pownall, T. Clegg, R. Morris and J. Leathwood. Mr. J. Woods gave a cornet solo in a finished manner. Mr. Harry Collins, of Liverpool, contributed several comic sketches and charrcter songs, which proved a fruitful souree of amusement. Refreshments were provided by Mrs. Riley of the Cocsa Rooms, and cigars were also dis- tributed, and altogether a most enjoyable evening was spent.

div.head: ____-4--__. PENKETH.
div.p: WESLEYAN CHAPEL RE-OPENING.

After service in chapel yesterday week tea was provided for the friends from a distance in the schoolroom. A goodly number sat down to tel. The tables, which vverie very prettily decorated with fiowers,presented a pleasing appearance. The tnbles were presided over by the following ladies:—Misses L. Routledge, E. Hobson, Cross, Seed, M. Garnett, F. Garnett, Walker, and 11. Garnett. The evening (musical) service began in the chapel at seven o'clock, when the pulpit was again occupied by the ,! Rev. F. L. Wiseman, B.A. After the first lesson the ' solo from the oratorio" St. Paul," "Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets" NI as effectively sung by , Miss Langdon. and after the 2nd lesson the anthem, "The Lord is my Shepherd" was sung by the choir. , Mr. Wiseman took his text from St. John, chap. 12, ' verses 31 and 32, and preachel a most excellent and impressive sermon therefrom.which was most atten- tively listened to. At the conclusion of the sermon the solo "Hear, oh hear my prayer 0 Lord," was given by Miss Langdon. A collection was taken at the close of the service in aid of the chapel exten- sion fund and realised a satisfactory amount. Mr. W. J. Wiwfield presided at the organ both afternoon and evening. The re-opening services in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel were continued on Sunday ; when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. G. Talalun Newton, of Manchester. At both the morning and evening services, there were large congregations. In the morning the preacher selected his text from St. John xvi. 32, preaching from the words, "Alone, and yet not alone." In the evening Mr. Newton selected his text from St. John i. 33 to the end. Collections were taken at the close of each service, in behalf of the extension fund. The total amount realized on Sunday was £l5 14s. 31. At the con• elusion of the service the sacrament of the Lord's Supper was administered. There was a large number of communicants. Continuation services will be held to-morrow (Sunday) and Monday, the Rev. R. Waddy Moss be- ing the preacher on the former, and the Rev. Charles Garrett preaching on the latter, day.

Mr. Blaine, a New York correspondent states, his declared that the difficulty with Chili is all over, and that the Government has no intention of strengthening the American naval forces in Valparaiso.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
Mr. Thomas Handley has been unanimously elected a member of Runcorn School Board in place of Mr. J. J. Howitt, who has resigned in conse- quence of his change of residence.
Mr. Eaton Speakman, third son of Mr. P. Speak- man, C.C., has received a commission as lieutenant of one of the Runcorn companies of the Earl of Chester's Rifles.

Dr. McDougall is one of the best known men in Runcorn, and for nearly the last quarter of a cen- tury has taken an active part in public affairs. Some of the most stirring scenes took place on the Board of Commissioners when he was a member, and he was generally in the thick of the fray, but now he is "yours respectfully" the Medical Officer of Health, and his thoughts and duties lie in other channels. This is all by the way. The fact is the worthy doctor contemplates leaving us and return- ing across the border to his bonnie Scotland. Such I gather from a remark he let fall the other night, when the ladies of the Ambulance Class gracefully presented him with a beautifal pair of gold-rimmed eye glasses. In acknowledging the gift he said they would greatly assist his eyesight when he was spending his declining years among the hills of Scotland. I suppose he has made his fortune in this dingy Cheshire town and now yearns to peace- fully spend his remaining years among the life- giving breezes of the romantic mountains of his native land. We shall miss him, but may he be happy when his foot is on his native heath.

Since the Board of Commissioners adopted the Technical Instruction Act the Committee appointed to deal with the question have not been idle, and there are indications that we are within measur- able distance of having a Technical Institute worthy of the town and of the cause. The scheme as first propounded it was estimated would cost .£3OO, but this was merely received and not adopted J and whether it will be adhered to or not is a moot j question, but that an Institute will be built may be J taken as a fact. Last week Mr. Lightburn and Mr. Lake (the Law clerk) paid a visit to London and had an interview with the chiefs of the Science and Art Department of South Kensington with a view to obtaining a grant towards the construction of a building and towards the purchase of appara- tus. The interview was most satisfactory and one result was that General Festing, the head of the Science and Art Department, visited the town on Monday,and accompanied by the Technical Instruc- tion Committee, inspected the proposed sites of the Institute, lie expressed his approval of the site, adjoining the public offices in Waterloo-road, and as soon as possible plans will be drawn and sub- j mitted for his consideration. 1 may state that the maximum building grant made by the department is 2. 6d. per superficial foot, which if the com- mittee are fortunate enough to secure will mean a very large sum •of money. It is to be hoped they will be successful in their endeavours.

It is usually stated that Mr. Hall Caine, the cele- brated novelist, whose last work "The Scapegoat" has created such a sensation, is a Manxman and was born in the Isle of Man. A Liverpool daily the other day mentioned Mona's Isle as Mr. Caine's birthplace, but Mr. J. D. Jones,the Runcorn Librarian, correete the error by stating that Mr. Caine was born in Bridgewater-et., Runcorn. A few months ago an article in the " Strand Magazine "gave Runcorn as the novelist's birth place, also mentioned that the late E. A. Sothern, the original Lord Dundreary, was born in Runcorn. In Nickson's history it is stated that between 1831 and 1841 Messrs Sothern and Co. (the family of Lord Dundreary fame) carried on the timber ship yard at Old Quay, until recently carried on by Messrs. Brundrit and Co., but no positive assertion is made that" Lord Dundreary" was born in the town.

on Monday evening Charles Thomas East, des- cribed as a "traveller "and "an old hand" was put in durance vile on a charge of violating the laws of his country by begging. Probably in the hope that the tender-hearted public would provide him with. a better protection against the coming winter, he tore his trousers into ribbons in the solitude of his cell, and next morning he was brought before the magistrates in a semi-nude condition. His worship instead of commiserating with him on his shorn condition, sentenced him to 14 days' hard labour in her Majesty's mansion at Knutsford, whither he was conveyed with a lime sack covering his pedal extremities. Charles Thomas will think his fate doubly hard if the prison authorities turn him out into the cold world in that condition when his " time "is up.

div.head: POLICE NEWS.
div.p: POLICE NEWS.
At Oakmero Petty Sessions on Monday the following Frodsham cases were heard.

INEBRIATED.—For lying on the road drunk at Kingsley , George Baker had to pay ss. including costs.—George , Spruce, Kingsley, butcher, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly on the 24th September. It was his ninth appearance, and he was mulcted in a penalty of 10s. and costs. Rebecca Brown and Samuel Brown, Frodsham, who were drunk and disorderly at Netherton on the 26th September, had to pay 7s. 6d. each. Samuel Brown, jun., Frodsham, for an offence com- mitted on the 11th October, at Helsby, was fined ss. Defendant was committed to prison for seven days with hard labour. DAMAGING A STEAM CRANE AT HELSBY.—Gelrge Spruce (aged 9) and Bernard Cobb (10) were summoned for committing damage to a steam crane belonging to the Runcorn and Helsby Red Sandstone Company, Limited, to the extent of 10s. The Bench ordered the parents of the two boys to pay a fine of 25., with 10s. damage and 9s. 6d. costs between them.

TIE CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL—On Sunday two special sermons were preached in the above chapsl by the Bev. J. Crewe. In the afternoon the service of song, entitled "Seed-time and harvest," was repeated, by special request. Members of the Cadishead Orchestral Band rendered their assistance. Mr. A. Whitfield was at the organ. The service was well attended, a collection being made at the close. SPECIAL SERVICES.—These services were continued at the Wesleyan Chapel. On Saturday night an experience meeting was held, and Sunday was a particularly full day. The evangelist, Mr. .1. Harkness, took for his sub- ject in the morning " Healing of the waters," and in the evening" Belshazzar's Feast." A mneting for men only was held on Sunday afternoon. All the services were well attended. On Monday, the evangelist took for his subject" l'our unemployed men." The work of the evangelist has been successful, and many have pro- fited by it.
DISASTROUS EARTHQUAKE IN JAPAN.

GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. HUNDREDS OF HOUSES DESTROYED. YOKOISAMA, THURSDAY.—A terrible earthquake has visited the southern coast of Nipon, the great island which forms the larger part of the Japanese Empire. Owing to the breaking of the telegraph wires, few details are forthcoming ; but it is known that the populous city of Osoko and Robe, the suburb of Hiogo, in which most of the foreign residents live, have suffered most severely. The shocks ' have passed in a westerly direction along the shore of the Bay of Osoka. Both at Osoka and Kobe, which are twenty miles apart, and are connected by a railway, the havoc caused by the earthquake was immense. The houses are mostly of light construction, and hun- dreds of them were destroyed. The telegrams at present received say that great loss of life has occurred, but no figures are given. Great damage has been done in other parts along the coast, but it is not so serious as at the towns mentioned.
A fight has taken place near the Montana frontier between the Canadian Mounted Police and a band of Blood Indians, one policeman and two Indians being killed.

PLEADS " Nov GUILTY " BUT CHANGES His MIND ON HEARING THE EVIDENCE. A young man named John White, who has been labourer on the Ship Canal, was on Tuesday charged at the Borough Court, with having stolen a pair of hoots, valued at 7s. 6d.. from the shop of Messrs. Scales and Son, Bridge-st. From the evidence it appeared that the boots disappeared from the front of Messrs. Scales's shop on Saturday night, and on Monday the prisoner wanted to sell the boots to Mrs. Leslie, a second-hand clothes dealer. Before this, however, the police had circulated a description of the stolen boots, and Mrs. Leslie con- sidered that the pair offered her coincided very much with the description, and as two policemen were pass- ing at the time, she called upon them, and the prisoner, 'whose answers to questions were not very satisfactory, wastaken into custody. When first -put in the dock White said he was not guilty, but after hearing the evidence he changed his mind and admitted his guilt. He was sent to goal for a month. The Bench com- mended the prompt action of Mrs. Leslie in giving in- formation to the 'police. THEFT OF BOOTS IN THE MARKET. At the Warrington Police Court. on.Thursdav' Thomas Farrington, ironworker, aged 17, residing at 10 Wright- st. ' Sankey Bridges, was charged with stealing on the privious day a pair of boots from the stall of Joseph Frisby. boot and shoe dealer, in the Market. Place, or receiving them knowing them to have been stolen. He offered the boots in pledge at Mr. Morton's, and the pawnbroker seeing they were new boots sent for the police. The defendant said he had received the boots from somebody else. 10s. and costs, or 14 days. MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICt COURT. SittitDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in he chair) and

Councillor VoThey. STEALING BOTTLES —Willaim Mulhall was charged with stealing from the lodging-house of William Gallop, Buttermarket-st.., some time between the 22nd and 23rd inst., 29 stone bottles, value 2s. 11d., his property. Pri- -setter was committed to toe Sessions for trial. MOND/Y.—Before the Mayor (Alderman H. W. Fran- comb), and Aldermen Sutton and Harrison. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Peter iirilason was 'Charged with being drunk in giaarge of a horse and cart in Bridge-street, on SaturaW afternoon. P.C. 39 who 'proved the case Said the'defendant knocked a carriage over, and a child was knocked on to the footpath and hada narrow escape from being killed. He was fined 55 and costs. Deimix AND DISORDERLY.—Wm. Jones, drunk and dis- orderly in Horsemarket-street, on Saturday night, was fined ss. and costs.—Wm. Coleman, in Mersey-street, on Saturday night, ss.—Ellen Kennion, in Buttermarket- street, the same night, a mouth's imprisonment with hard labour.—Henry Raynor and John Collins, in Bridge- st. that night, ss. each.—James Hayes was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bold-st., on Sunday morn- ing, and with assaulting P.C. Amson. P.C. Amson said be found the defendant near the Museum, drunk and using very bad language. He took him into custody and be became very violent, and took hold of witness's belt 'with one hand and struck him on the shoulder with the other. He had a struggle with !lira, and brought him to thepolice station.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to being drunk, but said he remembered nothing more.—Alder- man Wright, standing at the solicitors' table made a sworn statement, corroborating that of the constable. Mr. Gill's little daughter, he said, found the prisoner waving his arms, and acting more like an escaped lima, tic than anything else. -He used most filthy and abomin- able language. He applied at Mr. Gill's door, as he was coming out to church, to know where he could get drink, and Mr. Gill told.him he could get no drink there, and the next public-house was the Patten Arms. He made to go away, but tuined hack, and Mr. Gill removed , him, being satisfied that if he had not done so, the man I would have forced his way into the house. Mr. Gill and witness on afterwards passing him came in for a! considerable amount of abuse. The prisoner was sent to jail for a month.—James Bennett, drunk and dis- orderly in Tanner's-lane, on Sunday nirh, 54. and costs. —Wm. Bibby, iiißussellLet., on the 12th of October, who had broken three panes of glass, 59.—James Jordan, in Dolman's-lane,on the 17th October, b.—John Keenan, Cockhedge-lane, on October 19th, 103. FURIOUS DRlVlNG.—Richard Holcroft was charged with furiously driving a horse and cart, in Knutsford-rd., on the 20th of October. Mr. Browne. solicitor,appeared, for the defence, and explained that his client was absent because obliged to be at Crewe market. P.S. Taylor de- posed that the defendant was driving at the rate of 13. or 14 miles an hour, and took no notice when he shouted to him. Some people in a trap just before him screamed' out, but he drove past them. The horse had not bolted. P.C. Bell corroborated, and said the defendant seemed to be under the influence of drink. Chas. Bromley also gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Browne said the defendant was driving home along Wilderspool Causeway, and a luggage train was coming over Arpley Bridge, and he turned back to get out of the way. He was going to turn back again to drive home, when the horse, which was one of those animals that would not allow a horse to keep in front of it if it could get past it, bolted after another conveyance.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs. DISORDERLY LADS.—NOMaS Musgrove,John Manning, -and John Foy, boys, for being disorderly in the Market Place, on the 19th of October, were ordered to be de- tained till the rising of the court. FIGHTING.—John Hewitt and Richard Boscoe,for fight: in Wilderspool-road, on October 17th, were bound over to 'keep the peace and ordered to pay costs.—Mary Owen, Elizabeth Naylor, and Elizabeth Harbron were charged with fighting in James's-street, off Buttermarket-street, on October. 20th. P.S. Monaghan proved the charge. Owen and Naylor, he said, were under the influence of. drink, but Harbron was pober and not so much to blame as the others. The other women pulled her out of her house to fight. , Naylor said Owen came out with a poker and Harbron produced a handful of hair, which she said Naylor had pulled out of her head. She also said Naylor had given her a black eye, and bitten her. Naylor said, Harbron bit her. Owen said she had had a drink of whisky for the windy spastns.—P.S. Monaghan: It gave her spasms, then. She was falling about the street. The women were each bound over in the sum of £.5 to keep the peace, and in addition were fined costs, Owen Bs., Naylor 75., and Harbron-2s. - THROWING STONES.—Joseph Denmade, Michael Griffin, and James Lennady, were charged with throwing stones in Bewsey-road, to the danger of passengers, on, October 18th—P.C. 33 said the defendants were throwing at the bridge, and threw about 60 stones at it.--The defendants said they were throwing at a rat.—The Mayor thought a rat would have too much sense to stand to be thrown at so long. The defendants were fined ss. each. STREET Gammatio.--LThomas,-Joyce, ' Jeremiah Culler- ton, Thomas Oakes, and Williarirlircrderick, youths, were charged with tossing for rooneyin.Platt-st.;, on October, ltlth.—Joyce wasiined ss4having been twice before con- victed of a like offence, and the others were fined 2s. 6d.

each. TingsnAT.—Before Messrs. R Garnett and W. Owen, DIRTY PASSAGES.— Three women, named Stewart Armstrong, and Dooley, appeared in answer to sum- monses for having allowed the.passage andploset in con- nection with the houses 7,9, and 11 Buckley-st„ to be -in a filthy condition. The Corporation prosecuted, and it was slated that the passage and closet in question
were continually in a very dirty state. Armstrong, who had previously been sumainned, was fined 2s. 6d., and the other two had to pay is. each. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Holmes (chairman), and

Wright. UNSEEMLY BEHAVlOUR.—Catherine Carney and Matilda Watson, for unseemly conduct in Bridge-street, on Tues- day night, were sent to jail for 14 days each. WIFE Asseur.T.—John Edwards, 24, Dial Court, was charged with assaulting on the 24th of Octobar,his wife, Maria Edwards,who appeared in court with a black eye, and was a cripple in the left arm. She stated that 8 months since she had had a separation from him, and he had hit her more since then than during the whole 19 years she had been married to him. He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. THURSDAY.—Before Major Pi ckmere (chairman), Coun- cillor James Fairclough, Aldermen Sutton and Green- __ _ _ _ _

all, and Captain Ridgeway. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Jonathan Pilling,salt hawker, of Warrington, was charged with cruelty to a horse by working it while in an unfit state on Wednesday after- noon, in Wilderspool-foad. Inspector Dbvity, said he found the horse suffering from severe wounds,the saddle being saturated with blood and matter from them. P.S. Cox corroborated. He was fined 103. and costs, or 14 days. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —Charles Carney, drunk and disorderly in King-st., on Wednesday afternoon, ss. including costs. THREATBNING.—Henry Rayner, ship Canal labourer, was charged with using threaiening language to George Murray, manager of Mr. Bruchemire's lodging-house, in which the defendant lodges. The complainant had given evidence against him in a case in which Mr. Brtichetnire prosecuted, and this was the reason he threatened Murray. On the defendant promising to leave the town, he was bound over to keep the peace for sii months, and ordered to pay 9s. 61. costs, the defendant promising to remit the costs in a week from Runcorn, whither he was going. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder-
man Wright, and Dr. Gnrnall

FALSE DECLARATION' BY EX-SOLDIERS. —James Harold an Patrick Fagan were charged with having made a false declaration on being enlisted in the West York- shire Regiment, by stating that they had never been be- fore in the army. They were each sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.

OVERCROWDING A HOUSE.—Joseph Donnelly, shoe- maker, 8, Cropper's-brow, was charged by Ar. Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, with allowing his house to be overcrowded. Mr. Norman said the house was only adapted for habitation by two persons, and there were seven in it. It was in a. state of filth and squalor, and was not fit for habitation. Mr. Norman applied for an order to close the house till certified as fit for habitation, as well as the usual order. Orders were made to abate the nuisance within 24 hours, and for the house to be closed till certified.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF HIS•MOTITER.—Frederick Miles, wire drawer, a married man, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with non-contribu- tion for the support of his mother, Elizabeth Miles. He was ordered to pay 2s. per week. CRUELTY TO A HoRsE.--John Dooley was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S,P.C.A., with cruel usage of a horse by working it in an unfit state, in Winwick-road, on Oct 19th. Mr. Dowty said the horse was drawing a coal lorry, and was lame. He would not press the case if the defendant would not work the horse again till it recovered. The case was dismissed 9n that understand- ing. _

ABSENCE FROM SERVICE.—AN EPIDEMIC OF MONDAYISH- I NESS.—Bridget Hart, Ellen McCarthy, Mary Gleave, Catherine Melia, Elizabeth Ann Hart, Leah Matthew- man, Bodelia Towey, and Margaret Ryder, were summoned by John Platt. fustian cutter, for absenting themselves from work without permission. It appeared that the absence of the defendants in these cases was generally on Mondays, and in some in which it had been through alleged illness this had always occurred on Monday. The Chairman remarked that it was imredible that the illness should always be on Monday. Orders were made in each case for return to work and payment damage and costs, except that in Towey's case, damage was not claimed or allowed. ASSAULT.—Mrs. Jane Lightfoot, and Mrs. Elizabeth Fogg were charged with assaulting each other, on Tues- day morning. The parties live in the neighbourhood of Oliver-st. They were both bound over to keep the peace for six months and mulcted in costs.—Esther Wilson was charged with assaulting an the 19th inst., Rachel Rigby, who appeared with a black eye, which she said the aefendant had given her. The defendant said the complainant called her a "Liverpool stabber," and put , her hand to her nose several times, upon which she smacked her face.—Other evidence was given on bath sides. The defendant was fined the costs.--70har1es Forrest was charged with assaulting Annie Burehall, a married woman, on October 24th. 103. and costs.
DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
rIIESDAL—Before Messrs. W. Long (chairman), and H. Nield. . .

DRUNK. AND DISORDERLT.-Thos. Wilkinson, farm labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Stretton, on the sth of September. Mr. Jenkins de- fended. The defendant was fined ss. including costs.— Alfred Stringer, drunk and disorderly on the 28th of Sep- tember, in Warrington-road, ss. and costs.—John Host- age, drunk and disorderly on the 29th of September, at Stretton, was fined 103. and costs. DOG AT LARGE.—Arthur Hall,valet, for allowing a dog to be at large on the 30th of September, at Walton In- ferior, was fined 55., including costs. ALLOWING HEIFERS TO STRAY.—John Houghton was charged with allowing two heifers to stray at Little Leigh, on the 22nd of August, and fined 2s. and costs. KEEPING CHILDREN FROM SCHOOL.—Mr. De Prez, school attendance officer for the Runcorn Board of Guardians, prosecuted in the following cases :—Oa the case of Win. Henry Owen being heard, the Chairman asked Mr. De Prez whether all the schools in his district were free. Mr. De Prez replied that they were all free except at Stock- ton Heath, where the fees were ld. and 1-o.—The mag- istrates' clerk observed that if the parents could not afford to pay,the Guardians must still pay school fees.— The Chairman said now that education was free the Bench meant to enforce the law, and would be much more severe than formerli7.—The defendant was fined 7s. 6d.—James Mills, ss. -John Miller, Stretton, 10s. James Wilkinson, 2s. 6d. DnuNx.—John Johnson was charged with being drunk at Grappenhall, on the 12th of Sept.,and also with being drunk at Daresbury Court, on the 29th of that month. He had appeared in the box charged with the former offence, and being drunk, his case was adjourned, and he was now Charged. with the second offence in addition. He was fined the costs in the first case, and in the second fined IN.—Michael McLoughlin,' drunk on September, 20th at Little Leigh, fined as. ed. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.—EIIen Bower was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of her husband. Thomas Bower, of the Bridge Inn, Little Leigh, on the 17th of September.—P.C. Richardson deposed to finding the defendant drunk and unable to stand. She fell against the wall. She had been brought up five times before.—Annie Britland, servant at the Inn, for the de- fence said her mistress was quite sober on the occasion, and, during six months witness had been at the inn she had never seen the defendant worse for liquor.—The de- fendant denied that she was drunk.—The Chairman said if the defendant was hot ashamed of herself, they felt ashamed for her, to be brought up so often on such a frighful charge.—She was fined 10s., including costs. ASSAULT UPON AN OLD WOMAN.—AN EXTRAORDINARY CASE.—Samuel Buckley, lab.ourer,_ aged 23, and unmar- ried, son of Thomas Buckley, labourer,was charged with assaulting Sarah Barber, aged 84 years, at Antrobus, on the 10th of October. Mr. Browne appeared for the de- fence. The complainant stated that the defendant came into her house, put his arm round her, and made im- moral advances to her, offering her a shilling. Several witnesses were called on both sides, and Mr. Browne asked the Bench to believe that the case was one of de- lusion on the part of the complainant, remarking that such cases had occurred. The Bench consulted privately for about five minutes, and convicted the defendant. The Chairman said out of regard for the defendant's evi- dently decent father, and his own previous good charac- ter, they sentenced him only to pay the penalty of 503. and costs, and hoped this would be sufficient warning in the future. Funious DRIVING.—Thomas Kirkham,for furious driv- ing, at Stretton, on the 21st of August, was fined 10s. in- cluding costs.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT, On Tuesday morning, as a man was going to work on the canal near Runcorn, he met with a serious accident. He noticed an engine approaching him on the line, and in getting out of its way he stepped bn to another line, and was knocked down by a second engine. • He was removed to the hospital at Latchford at onae, Where it was found that his head was badly injured.
MITIPER AND MUTILATION IN BERLIN.

A shocking murder of the Jack-the-Rippor type was committed on Saturday night, says a Reuter's telegram, in a densely populated south-eastern quarter of Berlin, Where an unfortunate was found dead in her lodgings; The murderer had twice stabbed his victim, and after death atrociously mutilated the body. A man named Ernst Schulze, a commercial clerk, has been arrested on suspicion of having murdered the woman Nitsche. Several of the murdered woman's female associates iPentify Schulze as a man who was with Nitiche during the evening. The excitement amongst the women of the locality is intense.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.

hostilities right to the Rangers' line, where Jones and Radcliffe showed their -dexterity by a fine relief. Teare effected a grand save in his own quarters, and it was left to Heesom to clear by a screw kick. Both sets of backs then demonstrated their kicking powers, and after some scrambling play Bailey, Rowlands, Molyneaux,and Lawless rushed the game to the home 25: This enabled Warrington to look dangerous, but the style of play adopted by the visitors was quite irritating, and ulti- mately Lally passed to Heesom, whose drop at goal went yards wide. The drop-out was of little use to the • home side' for some loose work by Hampson, Teare, Rowlands, and Ikflolyneaux found the Rangers pressed, until a dribble by Higginbottom and Haslam transferred the scene of warfare to the Warrington 25. Warrington were play- ing in anything but good style, and the slip-shod attempts at anything like combination was most disheartening. Eventually a smart piece of play by Webster gained a lot of ground, Mather and Webster supplementing this by passing. Although Warrington should have scored re- peatedly, the miserable farces at packing exhibited by them and the indiscriminate mixing up of the combatants were absurd, and ultimately the monotony of this sort of football was relieved by the homesters conceding a minor. Manchester had to pay the penalty of too much zeal in the drop-out, but Radcliffe, getting a clear field, ran to • midway until stopped by Hamblett. After Flainpson, Russell, Lawless, and Knowles had been conspicuous, the Rangers returned to the attack, but their stay was only temporary, as Knowles, Barnes, Molyneaux, and Teare headed a rush well into the home lines. Russell then gave Webster a chance, but he was safely held, and half-time arrived with Warrington one goal to nothing. The home team resumed the game, and after Potts had returned, it looked as if Warrington had improved by the manner in which they now went about their work. Mather threw to Lally, who quickly made tracks for the goal posts, and Heesom, directly after getting the ball, punted grandly, and Birk's kick being charged, Teare secured a try. Soon afterwards Mather handed the ball to Heesom, and the latter, running well into the home quarters, passed sp!endidly to Lawless,but the expectant pass was not forthcoming and the rare chance was thrown away, a minor following shortly after this. Nothing of any note was afterwards obtained, and a miserable dis- play of football ended in a win for Warrington by 1-1-5 to 0-0-1. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. WIGAN Sr. JOSEPH'S IST. These teams met on the ground of the former on Satur- day, and the game resulted in an easy win for the home team. The visitors started operations, and the first half of the game was pretty evenly contested,no points being scored. Upon turning round, however, the Rangers quickly showed their superiority, and tries were secured by Loncrshaw, Hall, Ashton, and Hinchcliffe (2). The latter also dropped a smart goal, and the game finally ended—Rangers 1 goal, 5 tries, 3j minors, to nil. WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S V. ST. PAUL'S JUNIORS.—This match was played on the ground of the former. The visitors won the toss. Woods kicked off for the homes- ters, who at once pressed, Sanders scoring, Crosskill failing at goal. After the drop out the play was even up to half-time, the score being—St. Mary's, one try ; Juniors, nil. On changing ends, the home team, by good forward play, took the ball into the Juniors' 25. where Carey, from a scrimmage, passed to Threadgold, who ran round his opponents and scored a try, the kick at goat failiag. The Juniors again dropped out, but the ball was soon returned, and after some loose play Long- more scored, Helsby kicking a goal. Final result :—St. Mary's, 1 goal, 2 tries; St. Paul's Juniors, nil.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

* * Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrin,gton, not later than ten o'elock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY

PEMBERTON v. WIDNES ST. MART'S.—Played at Peril berton on Saturday. Final result: • Pemberton, 1 goal,' 2 tries, 4 minors ; Widnes St. Mary's, nil. FRODSHAM 2ND T. HELSBY.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday. A very pleasant game ended in a win for the home team by 2 goals, 2 minors, to Helsby 1 goal, 1 try. WIDNES ATHLETIC 17. WARRINGTON RaNGERs.-LPlayed at Widnes, and resulted. in a win for the Athletics by .6 points to nil. It is only. fair to add, however, that the visitors were heavily handicapped by playing 13 men throughout the game. RriNCORN A. v. WATERl.oo.—Played at Runcorn on Saturday. The game was very fast. The home team soon pressed the Waterloo full back, who failed to get the ball, Evans scoring. Resuming, Waterloo were kept in their half. After , desultory play, Lewis and Scholefield put in some good work for Waterloo, and Lewis landed under the home posts, Scholefield kicking a goal. Restarting Runcorn went right up to the Waterloo quarter, J. Faulkner passing out to Antrobus, and the latter scored a try, the same player kicking a goal. Score at half-time :—Runcorn 1 goal, 1 try; Waterloo 1 try: After the, interval, the hetne team soon pressed, Gayter scorihg- near the touch. Play then ruled even for a time, until a rush by the home forwards enabled Evans to pick up and score under the posts, Antrobus kicking a goal. Stubbs then scored,and in restarting, Jump got off and scored for Waterloo. Final score :—Runcorn, 2 goals, 3 tries; Waterloo, 1 goal, I try.

div.head: WIDNES y. CRONIPTON.
div.p: WIDNES y. CRONIPTON.

At Widnes on Saturday Plumpton was again Gn the field, and a good addition ho made. Peters played splendidly the whole of the time, both as regarded neat passing and fine running, no less than three tries being scored by him. Plumpton and Johnson also added to the result by a try each. The visitors, winning the toss, kicked off with'the sun shining in their faces, and before play had been commenced two minutes the ball was rushed to the Crompton line, and a try scored by Plumpton, which Brennan failed to improve. After several scrimmages and exciting play, Peters landed it safely over the line. Brennan kicked .a goal ; though the ball struck the 'post, it went over the bar. The referee, however, disputed the major point, although it was undoubtedly a fair goal. The ball was still kept in the visitors' quarter and Johnson next secured a try, Plump- ton failing at goal. The whistle now blew for half time, the score being—Widnes three tries, visitors nil. On play being resumed, the visitors seemed to brighten up, but they could not resist the fine passing and running of the home team. Scrimmaging took place near the visitors' line, Plumpton picked up and passed to Brennan and Brennan to Peters, who landed the ball 'once more over the line, amidst loud cheers. Again the attempt at goal was unsuccessful. In a short time Peters scored again. Play was centred in mid-field, when the whistle blew with the final score :—Widnes, 5 tries ; Crompton

nil. OLD EDWARDIANS T. RuNcoaN.—This match was played at the County Ground, Edgbasion, Birmingham, in the presence of about a thousand spectators. The Old Boys were strongly represented, but the visitors were vrithout Faulkner and Crompton, whose places were taken by reserve team men. A capital game was witnessed; but at the outset the visitors were a little the stronger side, and after keeping the ball well in the home teams territory, Pendlebury secured a try as the result of a fine run. Houghton made a capital attempt to convert, but the kick was from a very difficult posi- tion, and he was unable to place the ball accurately. , From this point the play of the home,team showed a marked improvement, and Auster, Badger, and Charles were conspicuous with some very pretty passing. Just before the interval: Anster passed the ball nicely td Badger, who was enabled to score a beautiful try, which Adams had little difficulty in converting into a 1 goal. At half-time the Edwardians led by five points to ' two. On recommencing, the Old Boys continued to have slightly the best of the play, but were unable to break down the sturdy defence of the visitors. The latter at length bore back the Opposition, and Robin- son secured a splendid try, which Houghton improved, and thus placed . the visitors ahead. This reverse stimulated the Old Boys to renewed efforts, but, try as hard as they could, they were unable to score ; whilst just before thefinish Abrams obtained a third try, but It was in such a difficult position that Houghton was unable to turn it to any greater advantage. The Run- corn men thus won by 1 goal and 2 tries (9 points) to goal (5 points). WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

The first match of this annual engagement took place at Wilderspool,on Saturday. The Rangers have never beaten the Warringtonians, but still, for all that, they are favourites with Warrington spectators„ their opeft play having gained for them a host of admirer.. To enter into details of both clubs would be stale news z.• suffice it to say that the Rangers have only been credited with one victory this season. The Manchester team came one short, but a capital substitute was found in Davies, captain of the " A "team. Warrington played as originally selected, and Nevins kickedoff towardsthe pavilion goal. A mull by Okell almost had a. disastrous result, but Sabin was handy, and a capital run found play at centre before Barnes. stopped his career. Taking advantage of loose play by Warrington, who were again slow in commencing, Par- lane made his mark from a return by Boscow. Sharp rushing by Comman, Pollard, and Pearson took play on the Warrington line, and the homesters now realizingthe honest intentions of their rivals, packed somewhat bet- ter ;and individual dribbles and rushes, led by Thornley, Berry, and Lawless, pressed the Rangers back to their lines. Bate made off, and his kick was well returned by Grange; but Boscow was safe as ever, and Warrington still attacked. Evans proved too much for Sabin when the latter had a fine chance, but Lawless ought certainly to have romped over, after some passing between Bate, Antrobus, and Evans. Okell got the oval away. only to, find Holmes, Ashton, Fair Turner, and Donohue at the I Rangers' goal again and although Sabin got clear on one occasion, Barnes tackled him finely before he could cross the half-way line. Bate and Okell exchanged kicks, and Evans, being the last recipient, was promptly.tackled by Parlane before he could get into his stride. A fine pass- ing movement by Antrobiis, Bate, and Evans was neutralised by Grange and Okell, and from a catch Evans injudiciously kicked the oval dead. Following this mile a long pass from Evans to Barnes, the latter promptly throwing to Lawless, but the chance was mulled, and, Grange kicking well, the Rangers breathed more freely. Their hopes were, however, 'doomed to disappointment, for no sooner had the relief been effected than Warrington were at their old game again, and Bate securing from a pack wriggled through, gaining a line try. Nevins was called up, for the place, and, niuch to the surprise of the home enthusiasts, kicked a fine goal. A faint reply to the kick off gave the Rangers a sight of the home goal, but a 'couple of movements, in which Bate was the chief operator, saw Pollard mulling, a like ill luck attending Turner, when the, latter endeavoured to pass. Grange was applauded for a fine run,but Warrington certainly missed a splendid opportunity when Evans in relieving kicked to Okell. A sharp follow up baffled the Rangers' custodian, but in their eagerness that all should partcipate in the score, the chance was thrown away, and Haselham saved. It was now the Rangers' turn to have a look In, for Ent- wistle, dribbling single-handed through the opposing backs, finally beat Boscow in (he race over the line, giv- ing Haselham the opportunity of placing the sides equal, which he did with a smart kick. Tlika evidently livened Warrington up, for on the restart a- run and kick by Barnes was seconded by Bate, and eventually Lawless registered the second minor. Bate next dropped at goal; the oval falling short by about a •yard. Donohne was next prominent in an effort near the line, but..combina- don had apparently been ignored by the Warringtonia.ns now, chances being several times missed near the line. A fine cross dribbling movement, initiated by Jolley,and taken up by Nevins, Thornley, and Berry, was followed by a similar one on the part of Bate, Barnes. and Law- less, but Parlane luckily ran the oval out, and half-time • was sounded with the score as Warrington 1-0-3, Ran- gers 1-0-0. On resuming, Jolley and Turner were pro- minent, but a long monotonous spell of uninteresting play followed. In fact, the game had a tendency to be- coming wearying to the most patient, but eventually a rousing cheer was accorded the Rangers for a fine pass- ing display, Entwistle being pushed into touch a yard from the line. Play in this half had gone fully 25 minutes before Warrington showed anything like their proper form, and the home supporters, calling for an effort, had their wishes gratified. A sharp rush headed by Ashton, found the game at the Rangers' end,and Bate passing across to Evans. The latter threw to Barnes, who preferred having a shot at goal, with a successful result. With four points to the good, Warrington kept up the attack, but chances from a forward rush and passing movement in the last minute were missed. Final result, . Warrington 2-0-4 (nine points) ; Manchester Rangers 1-0-0 (five points). Teams :—Warrington, J. Boscow, back ; T. Barnes, J. W. Evans, and P. R. Lawless; three-quarters ; James T. Bate and W. Antrobus, half-backs; H. Ashton. Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Berry, W. Nevins, W. Bandies, T. Donohue, J. 'Holmes, and J. T. .Thornley, forwards. Rangers:. Okell, back; Sabin, Grange, and Pollard, three-quarters; Parlane and Entwistle, half-backs; Haselham, ,Comman, Ashton, Reece, Westbrook, Pear- son, R. Hariablett, H. Hamblett, and T. Davies. Refereee, Mr. Williamson, Salford. WARRINGTON LV. MANCHESTER RANGEES.—At Rus- holme. It was considerably past the 'advertised time when Heesom, for Warrington, started the combat, and the visiting team were quickly initiating an attack. A dribble saved any further invasion, but,not to be denied, a screw scrimmage, headed by Knowles, Bailey, Teare, and Barnes, carried .the leather, over the line, Russell fiecuring a try, from yi,1444 *tsp. japded . a goal. ,A clever movement by tames, Heesnm, and Webster took

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FLOODS IN FRANCE.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FLOODS IN FRANCE.
GREAT LCSS OF LIFE.

PARIS, SUltDAY.—Further accounts of ravages caused by the floods in the South state that at Limoux the swollen waters of the Ande undermined several buildings, which to-day collapsed, twenty of the inmates being killed. Nine persons are still buried beneath the ruins. The bridge at Limoux has also been carried away, and the crops in the neighbourhood are completely destroyed. The railway line between Cette and Torthon has been cut, and the traffic at Size is interrupted, except on the line to Bordeaux. A telegram from Perpignan states that the rivers Agly and Roboul have both overflowed, and are causing great damage, several small houses on the banks of the Agly having been swept away.
THE STIPENDIARY -MAGISTRATE QUES- TION AT WARRINGTON.
REPORT OF THE TOWN CERIi.

The following report of the Town Clerk to the General Purposes Committee on the question of appointing a stipendiary magistrate for Warrington came before the Town Council, on Tuesday :—Pur- suant to the instructions of the Council of the 2nd of June last, I beg to submit the following particu- lars of the appointment and emoluments of stipen- diary magistrates at present holding office. The total number of stipendiary magistrates appointed is 19'..

LIST OF SMIPIINDIAIIT MAGISTRATES APPOINTED , UNDER THE MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS ACT. Population. Date of Place. 1891. Appointment. Salary. Birminghana 429,171 ... 1888 ... £l,OOO Brighton Ceirdiff Kingston-on-Hull Leeds. 367,506 ... 1869 ... 1,250 Liverpool 517,951 ... 1860 ... 1,000 Manchester Merthyr Tydvil Middlesbrough Sheffield Swansea LIST O,F STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATES APPOINTED UNDER
LOCAL ACTS. Birkenhead Bradford 216,361 ... 1889 ... 1;000 Chatham and Sheerness Manchester County Division — ... 1885 ... 1,200 Pontypridd Salford Borough _ .

Staffordshire, -Potteries, Stoke-on-Trent West Ham 204,902 1887 ... 1,000 Wolverhampton The Municipal Corporations Act provides that if the Council desire the appointment of a stipendiary magis- trate, they may present a petition to the Secretary of State, whereupon the Queen may appoint a barrister of seven years' standing, at a yearly salary not exceeding that mentioned in the petition. A stipendiary is by virtue of his office a justice of the peace for the borough, and he i empowered by the Licensing Act, 1872, to act as one of the licensing justices. A stipendary can act alone where two other magistrates are required. I wish to point out that the lowest salary paid to a stipendiary is £7OO per annum, this being the sum paid at Ponty- pridd and the joint districts of Chatham and Sheerness, and in each of which places the population is much be- low that of Warrington. That in no case has a stipen- diary magistrate been appointed under the Municipal Corporations Act to act for more than one borough, and the only two cases in which. such an appointment has been made have been under Local Acts. There is con- siderable doubt as to the power of the Home Secretary Ito appoint a stipendiary for more than one borough, and having regard to the salaries paid in other places. I doubt very much an appointment being approved at a salary less than £7OO per annum. Beyond the amount of the salary paid to the stipendiary, I know of no other ex- penses incidental to the office.
GRAVE CHARGE AriAINST A WIDNES
YOUNG Af&N.

A young man named John Rylance, 19 was brought before Mr. Deacon, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, to answer to a charge of having at- tempted to procure abortion by administering several doses of a drug to Louisa Hutchinson, a young woman whose home isat Ditton. Mr. Know- les, who defended, suggested that the case should be heard in private, as it was one that should not be advertised.—Mr. Deacon said he did not care to hold a private inquiry but by his instructions all young persons were ordered from the Court.—From the statement of the prosecutrix who is 19 years of age it appeared that she commenced to keep com- pany with the prisoner in January last and from that tim,e he had frequently taken her from the theatre at night to her home at Dittou. In conse- quence of what she told him in July last, he pro- cured some stuff for her to take. At first she refused to take it, but he persisted in her doing so. He then poured some of the liquid into her mouth, but afterwards she spat it out into her handkerchief. He continued to administer the doses each time he met her, but on each occaf ion she spat the liquid into her handkerchief. At last he gave her three bottles containing some liquid in order that she might take the doses at home and save the trouble of meeting him. She did not drink the contents, however, but placed the bottles in a box and in the course of a few days showed them to her stepfather, George James. On the 13th inst., she went with her father to the Police Station, at Widnes, where the bottles were handed to P.C. Thompson who sealed them in their presence. Subsequently they were sent on to Mr. Edward Davies analytical chemist at the Royal Institution, Liverpool, who described the contents to the magistrate. On the 21st inst. the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Thompson and in answer to the charge, said he had expected some proceedings to be taken.—Mr. Knowles having made a speech on the prosecuter's behalf, the prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial, bail being allowed.

RUNCORN PUBLICANS AND MR. BRUNNER, M.P. A deputation from the Runcorn Licensed Victual- lers' Protection and Benevolent Association have presented the following memorial to Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. for the North wick Division :—" We appear as a deputation from the licensed victuallers of Runcorn and its neighbourhood, appointed by their association, and we desire to make a few ob- seivations on the liquor trade, with the control of which you have recently identified yourself. The Licensed Victuallers' Association has been forced in- to existence by the aggressive action of the extreme teetotal party. It is non-political in its. character, and has for its object the protection of the trade, and not the encouragement and success, of those whose illegal conduct has brought them into con- flict with the authority. At the outset,we emphatic-- ally state we have no sympathy with intemper- ance, and look upon a drunken person as our ' greatest enemy. If we understand direct veto aright, it gives the inhabitants the power of determining by a given majority of votes the number of licensed house-s, if any, that shall exist in theirdistrict. It will be observed this regulates the sale as opposed to the consumption of intoxicants in any district, so that persons who are rich enough to keep a wine cellar will not be affected by the direct veto, but the minority of a district who are poor, however moderate in the consumption of intoxi- cants,will have their cellar, which is the public-house, closed against them; Te be just, therefore, the consurnp- time as well as the sale of intoxicants should be affected by the direct veto. If some scheme could be adopted that would limit the number of licensed houses, and those suffering from loss of property and occupation be. compensated, it would be more equitable, and less liable to alienate those who desire the reduction of public houses but will not be a party to confiscation. With re-- ference 'to compensation, we would briefly refer to the I change in the interpretation of the law on the subject et I magisterial power which, has taken place during: ,t1:)e last two or three years, and the amount of capital sunk before that time, to the unanimous opinion, in favour of full compensation, as expressed by Mr. W. E. Gladstone and all other leading politicians, and to the , fact that the magistrates who, in the first instance, granted licenses, had co-ordinate power with those who I now have to deal with them,. We also desire to point out that legislation never intended that beerhouses, sup- I posed to be the greater evil,, are, during good conduct,. I practically out of the control of the magistrates, whilst fully-licensed houses, tho lesser evil, are not placed on the same basis; and finally the House of Commons I affirmed the principle of compensation (luring the last session. We desire to statethat no one, we believe, con- siders Sunday closing entirely satisfactory, as we are more or less in ignorance et its effects, as it is practic- I ally outside police supervision. Altering the hours of opening, say from 12.30 p.m, to 2 p.m., and from 8 :to 10 p.m.., would give all an opportunity to attend religi- ous services, would avoid bogus clubs, and drinking in private houses. The relation between the owner and' ' occupier of the licensed premises might be left to regu- I late itself if the fine was attached tsi the premises instead of the occupier. In this case a change of occupier would' Ibeof no advantage to the owner. This would give the persons interested means of getting rid of a drunken or careless tenant, and so be an, advantage to the cause of temperance. Se far as Runcorn is concerned, the ag- gressive and ill-considered conduct of some of the tem- perance party resulted in the fact that in the last local election the temperance vote did not equal one-half of: the votes given in favour of persons interested in the liquor trade. We have submitted the above facts and considerations to you, believing that your sense of jus- tice will give them the attention they deserve." :Mr. Brunner has irtimatect his intention to reply in full by letter.

CO-OPERA.TIVE CONFERENCE AT WARRINGTON. A conference of the Executive of the Cheshire and North Wales District Co-operative Association' and delegates from societies in Cheshire and North Wales and other gentlemen favourably disposed to co-operation, was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st,, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. T. Birchall presided.. The Chairman said on behalf of the Warrington Society,lie had great pleasure in giving the delegates a very hearty welcome. These meet- ings, which were held ci:parterly, were for the pur- pose of taking counsel to see how best they might spread the principles of co-operation, which they had so much at heart. It might be said they were very persistent in proclaiming their principles, but they were so because they believed in their power to bless their fellow-men,and to promote peace and, happiness and contentment among them. There- fore they had to be continually giving ,line upon line and precept upon precept upon this old subject of co-operation. When they saw the great bles- sing. it had been ,in this country, they were en- couraged to try.to extend its blessings to districts where it was at present unknown. . There.was.a. tendency on the part of societies, as well as-indi- viduals, to be somewhat selfish in these matters.. Now, no organisauion no more than any individual, could become solely devoted to self-interest,, and ignore the condition ei'.'those less fortunate,without deteriorating verY seriously. It was very much like members of religious societies: :their whole thought seemed to be to save their own miserable souls, but they did not care for anybody else'*. A man that cared unselfishly for others- need, not trouble very much about his own individual wel- fare, so far as the next world, was con- cerned.. There were co-operators who were such simply. because they made so much dividend. That was a very desirable and useful thing, the backbmeof their society, but those who were co-operators for dividend only failed to make co-operation that. humanising and elevating influence that it could and ought to be made. The Chairman mentioned that at the last quarterly meet- ing there had been discussed the desirability of paying towards scholarships in technical schools, to induce their members to make the most of their education, and thus rise in the world in all directions. The Chairman also referred to the speeches of Mr. Gladstone-and Lord Rose- bery on co-operation, as proof that the subject was at- tracting attention in the highest quarters. These men he said who had been trying all their lives to ameliorate the condition of mankind were delighted to find that the co-operators had found a plan by which' they could help men to help themselves, the best of all•possible ways to help them. Co-operation did not require governments and special legislative measures to help them to help each other ; their motto was all for each and each for all. (Applause.)—The Secretary, Mr. R Wright, of Garston, read the minutes of the last conference and the Execu- tive Committees report of the Warrington conference held in October. These were adopted by the meeting.— The Chairman then read a lengthy printed paper, read by Mr. Sydney Webb, L.L. 8., of London, at the congress held at Lincoln at Whitsuntide, 1891, on "The best method of Winging co-operation within the reach of the poorest of the population." The paper in the commence- ment, 1,3 t,stB stores,ar dthat there were a million co-operators, and 12 millions capital, but pointed out that there were "still sad blanks on the co- operative map, the rural districts and the south of England being wall nigh barren of co-operative activity. Those among the wage earners who needed co-opera- tion least had got it the most, and those who needed it most availed themselves of it least. This was the co-operators' side of the great'social problem. How could they best render General Booth's scheme unnecessarry by bringingthe " submerged tenth " into their own ranks ? But for the co-operators- there was not alone a "sub- merged tenth" to struggle with,but at lea.st a submerged five-sixths. A large part of these might be reached by an increase in propagandist activity. Trade unions, working-men's clubs, local benefit societies,and mothers! meetings,might be utilised for this purpose,and churches and chapels were not made half enough uE,e of for that object. Every co-operative society should have a stand- ing propaganda committee. Why should not some notice of co-operation be inserted in the school reading books ?' Lectures were also recommended, as another means, and the use of a co-operative travelling van to traverse the rural districts. The making of co-opsra,tive stores more socially attractive was advocated. It seemed time, said the author, that the co-operative societies began to take their rightful part in municipal and Par- liamentary elections.—Mr. T. Charles, of Brymbo,Wrex- ham, chairman of the executive comreittee, opened the discussion. Co-operation had not spread in Wales because the gospel of co-operationhad not been brought there.— Mr. H. J. Watson, of Farnworth, member of the Central Co-operative Board ,also spoke,after which Mr. Crowt her made seine remarks. He considered that co-operative stores would derive, much benefit if they would employ more shopmen so that custorners.could be supplied more promptly. Mr. Thomas Kelly, St. Helens, proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. X. Boyle, Run- corn, seconded.—The Secretary supported the motion, I as also did Mr. Howarth, of the Co-operative Insurance Society, Manchester. The latter descanted on the pauperism of thb country, which he said cost four millions per annum more than the capital of co-opera- tion amounted to; and urged that it was the duty of co-operators to work hard to alter this state of things. —Mr. Wilson,president ofone of the Liverpool societies, supported the propositin. He thought there was not much good to be done in the way of advancing co- operation in the present generation : they must get hold of the children and train them up to it. He hoped to see some co-operative men in the Town Council of War- rington.—After scale further remarks by Mr, Watson and a gentleman from Leicestershire, the vote of thanks to the Chairman, was carried and responded to by him. The question off fixing date and place for the next con- ference stood over. Tea was provided on the premises for the delegates after the meeting by the Warrington Co-operative Society.

THE •SSHOOKING DEATH OF A WARINGTON MAN.
INQUEST AND BURIAL..

The inquest on the body of Albert George, aged 25, whose parents live in Wellfielthst., unkey Bridges, a guard in the employ of the Mersey Rail- way Company, and whose body was found on Thursday evening last, in the tunnel between Hamilton-square and James-et: Stations, was held on Saturday, at the Queen's Hotel, Park-entrance, , Birkenhead, before Mr. H. Churton, the Birkenhead ' coroner. Mr. Maples represented the Mersey Rail- way Company, and Mr. R. B. Moore appeared on behalf of the widow of the deceased. Mr. Ma,pies said he appeared on behalf of the Mersey Railway Company, to give the Coroaerall the assistance he could in the inquiry, and at the same time to give espression to the feeling of great grief on the part of-the board of directors and the superior. °Ricers of the Cbm- pany that this accident should havehappened. The de- ceased was, in his station, as good's man as was in the Company's service.—The first witness called was Fra.n.lt Glass,. a ticket collector stationed at the Elamilton-squace Statien who said the deceased was guard on the train friatn.Rt;ck Ferry to Li verpool,which arrived in Hamilton- square-Station at 6.53 p.m. The train, which consisted of eight coaches and an engine, remained at the plat- fcirm..abeut half a minute, the time allowed.- Witness ' saw the deceased, and gave him the signal to start the train,, but had no conversation with him ;,and then saw , him get into the van, the door of which ebsed from the- inside. A telephonic message was sent from James-st. that the-deceased waS missing-on the arrival of the train there,. and witness, in company with several others, went down the tunnel in search of him. They found the deceased about 300 yards from Hamilton-square Station, ; lying inside the rails alive, but insensible: His skull was fractured...and both legs were cut clean off above the knee. Withess could not form any opinion how he left the van._ He could not fall out if 'both doors were pro- ' perly fastened. In answer to a juryman, witnesssaid ,that the guard's compartment was free froubpissengers. There wasa door on each side of the compartment, and deceased was found on the outside rail to Liverpool. It L'must have been the 'train from -Hamilton-square to Liverpool,, which followed four minutes • later, that passed over the deceased.—Mr. Maples, in answer to a question from the Coroner, said the actual space between the outer rail and the wall as :five feet.—A Juror re- marked that if the door of the van openedfrom the-in- side he cou4d not see how the door could fly open unlet3s- the deceased opened it himself.—Robert M'Cormick, signalman at James-st. Station, said he saw the train of whieh deceased was guard arrive at James-st., and, wishing to speak to the deceased, he went to the guard's - "van as soon as the train arrived. He found the door open and the guard missing. The door which-was open was not the folding door; there was a catch for the-open door, and the door was thrown back and the catch up. He could not give any opinion as to the cause of the ac- cident. All traffic was at once stopped until the tunnel was searched.—Mr. Maples remarked that it was possible that the door, not being properly fastened, might fly open,,and if the deceased was standing. writing, as he 'might have been, he might fall through the open door, but it was all conjecture.—The Coroner said ho-could not see-the utility of pursuing the inquiry further. They had no evidence to show how or by what means the de- -ceased had come by his deaf h.—The jury expressed their concurrence in this view, and returned a verdict of " Accidental death." _ _

Much regret at the sad death of George is expressed at Sknkey Bridges' Warrington, where the deceased. had lived nearly all his life. He , was secretary of the local Sunday school, and a member of the choir,, and was 'much respected in the locality. The funeral took place at Warrington Cemetery, on Mcinday, the. body •of the deceased having been 'brought froth -Birkenhead to his parents' .residence in Wellfield-st. Wreaths had been sent by the c,boir of the Sankey Bridges WeSleyan Chapel, and by the deceased's fellow workmen. The fitheral was largely attended, there being present a deputation of workmen from the Mersey Tunnel Railway. The Rev. J. Gunnell was the officiating minister.

Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable of Warrington, has. submitted his report to the Watch Committee.on the police establishment and state of crime in the , borough for the year ended 29th September. .Thisis. Mr. Hunt's 25th annual report. The sentences -upon these, of- -fenders were-1 eight years' penal servitude, I fire years' ditto, 1 eighteen tnonthe hard labour, 4.. twelve months' hard labour, 1 nine. months, I. eight mouths, 6 six months,and 3 three months.; 2 *ere acquitted,9.dis- charged for want of evidence, sSzc,, and 2 are pending trial.. The number of persons convicted for drunkenness is 667, last year 738, ecrease 61.; : for • assaults on police, 57; last year 23, increase 34 .; , cemmon assaults, '137, last year 102, ~increase 35;: breaches of the peace, 145, ;last year 190,, increase 36; Elementary Education Acts, 441,Jast year 347,', increa.se 94; Local Acts and 'loran& By-laws, 305,..1a5t year 276, increase 29; petty larceny,' 150, ,last year 122; increase 28; vagrancy, 86, last year 106, decrease 20. The total number of persons summarily , convicted is 2,385., last year 2,146, increase 239. Of these 254 were sent to gaol without the option of a fine; 7 children were sent to reformatories and 25 to industrial, schools, I.:46s6persons were fined, 28 children (boys) were whipped, 171 per- sons were ordered to find sureties, .31. soldiers were delivered to the Army and Navy, and 169; persons sub- jected to other punishments. The number of children at pre sent detained in industrial schools is 30,i and in refor- matories 11, total, 41; the parents of whom have paid for their part maintenance for the year the sum of £75 55., which has been remitted, As required,. to the Home .Office, London. , Eighty pedlars' certificates, and nine chimney sweepers' ditto, have been issued during the year. Five persons have been summoned for , keeping dogs without licenses, all being convicted and fined. Under the Rabies (Muzzling Of Dogs) Order, 1889, 100 dogs Were seized, and owners of- 209:reported, total 309 dogs; 58 being destroyed, 24,501 d, 174 given, up to owners on payment .of detention fee, 24 given up to owners who were simply. cautioned, and 6 escaped. Twelve owners ,of dogs were summoned, not having paid detention fee, 2 , being. dismissed, and 10 con- victed and fined in the.. sum of £2 13s. 6d. The owners and purchasers of dogs paid during the year the sum of £24 is. 6d. With regard to sudden vio- lent, or. unnatural deaths of persons which have been , reported to the p01ice,,59 inquests were held, 62 referred to theregistrar, and six certitied.by the medical gentle-, nien,,by consent of the Coroner;: total 127. Where in- quests were held the. .verdicts were—accidental, 37; natural causes, 10; suicide during temporary insanity, 3; excessive drinking (chronic alcoholism), 3; follnd drowned, 2; stillborn, 1 ; shock: to system through im- mersion, 1.; and open verdicts,. a. Nine fires were re- ported as having taken placein the borough, the dam- age amounting to • probably £550, and is covered by • insurance. There are 15. cab. and hackney c4rriage owners, and 75 cab , and omnibus drivers, 6 dealers in gunpowder,and aldealersin small fireworks; 12 marine store dealers, and 21_ common lodging-houses in the borough ; the average number of tramps accommodated in these houses .monthly is 11,827, or over 380 per night. Lost children to the number of 56 were found, and restored to their parents, and 50 hcmes, cattle,. and sheep. found straying were pnt into .the pinfolni nail owned. One hundred and ninety houses, shops,, and warehouses were found unsecured by the police ,on duty at night, by reason of the occupieli not having 1 fastened doors or windows. • One hundrediand fifty-seven warrants were issued, and 139 exec4ted this year, against IES issued and 131 executed last year,.. The borough contains 85 public-houses, 48 beerhouses, and 7 off-licensed houses, total 209, being 1 .house to each 251 of the population,. which at census taken this year is 52,742, the number of houses being 94631, acreage 2,004, rateable value £157,916. The Borough Boundary Extension Scheme having come into operation on Oct. 30th, 1690, necessitated the increase of the force by four Men, to cover the. additional. beats create 3,. and the lengthening, of some of 'the original ones ; this was done in due course, arid the strength is now 52 .men, viz.., 1 chief constable, 4 inspectors, si.sergeants, and 4/ con- stables. The, variations in the force are—resigned, Ito go back to his trade ; 1 through ill-health, and 1 claimed his. resignation and pension after 31, years service disnasssed, 4 ; total, '7; In place of these 7 men were appointed, and 4 new men were placed on the strength through augmentation, from. 48,t0 52, all told. Leave of absence' to all ranks was 513-days; sick leave, 463 days:: hurt upon duty, 21 days. The value of the Police Superannuation Fand on March, 25th, 1891, was £7,aa is. lid.; a charge of 19a. 4th per week is all that is against it at present. The cost of the police establish- ment for 1891 amounted to £4,684 Os. 2d., as against £4,344 ss. 4cl. in 1390. St. John ambulance class Number holding certificates. 3he success of the League system in the Association game is demonstrated every Saturday. At the match at Blackburn between the. Rovers and Preston North End there were fully 10,000 spectators ;. at Bolton where the Wanderers were engaged with 13urnleyrthe attendance was returned at upwards of 8,000,. and the gates at the other five Lrague fixtures were equally satisfactory. The guarantee that the best possible teams. wind° duty largely adds to the interest. of the gameat as good foot- ball is always assured.

By their victory over Burnley. the-Bolton Wanderers are now credited with 14 points. It was a. tough battle throughout,. and the Turf Moor men. were practically beaten, by the Superior goalkeeping of Sutcliffe, who never naade a mistake. 'Hillman' though twice defeated, did remarkably well under the Burnley crossbar. Not many anticipated succese of the Forth, End at Ewond Park. Indeed the Rovers obtained their two goals early on, but they once more fell away and allowed their great rivals to vanquish them ny four to two. The Prestonians improved as the game proceeded, and were - vastly hatter than the cupholders in. the last twenty minutes,

Darwempaid the penalty of taking a very weak teem to Trent Bridge, where Notts- county ram away witti them to the tune Of five goals to nothing. Entwistle, one of the forwards, acted as g,oalkeeper,. and five of the , -best men were absentees. Thi&accounts• for the irxliffer- ant display. Sam Thompph joined Accrihgton for the first thne,.and was largely inetruiciental7m defeating Wolverhampton Wanderers, after a hard game, by three goals to two. Stoke were surprised at the form shown by Aston Villa who managed to- come through sacceits- fully by a goal only. The contest took place on the Stoke ground. Bunderland received &visit from West 13romwiCh 'Albion,and defeated Clem for the second time
in. eight days. The superiority, of the; Wearsiders is ezfily peen by the fact that in the two engagements they have totalled nine goals to two.

With, regard to the more nota,We• Rugty matches of Saturda,y,. Bradford, as was to be expected,. defeated Manchester O':C.'at Whalley.Rangs;:but, as was not to be expected, Stoughton beat Swinton on their own ground, and Broughton Rangers upset Salford. Swinton and Balford,:the quondam " crack " team, are surely on the down grade. Oldham were again victorious, defeating Carlisle ;; Wigan had the best of Brighouse- Rangers ; St. lii3lens went down before Newpprt, but Runcorn brought off: asubstantial win against the,old Edwardians.

When we find no fewer than afteea players brought up,for rough play at one sitting of the Yorkshire Rugby Union it is clear that football is-not always a harmless pastime as carried on in the neighbouring county. The conduct of some of these offenders was considered to be 'se outrageously bad that they were- suspended sine die. There was mlre rough play on Ssturday, three-men being ordered off the field at Holmfirth.

• The trial match between two-teams of the leading Rugby football players of• Lancashire took plaze on-Wed- nesday at Whalley Range. Ono side—the Probables-- •was mainly composed of the available county players of the last season, whilst. the other—the Possibles—was made up of the pick Of the team,,that played in the trial .game the previous week. The-ofterneon was-Rae, apd, a large number of spectators,was present. The sides were • pretty well balanced, though. the Probables were the stronger of the two; and won easily by fourteen points to tw. Among the Possibleswere again two Warrington players, J.T. Bate at half buala, and J. Jolley amongst - the forwards. Both again distinguished themselyes,Bate in particular, as he scored the-only try obtained by his . side. As a.result he has been, ehosen to Ilay for the 'county against Cambridz, University on Wednesday 'next, Jolley being put upon the-reserve.

At the Warrington,,Borotigh Magistrates' court,on , Monday morning, Mr.. Greenall, solicitor, said he appeared on behalf of Messrs. P. Walker and Sous„ , Limited, with reference to the application as to the Lion Hotel. The company wished to make very slight alterations to the hotel,. leaving at present the hotel proper ,as it stood. They wished - to alter the lower portion of the betel and open out- the present lower room used for ball purposes and make a permanent doorway, and close up. the archway. .which now led up, to the ballroom stairs, also open: out a door into the Ship yard, where at present) there was a large window. The Company had given notice of the alterations to the.. Chief Constable, And submitted their proposals -to ~ hi, and it was understood that, he had no objec- tions. Mr. Hunt said he had ,none. He did not know thatiit, would have any effect if he had. As. 4 to the door opening into the Ship yard tliat, yard was very much the acene of rows anC disturbances, Re would rather there had been , no more vaults in Bridge-street, particularly, open,- ing into Ship,Yard. ..At the- same time he didi I not know Cut,. he could offer-any objection.—Mite.
