I •• port In ,up to the Corporation.—The Mayor,:: We shalt be very pleased if von give us the other.portion too-.-Alderman Sutton endorsed this remark:,--Mr. Greenall promised to lay their statements before the Companzr, and he thought they would giive the 1 matter their serious consideration. div.head: PAPA TOPAZ
div.p: PAPA TOPAZ

BY HENRY AVERY. "'Why do we call him 'papa ? " said Hoolihan to me. "Because long, long ago, when this train passed a certain crossing some fifty miles beyond • here, there was a little child with yellow hair and blue eyes. As we went whirling by she would wave a hand to our engineer and call out: 'Bye bye, -papa; bye bye.' The boys took it up after awhile, and ever since he has been known as 'Papa' Topaz." In 1876 the youngest engineer on one of the western roads which pierce the heart of the Rock- ies, was Gervais Topaz, or, as he was better known, "Papa" Topaz. He was a handsome, rosy-cheeked fellow, with muscle and nt-,rve and brain to make him popular, and a favoured employe. He had worked his way up to the post of engineer of No. 5, the fast express, from the bottom of the ladder, and no one begrudged him his good fortune. At twenty-five, possessed of a charming wife, a little child, who adored him, and a home whose comforts fringed life's circle with gold for his joy, "Papa" Topaz felt that his cup was full, and the sun of his happiness in the zenith forever. Day after day, and month after month, as his train swept through the village where he lived, he would look down from his cab window to his baby's face and carry away into the distance that tender , cry: "Bye bye, papa; bye-bye." "Am I not happy ? " he would say to himself. "There isn't a king on earth so happy as I." In his joy he would press the shining throttle and the great engine—straining every iron band to do his will—would leap to the beat of his heart. Several years passed, and the face of "Papa" Topaz had grown so rosy and bright that when, one day, a shadow rested upon it, every one noticed the fact. When it was there a second day his friends spoke of it. A week of its presence made them anxious, he had grown so silent and sad. Some one noticed, too, that at the old familiar crossing there no longer stood a little child. Sparks, the fireman of No. 5, told the conductor that when they passed the spot "Papa" Topaz turned his head <away and tears ran down his face. "Is the youngster sick V' asked Sparks of him, .one day. "Papa" only looked out of the window, and made no reply. But the trouble could not remain a mystery for all time. Some one heard this, and some one heard that, and the two were put together. "It is this," said Sparks, in a confidential tone, to a group. "There's a handsomer man than 'Papa' Topaz gone off with his wife, and the woman took the child with her. It beats all how mean a woman ean be when she starts out to ruin a man. Course, 'Papa' loved her, but he wouldn't have suffered so if she'd have left the girl behind. Who'd she ran away with ? A store chap with a soft tone and white hands. It takes a fool to catch a fool." Various words of sympathy reached the ears of "Papa" when his sorrow was understood, but he paid no attention to them. His face grew thin and white, and deep circles set his dark eyes. But he did not fail in his duty, and No. 5 came and went just as swiftly as in the days when a child's smile had sunshined the way of her tender en- gineer. The express was coming into the place where "Papa" had his home one day under a full head of steam, for she was behind time. She was nearly up by the old crossing, when Topaz, looking out of Ito window, saw standing there a little child, hands waving in the air, treble voice crying out the familiar farewell. With a leap he reversed, shut off, applied the air-brake, and with a jostle and bump No. 5 came to a dead stop. The passengers looked out, and the conductor ran ahead, but all there was to be seen was a dust-begrimed man by the way, sobbing and laughing over a little child, whose arms were about his neck. The delay was not long. "Papa" Topaz sought for no explanations as to how his child had come back. Perched on his seat she made the trip with him, and then he placed her in safe hands to be cared for. Something of the old sadness fled from him. While he still was reserved, the mist over his eyes faded, and a second manhood came back to his face. Every spare moment he gave to his little one. She grew out of babyhood to the years of a child, and when the gray had begun to tinge his hair, she was a young woman. The affection he lavished upon her was returned, and if she was his idol, he to her was the loving, cherished "Papa" Topaz of all time and eternity. The men on the road felt a proprietory interest In both of them. The mother had long since been forgotten by all but "Papa." He never spoke of her, and no one ever questioned. She had chosen her way, and the path did not run as theirs. The summer of 1887 was marked by many fatal railroad accidents, and " Papa " said, with a shiver, to Sparks, that he hoped their turn was a long ways off. The best of the engineers met with disaster in an unaccountable way, and in the crash of wrecks brave souls went heavenward from the post of duty. Sparks was more than usually attentive; "Papa studied every dangerous point. The days slipped along, and still no trouble for them. A Saturday came with the tracks crowded and delayed trains. No. 6, an hour behind time, was on the home stretch, with every driver doing its utmost. Her long shadow crossed the plains like a vision; her sparks died in the forests after she was miles away. The etho of her whistle in the valley was stiff ringing when she was out of sight and hearing. Up the grades she panted and beat the hot rails; down the grades she skimmed like a bird racing with the winds. Sparks was looking ahead; "Papa" Topaz had his eye on a distant curve. Now they were on it and around they swung—Crash 1 The instant of collision between two trains meet- ing at high speed is a contact of Titans. The combined forces of man and Nature meet and wrestle in deadly embrace. Steam escapes, rends the air with awful screeches; tears iron and steel apart; sprays over frail bodies, scalds and boils them into nothingness. Timber batters timber, and fire leaping over their barricade illumes the scene for the final tableaux of a terrible tragedy. Huge drivers fan the air, spinning in im- potency, as if turned by giant hands. There is an upheaving and overturning of all order; Chaos and Death come in their chariots. In the midst of this cataclysm are human beings, pigmies before the engines of destruction builded by their own hands. Strange that at such a moment the kingly nature of man is abased by the very elements that gave him a king's estate. In the shock of the collision " Papa " Topaz was thrown to the right, Sparks to the left. The latter never breathed again to tell the story of that wreck. Bruised, but not injured, Topaz gained his feet and started for the coaches to aid the wounded. Here and there he released a pinioned body. The groans and curses sickened him. He pushed through the dibris to where he saw the skirt of a woman's dress. Heavy timbers lay across it, but with patience he pushed them aside. She was lying face downward, only an occasional moan giving sign of life. At last he had her free, although he saw that death was near to her. Lift- ing her up and turning her oyqr, he looked down into the face of his wife. Thus, unconscious of his pres- ence, she died in hi fi arms.

A Swiss inventor has pefected a method of making artificial boards, and is advocating their use in building. They are made of a mixture of plaster of Paris and reeds, pressed into shape by hydraulic process. The material has the advantange of incombustibility and lightness, and will resist the warping action of atmospheric changes. PEorias: talk of liberty as if it meant the liberty of doing what ama it likes. The only liberty that a man, worthy the name of a man, ought to ask for, is to have all restrictions, inward and outward, removed, to prevent his doing what he ought. I call that man free who is master of hi,F; lower appetites —who is able to rule hitriseif.—F. IV". Robertson.

div.head: trtttrs to the attor.
div.p: trtttrs to the attor.
THE HOURS OF BAKERS.

Sir,—Permit me a short space in your valuable paper in reply to Mr. Forshaw's letter on "The Club Bakers of Warrington." In the first place I cannot call him a Christian, nor can he study his fellow-workmen, for, if he did, he would study the fourth commandment, where it states six days shalt thou labour, and rest on the seventh day, which Mr. Forshaw has certainly overlooked. Again, if Mr. Forshaw's mode ot working includes gett- ing part ef Monday's labour done on Sundays, to reduce Use hours of labour from 16 per day to 10 and 11, I must certainly say it is a poor mode that he has, and I hope that the law will punish him and all such like who make such breaches of the law.—Yours, &c., one who studies his
FELLOW-WORKMEN.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON. Sir,—lt was with feelings akin to disgust with which I read in your valuable paper of an account of the meeting kithe Old Conservative Club, and of the deputation that waited upon Sir Gilbert Greenall to ask him to again Contest the Borough at the next General Election. Now, air, I think it is an insult to the town and to the common sense of its working-men to again ask a man who has now close upon his 86th year, and has ceased to vote, or speak,or give an account of his stewardship,to contest the town. If the town is Conservative, let us have cne that can do the work that is required of him in the House of Commons and by his constituents. Surely there is such a one among the Tory party, say a White, a Sutton, or a Roberts.

And I notice the deputation told Sir Gilbert that the feelings of the borough towards him were not only friendly but affectionate. Now,' do not attempt to deny that Sir Gilbert is held in great esteem as a gentleman, but I cannot think there is much affection on the part of his party when they would again drag Sir Gilbert through the turmoil and excitement of another election, endan- gering his health and, may be, shortening his life, seeing that they know, or ought to know, that the last time he voted in the House of Commons he had to be taken in a Cab and in blankets to vote on the Publicans' Compen- aation Bill. Other bills have had to be totally disre- garded by him owing to his health. I think if his party had any esteem and affection for him they would allow Sir Gilbert to spend his last few days at Walton Hall in peace. But lam persuaded to think it is not him so much as the bag he has for which they have so strong an affection, or else that they are afraid to contest the borough by any other means than through a bung hole .or beer barrel.—Yours Warrington, 22nd Oct., 1891
IRONWORKER.
PRAYER AND PERVERSITY. As you may take a horse to the water, But cannot make him drink; So, you place reasons before a man, But cannot make him think.

Sir,—The reading of " Gnostic's " letter of 19th inst. convinces me that he is ignorant, shifty, and untruthful. As I dislike assertion without proof. I will produce mine. 1. As to his ignorance, natural or assumed : The evid- ence of this lies open and palpable in his opening para- graph, where he pretends to define Agnosticism as ignorance. Now.an Agnostic is one sufficiently advanced in knowledge to know that there are many things he does aot know, and so far is an Agnostic an ignoramus. The Gnostic on the other hand professes to know everything —from the existence of angels and how many of them can dance upon the point of a needle, up to the wants and wishes tastes and attributes of an Infinite Being. Pro- fessor Huxley may be styled an ignoramus in so far as he does not profess to know everything. On the other hand, " Gnostic," at the other end of the scale, may be justly regarded as one, inasmuch as he does profess to know the Unknowable.

His second paragraph justifies my epithet of untruth- ful. In it he says—" The question is not the logical . position of prayer, but the logical position of the laws of nature." Now, overlooking the fact that I am quite unable to grasp the meaning of the phrase I have italicised (is it purely scientific, by the way?) I reiterate any assertion, that the point at issue all along has been the unreasonableness of prayer for change of weather—the Prince of Wales, or indeed past praying for. As a proof I quote the letters, "Prayer for fair weather," by H. T. W., followed by one from me on "Meteorological supplication." Then Gnostic , favoured us with one on "The laws of Nature I and theism." Thus, the first deviation from the subject comes from himself. Indeed, it was never my intention to discuss "the logical position of the laws of nature," that being, like" Gnostic s " moditication of gravitation by the laws of chemistry," a thing existing only in his =unformed and too exuberant imagination. "Gnostic" does not display much of his "purely scientific" capacity for logical argument when he would erect a mere inci- dental reference into the position of the main argument, eny reference to the laws of nature being made solely with the object of enforcing my opiniun as to the folly of trying to change them by futile supplication. And then our friend sends up a wail of lamentation because I will not " discuss the question on purely scien- tific grounds." I have two good reasons for not follow- ing this red herring which" Gnostic" has "trailed across the scent." First, it is not the matter in hand; se- condly, because my experience of " Gnostic " does not warrant me in thinking "him capable of conducting, or even understanding, an argument of a purely scientific character. Take,as an example,his statement that" the law of gravitation is absolutely universal. Not so with

the laws of chemistry." Now, as one having Agnostic tendencies, I say that I do not know that the laws of chemistry are universal, much less am I prepared to as- sert that they are not so. But I have good inferential evidence as to the high probability of their being univer- sal. My own personal experience tells me these laws are in force in England, and I have had the same expe- rience in Canada and the States. I have good reason to think they obtain in all other parts of our planet, be- cause our text books of chemistry are in use there, and any change of property and re-action would soon be noted. So they apply to the whole earth. Now,spectum analysis proves the sun, fixed stars, &c., to be materially of like composition with the earth. Is then—" The same materials the same laws" an unreasonable inference? I think this disposes of two assumptions of "Gnostic's." I. That the 'taws of chemistry are not universal; and 11. His ability to "discuss the question on purely scienti- fic grounds." Let " Gnostic" leave pure science and give us the logic" deductive Gr. inductive" which warrants payer for atmospheric conditions ! Herein I am eat rely an Agnostic, and confess I cannot find any si ek .sar- rant ; let the " Gnostic " do this for us; if he dces not, surely it is because he cannot ! Meteorology is unfor- tunate in that it is passing through a phase of its history similar to that passed through by astronomy, when its phenomena were regarded as being the result of caprice rather than of law. Science now regards even the most apparently capricious phenomena of Meteorology as being as strictly the result of law as the occurrence of an eclipse. Yet who would think of pray- ?ng for the prevention of an eclipse ? And yet the one set of laws are just as likely to be set aside for us as the other. But, sir, prayer for such objects as this is likely to continue so long as it forms part of the stock in trade of the prayer-mongers. One of these has lately issued what he styles a " Call to Prayer." It is a two page leaflet tinted a washed-out green. Perhaps this may be delic- ately symbolical of its intended readers,who may be sup- posed to be similarly tinted. This precious document is characterised by two main features ; an utter absence of any reasoning and a plentiful abundance of hysterical fanaticism. Take one example," Persistent, believing, united prayer will bring upon us showers of blessings, nothing else will." It is almost past belief that any man could be got to pen such a manifest absurdity and evid- ent untruth. This Methodist muezzin finishes quite char- actically by a little tpyographical crescendo—Pray, Pray, PRAY The mind of man is surely a strange anomaly when such rubbish can find a place in it. Yours &c., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, October, 1891.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
THE STRUGGLE GROWS KEEN.

Both political parties recognise that the present municipal struggle is one of the most important which they have ever been engaged in in Warring- ton, having in view the fact that theresult may have considerable influence upon the Parliamentary con- test which is expected to take place next year. Both sides are, therefore, displaying great energy, and, as the phrase is, leaving no stone unturned to secure the return of their various candidates. Judging from the placards and handbills that have been issued it is obvious that the struggle has been getting keener each day during the past week, but it is satisfac- tory to know that, thus far, it has been conducted with fairly good temper. Public meetings have been held in a number of the wards, while in other wards the meetings have been confined to workers, the feeling being that the time would be quite as well spent in looking after doubtful votars. As will be seen from the detailed particulars which are given below,both the temperance party and the labour party have put questions to candidates— questions, which, without a single exception, have been answered in the affirmative by the Liberal can- didates. The canvassing on both sides may now be regarded as complete, and both sidos seem equally confident ot victory at the polls. We can speak for the Liberals in saying the canvass is throughout one ot the most satisfactory character, and that they have every reason to expect, if every Liberal does his duty, that they will return a majority of their candidates on Monday next. Most of the ad- dresses of the candidates will be found in our ad- vertising columns. The candidates are arrayed against each other in the following order : WARD. LIBERAL CONSIIEVATITE
CANDIDATB. CANDIDAT.B. Town Hall Wm. Pierpoint.... ..... Jas. Smethurst St. Austin's '3. J Holmes Jas. Pairclou,gh St. John's Jos. Garner Jos. Dobson

Bewsey Thos. Flood W. J. Shaw Fairfield Wm. Walker Thos. Hutchinson Howley Jos. Mounfield, Jun Wm. Bolton Orford John Bonnell W H. J. Jenkins Latchford S. B. Stringer Wm. Tinsley Whitecross Geo. Plumpton Win. Belliaa In Howley Ward Mr. Diggle is also in the field as an independent candidate.
THE TEMPERANCE FEDERATION AND THE
CANDIDATES.
The Warrington Temperance Federation sub- mitted the following questions to each of the can- didates :

(1.) Will you, if elected, vote against any person connected with the Liquor Trade having a seat upon the Watch Committee? (2.) Are you in favour of the Chief Constable being instructed to systematically enforce the Licensing Laws, with a view to reducing the drunkenness which prevails in Warrington? In every case the Liberal candidate has answered "Yes," to both questions,but answers have not been received from all the Tory candidates, and those who have answered, answer in various strains. Mr. James Smethurst says,with regard to the first ques- tion, "I prefer men who will do justice to all, and not bigots on either side." To the second question he answers "Yes." Councillor Jenkins replies to both questions as follows :—" (1) I regret that I am unable to answer the interroga- tories addressed to me by your Federation in the form in which they are put, but my opinion is that no licensed victualler, or other person immediately connected with what you term the "Liquor Trade," or any person holding strong teetotal opinions, should seek to be placed on the Watch Committee.' "(2) I am under the impression that the Chief Con- stable is instructed to systematically enforce the licensing laws." To the first question Mr. James Fairclough replies by asking another question, namely, "What about the total abstainers?" The second question he answers in. the affirmative. Councillor Hutchinson is diplomatic in his answers. To the first question he replies " wonld not support any person for the position connected with the drink trade." To the second question his answer is "If fairly defined not to harass respectable and well conducted houses, 1 should be with you." These answers have been construed to mean affirma- tives, and therefore with regard to the election in Fairfield ward the Federation takes up a neutral attitude. As Mr. Dobson answers " Yes " to both questions, the Federation is also neutral in St. John's ward. The Tory candidates for Bewsey, Howley, Whitecross, and Latchford wards have not deigned to reply to the questions, and therefore the Federation has declared against them, as well as against the Tory candidates for Town Hall, Orford, and St. Austin's wards. The appeal of the Federa- tion to the electors is "To help in removing the stain of drunkenness, which has so long brought discredit on our town, and to set aside all consi- derations of party."
THE TRADES COUNCIL AND THE ELECTIONS. CANDIDATES RECOMMENDED.

The WarringtonTrades Council submitted the follow- ing questions to each candidate: (1.) Will you (if elected), promise to vote for all Cor- poration work and contracts being given only to those employers who pay the standard rate of wages ; and for all such work and contracts being given (as far as prac_ ticable), to Warrington persons, firms, or companies ? (2.) The better paid servants of the Corporation are ' allowed holidays and are paid for the same. Will you vote that the poorer paid servants should also have holi- days and be paid thew wages for the same? (3.) The members of the Warrington Trades and Labour Councils are of opinion that by the insertion of the Fair Wage Clause in all public contracts, it would be ene great step towards abolishing that cruel evil known as the" sweating system." Would you (if elected) vote for such clause being inserted ? The Trades Council having considered the replies, at a meeting which was held on Wednesday night, re- commend candidates to the electors of the different wards in the following terms : Town Hall Ward : Mr. Pierpoint. Whitecross : Both candidates favourable. Bewsey : Both candidates favourable ; Mr. Flood has served us in the past. Orford: Both candidates favourable; Mr. Jenkins has served us in the past.
St. John's: Both candidates favourable. Fairfield: Both candidates favourable ; Mr. Hutchin- son has served us in the past. - -
Howley: All three candidates favourable, but Mr. Bolton's past conduct does not warrant our support.
St. Austin's:. Mr.C. Jackson Holmes Latchford: Mr. S. B. Stringer.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1891.
The Trades Council earnestly appeals to all working- men to be true to their principles on the day of election.
REMAINING NOMINA'IIONS.
Saturday was the last day on which nominations could be received and on that day the following papers were handed in :

Charles Jackson Holmes, 17, Folly-lane, tailor and woollen draper, nominated for St. Austin's Ward by Mr. Julian Winser, and seconded by Mr. A. Browne, and as- sented to by Messrs. James Henry Kisbey, S. Dunbobbin, J. Yonge, J. W. Johnson, J. P. Jones, T. Knowles, W. Malone, and W. Roberts. Samuel Bennett Stringer, 150, Wilderspool Causeway, gentleman, nominated for Latchford Ward by Mr. J. Strange, seconded by Mr. T. Barnes, and assented to by Messrs. J. E. Richardson, A. Wright, T. A Ward, J. Copeland, F. W. Wright, T. Hewitt, J. W. Longworth, W. Speakman, junior, W. Kirkham, and W. 'fwiss. In a second paper, Mr. Stringer is nominated by Mr. John Lunt and seconded by Mr. E. Johnson. William Bolton, Chester-road, Appleton, brewer, nomi- nated for Howley Ward, by Mr. H. King, seconded by Mr. J. Birchall, and assented to by Messrs. T. Hatton, W. Jacksom, J. T. Jon, J. Liddle, T. Peacock, J. Parr, G. Spa lrer, and J. P. (Oxley.

never large, and both candidates are well known and highly respected, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, the Liberal candidate, has, however, the advantage, as is the cage with other Liberal candidates of having the support of the temperance party and the Trades Council, Mr. Fair- dough being amongst the councillors who voted against the fair-wages resolution when it was last before the Town Council. Meetings of the supportera of both can- didates have been held daring the week. Mr. Holmes addressed the electors, on Thursday night, and made an excellent speech in which he briefly but clearly deak with various topics of interest to the electors. By way of exposing Tory tactics a poster has been issued on be- half of Mr. Holmes which says :—" The Tories are doing all they can to prevent the Liberal electors having equal rights and convenience on the day of electioa. They are not only having the use themselves of the Pblling Station School for a Committee room and refusing it to the Liberals ; but are also refusing the use of any of the spare land which surrounds the school. Electors of St. Austin's Ward! vote for Holmes and fair-play on Mon- day next.

Councillor HENnY ROBERTS, in supporting, the resolu- tion, said it was not the intention of the Warrington Temperance Federation that the respectable publicans of Warrington should be harassed by any action of theirs. Meer, hear.) Such men really needee protection against the improper action of publicans whose conduct was winked at by the police from day to day. They wanted to rid Warrington of its" black spots," and by that he meant those public-houses which were neither respectable in appearance, respectable in management, nor respectable in any other sense. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Holmes, their candidate, came of a father of whom War- rington might well be proud. (Hear, hear.) Alderman. Holmes had now rendered services to Warrington ex- tending over a period of years which many of them on the platform and in that room could not claim to have seen In season and out of season he had devoted him- ) fief unselfishly to the interests of the town, and from . what they had seen of his son he was likely to have a 'eon worthy, of such a sire. (Applause.)—Mr. ROBBFTS 'then referred to the question between the Corporation and the firm of which Mr. Fairclough is a respected member as to the right of way at Bank Quay. The Cor- poration had done everying they possibly could to avoid a/conflict, but Messrs. Fairclongh did not seem disposed to give way one iota, and the question would therefore, have to come to legal tribunal for settlement. He would not believe that Mr. Fairclough would use his position in the Council itnproperly, but at any rate until this ques- tion ia settled it would be better if the Faircloughs were outside the Council rather than in it. (Applause.) Mr. G. J. HoLatas, the-candidate, was received with loud applause. He said he did not think there was any ward in the town which he would sooner represent than St. Austin's. There was a double reason why he. should particularly wish to represent that ward. In the first place it was the ward in which he was born, and it Was the ward which many years ago, as the old south-west ward retarned his father to the Town Cbuncil. (Hear, hear, andi applause.) Therefore, he should feel it a very great honour indeed to be thought worthy of following his father's steps,and if they returned him he was sure it would be a great compliment to his father as well. (Hear, hear.) Although he could not refer, as Mr. Fairclough did, to. past experience in the. Town Council, he could at any rate say he had for years. and years taken a very great interest in the municipal life of the town, and in all matters appertaining to the good of the town. Owing to thevery close' relationship that had 'existed between himself and the Council for such a number of years,he had almost looked upon him, self as part and parcel of it. (Hear, hear.) It was to. him a matter of personal regret that he had to oppose Mr. Fairclough on that occasion, but he WAS sore Mr. Fairclough would! be the first person to agree with him that it was• not in any sense a personal fight, as between man and man, but simply a trial of strength between the two great politi- cal parties of the ward. (Hear, hear.) Why did Mr. Fairclough leave Latchford? The only conclusion was that he was moat anxious to have a political Eght, and he should have it. (Applause.) With regard to the questions sent to him by the Trades Council,. his friend Mr. Mid had bold him that his answers were entirely satisfactory to the Council and that he should therefore have their support on Monday aext. (Applause.) His answers to the Temperance Federation. had also been satisfactory, and they recommended him as the most suitable candideke in that contest. (Applause.), Speak- ing with respect to the Intercepting Depots), he thought no householder or owner of property would like to have an Intercepting Depot placed anywhere near his dwell- ing, and while txpagreed that the sanitary business of the town was well conducted bethought that, before any. further capital expenditure was incurred at Longford, a most thorough and searching inquiry should be Made into the mannerin which that place is conducted. (Hear„ hear.) As to the widening of Bridge-st.,, which affected one part of that ward, he was of opinion that the street could not be much longer left in the condition it was now in, as the traffic on Saturday nights was so great as to be almoat impassable. Another question was that of meter rents. (Hear, hear.) He believed they had in the gas. works a magnificent property, but,. under the able management of Mr. Haddock, he felt sure there.was still room for great develcpment. The only way in which the undertaking could be made of greater profit to the town was, in his opinion, by selling a greater quantity of gas, and he thought if there was a revision ef meter rents that would be one way of attaining that object. He was glad to. be able to say that the Gas Committee had under consideration at the present time a scheme for the revision of meter rents, and he believed the meter rents for cottagers and small consumers would be entirely done away with. He should be most happy to support that plan. (Applause.) Mr. Holmes alto spoke in favour of the provision of open spaces in various parts of the town, and in conclusion, said he shouid support all measures which were for the greatest number. (Loud applause.) Councillbr Plumpton and Councillor Flood also sup- ported the resolution, which on being put to the meeting was carried unanimously with acclamation. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meet- ing to a close. COUNCILLOR FLOOD'S CANDIDATURE.

MEETING LAST NIGHT. A meeting of the supporters et Mr. Thomas Mood, the Liberal candidate for Bewsey Ward, was held last night in—Wycliffe Hall. Mr. Thomas Morris presided,.and on the platform were the candidate, Mr. T. Flood, Messrs. J. Shaw Green, Malkin (Warrington Trades Council),and others.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, apologised for the absence of several prominent supporters, who were unable to be present, and speaking of the candi date said it would for ever redound to his credit that he , was the means of getting passed by the Town Council the fair-wage clause in Corporation contracts. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Flood was a well tried man, while his opponent was young and untried, and he urged those present to vote for Mr. Flood on Monday nest. (Ap- plause.)

- Mr. MALKIN in proposing that Mr. Flood was a fit and proper person to represent the Bewsey Ward remarked that when he lived in Bewsey it was a sludgy dirty hole, but now through the efforts of Mr. Flood in the council the streets were paved, clean and decent. (Applause.) Mr- OweN then seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimousty. Councillor FLOOD in reply said he was the first work- man representative in the Council, and he had tried to walk in the path of rectitude and he believed that he had never lost his independence of character. (Ap- plause.) It was in Committee that the bulk of the town's business was transacted, and he ha I there endeavoured to do his best for the interest of his fellow ratepayers. He claimed that it was through his endeavour that Bew- sey Ward had been property paved and sewered. Touching on the promise of Mr. Shaw to reduce the rates, he (the speaker) maintained that it was almost impossible at present,when the town was launching out into great improvements. As for the Waterworks, he considered they would be a great acquisition if properly managed. Mr. Shaw promised to try to abolish the meter rents. From these rents the Council derived an in- come of £l,lOO per annum. How was Mr. Sliaw going to replace it? If the amount had to be made up out of the rates, 2d. in the £ would have to be raised They were in for another difficulty,a widening of Bridge- st., A serious blunder was, made in Lower Bridge- street. There was scarcely 20 square yards of the laud there but had passed through the hands of two or three members of the Council. That was what he meant. by saying he had no axe to grind if others had. Mr. Flood next dealt with the question of the accept- ance of tenders,condemning the preference of those with a heavy discount tacked to them as a bait to get them accepted. No honest tradesmen would attempt this. Contracts had gone out of town which should have been accepted in town, and men in the town were deprived of employment. The resolution he had carried in favour of the fair-wage clauses, he said, would mean, that there should be no trimmers or bummers, and the like, but honest and straightforward tendering. If he had failed in fulfilling the obligations he had laii down for himself, it was for those present to question him on the point. He claimed that independency of character and straight- forwardness of purpose had marked every action in his career for three years. (Applause.) Mr. Councillor SHAW-GREEN and Mr. SALT Subse- quently addressed the meeting, which closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: if.) OBJECTION TO NOMINATION PAPERS.
div.p: if.) OBJECTION TO NOMINATION PAPERS.

The Mayor attended at the Town Hall, on Monday afternoon, to adjudicate upon the validity of the voting papers. There were also present—Messrs. George Plumptan, James Smethurst, William Bolton, C. Jack- son Holmes, and William Diggle (candidates) ; Councillor Henry Roberts ; Mr. John Clayton (Liberal registration agent), Mr. John Hampson (Conservative registration agent), and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle). The proceedings, which were of a very formal character, only occupied a few nvinutes.—the Mayor said he had been advised by the Town Clerk that all the nomination papers were. correct, as far as appeared on the face of them. Ile vi ished to know if any gentleman present had any objection to any of thern.—There was no reply and the Town Clerk announced that there had been no withdrawals,and none could be made now.—The- Mayor declared that the nomination papers were valid, and that all the candid- ates would have to go to the poll.—Councillor H.Roberts thanked the Mayor for his courtesy,and for the impartial manner in which he had discharged his duties that after- noon.—Councillor Bolton seconded, and the !notion was carried.--The Mayor, in reply, said during the past two years he had tried tube thoroughly impartial, and if he had made such a blunder as not to have been impartial in anything,,it had been unknown to him. He hoped the election would be conducted in a good spirit, and there would be no personalities, and that when the fight was over all the candidates would be able to shake hands most heartily. (Hear,. hear.)—The proceedings then terminated. TOWN HALL WARD.

There have been no tmetings held during th• week in Town Hall Ward, but both candidates have issued plac- ards, in addition to their addresses, appealing for the support of the electorsi. Mr_ Pierpoint's poster runs— " Vote for Pierpoint ! for nine years your tried and trusted representative." Upon the polling card which has been issued on his behalf,Mr. G. Clay, the chairman of the ward, says,—" You, are requested to vote for Mr. Pierpoint who for nine years has been an independent, able, and trusted representative- of the ward, and who is a man of first-class business capacity, in preference to one who has had no experience in municipal and public work, and who, if elected, could not render very much assistance in the management of the affairs of the borough." Wit ITECROSS WARD.

As will be seen from our report,Councillor G. Plumpton, the Liberal candidate, held a meeting in the ward last night at which he made a, vigorous reply to the Tory mis- statements at the meeting which was held by the Tories last night week. By way of showing that he has made every effort to redeem his promises during the short time he has been in the Council, Mr. Plumpton is issuing a circular in which he qtaotes from the speeches he has made in the Council with reference to the Longford and intercepting depots, the fair wage question, and the proposed new baths. He adds that, if re-elected, he will pay attention to the neglected streets of the ward, and make a request for more lamps, and he explains that he is in favour of deferred payments of the cost of street making, believing, as he does, that it can be arranged without loss to the ratepayers.

div.head: BEWSEY WARD.
div.p: BEWSEY WARD.

Mr. Shaw, the Tory candidate, held a meeting. in the ward on Thursday night, which was followed on by Councillor Flood hotiing a meeting last night. From the statements made at Mr. Shaw's meeting, it would seem that, as he is a beerseller, his supporters are alarmed at the action of the Warrington Temperance Federation, who had called attention to the fact that lie had not sent any answer to the questions they had submitted to him, and appeal to the electors to vote for Councill or Flood. Mr. Flood's voters' card says: "You are re- quested to vote for Mr. FLOOD, who for three year s has been an independent, able, and trusted representa- tive of the Ward, and who, as a working-man represen- tative of working-men, is in every way better qualified to serve the electors than one who is almost unknown to them."

div.head: ORFORD WARD
div.p: ORFORD WARD

The Liberals have every reason to be satisfied with their progress in Orford ward, and Councillor Jenkins has felt it necessary to issue a placard urging the elec- tors not to pass what would be a vote of no confidence if they failed to return one, who, as he urges, has served them so well in the pass. In reply to this the Liberals have issued a poster asking them to vote for Mr. John Bonnell who has for 40 years been amongst them as their friend and neighbour. During the week copies of a letter signed by "A Conservative" have been circulated, the writer of which says he has known Mr. Bonnell " for many years as an honourable, upright man, and one anxious upon all occasions to render any service he can for the benefit of his fellow workin..-men." Be also remarks that, as an engineer, Mr. Bonnell's long and pratical ex- perience and knowledge of machinery would be most helpful to the sanitary Committee and assist them in removing whatever nuisance may at present exist. No meetings have been held,but both Committees are work- ing exceedingly hard, and there is every prospect of a large poll with Mr. Bonnell at the head of it.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD.

Councillor Garner,the Liberal candidate for St. John's ward, is well known as an almost life-long resident in the district, and he is highly esteemed as a tradesman who was so many years in touch with a large portion of the electorate of the ward. Mr. Dobson,the Tory candi- date,resides at Lumb Brook, and is regarded as somewhat of an intruder. He claims, however, that he is a large ratepayer in the town, and that if he is sent to the coun- cil, he will speak as well as vote,on various questions. Mr. Garner has issued a circular handbill in which he explains that he is in favour of cheap and good gas, of no meter rents, cheap and free baths for the people, free education, and of the sweeping away of the intercepting depot which is in the ward. He elaims that although not a speaker, he attends .to the work of committees and is in the position of having attended more meesings of the School Attendance committee, during the past year, than any other member. The electors are asked to vote for him as one who has been " tried, trusted, and found true," and "as an old representative and the working-man's friend." FAIRFIELD WARD.

Councillor Hutchinson, who seeks re-election in this ward, has found it necessary to considerably advance his position on various questions. He finds himself hard pressed by the active Liberal candidate, Mr. William Walker, who has issued a second address in sending out his polling cards, with the object of criticising his op- ponent. FTc asks the elector; to consider what use Councillor Hutchinson has made of his opportunities as a member of the Council. He says" Has your retiring member ever called attention to evils, and has he really given attention to all matters affecting your interest and comforts ? I think not, and, therefore, Ladies and Gentlemen, I ask you for your votes, promising, that if you do me the honour of sending me to the Town Coun- cil. I shall at once direct my efforts to bring about these much-needed improvements, not waiting to the end of my term before awakening to the fact that such griev- ances exist." He expresses himself, too,as in favour of dealing with the intercepting depots, and will vote for for the abolition of meter rents. HOWLEY WARD.

The contest in flowley ward is being watched with especial interest. Mr. Bolton, as abrewer and a publican, has not thought fit to reply to the questions of the Tem- perance Federation, and, although he has been con- strained to answer the questions of the Trades' Council in the affirmative, it is well known to the electors that originally he spoke of the fair wages resolution as" ridi- culous," that he walked out of the Council to prevent its discussion,andthat,when it was again brought forward, he failed to vote for it. .Mr. Joseph Mounfield, the Liberal candidate, is a well known temperance man, and as he has answered the Trades Council to their satisfac- tion be has the support of that body in the present contest.

div.head: LATCHFORD WARD.
div.p: LATCHFORD WARD.

_ Mr. S. B. Stringer. the Liberal candidate, is prosecut- ing a vigorous canvass in Latchford Ward, which is a noted Tory stronghold. He made a good stand when he fought his first battle last year, and there is every prospect of his doing even better on Monday. Unlike his opponent, Mr. Wm. Tinsley, Mr. Stringer has answered satisfactorily the questions both of the Temperance Federation and of the Trades Council, and he has, there- fore, the active support of both those important bodies. good deal is being said in the ward about the way in which Mr. Tinsley thought fit to resign his seat about twelve months ago, because the Tory party had treated him badly, and a circular has been issued calling atten- tion to this fact, and to the fact that Councillor James Fairclough has been taken out of this ward in order to make room again for Mr. Tinsley. The circular adds— " Workingmen—What was Mr. Tinsley's action in Oct. last, in regard to Councillor Flood's motion against ' sweating ?' Mr. Tinsley was one of the Tory members who walked out of the Council Chamber, and prevented the motion being discussed. The Trades' Council there- fore recommend the electors to vote for Mr. Stringer, who has replied in favour of their proposals."
ST. AUSTIN'S WARP. • It is a matter of course to say that a neck and neck race is being run in St. Austin's Wardas the majority is

div.head: ELECTION MEETINGS.
div.p: ELECTION MEETINGS.
MR. FAIRCLOUGH'S CANDIDATURE. MEEXING IN TRINITY SCHOOLS.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the electors. of St. Austin's Ward was held in the Holy Trinity Schools; in mopport of the candidature of Mr. James Fairclough, for that ward. Alderman Sutton presided, and was sup- ported on the platform by Alderman Wright, Councillors Bolton, Muir, Heaton, Jenkins and Hepherd and Ames Fairclough and Mr. B. Pierpoint, president of the Con- servative Association. There was only a poor attendance. Th&Chairman read letters of apology for absence, from a number of gentlemen. The Chairman then addressed the meeting. Both the candidates he said, Mr. Fair- dough and Mr. Holmes, were good men, but he consi- dered the former kad the superior claim as a large ratepayer in the ward, and in consequence of being so he must be interested sn everything that was beneficial to the ward. The paving, sewering, and lighting, and general condition of the streets, and the health of the borough would have his attention. In the second place Mr. Fairclough had, already represented the ward for several years, during which time he had gained the esteemand confidence of every party and class. When he consented tolstand for Latchford the Liberals did not oppose him. In the third place as representative for a short period for Latchford ward he had gained the esteem of the Council and ratepayers. Mr. Holmes was a reluctant candidate, and as such the ratepayers would understand the difference between Mr. Fairclough and a man who came forward merely to benefit his political party.—Alderman Wright moved a resolution accepting Mr. Fairclough as a candidate.—Councillor Heaton seconded. He advanced as one reason in favour of Mr. Fairclough that Mr. Hohnes was a bachelor and would not be able adequately to represent his female constitu- ents. (Laughter.) Councillor Muir supported, urging that as the Parliamentary election was not distant there was a special reason for being anxious to return as many conservatives as possible to the Council, and therefore electing Mr. Fairclough.—Councillor Bolton supported, and Mr. K. Pierpoint followed in support of the motion;with a lengthy speech, largely devoted to imperial politics.—Mr. JAMES Fairclough thou addressed the meeting briefly. and the motion was carried. The tweeting closed with votes of thanks to the Chairman and to Mr. Pierpoint.

div.head: MEETING OF MM. BOLTON'S SUPPORTERS.
div.p: MEETING OF MM. BOLTON'S SUPPORTERS.

A meeting in support of the cannidature of Mr. W. Bolton, for Howley Ward, was held, on Wednesday evening,in the National Schools, Church-st. Dr. Cannell presided, and amongst those present were Mr. R. Pier- point, Councillors Roßon, Heaton, Hepherd, and Muir. There was a good attendance. The Chairman said Mr. Bolton was an excellent repre- sentative, and there was no man in the Town Council deserving of more respect. He thought the electors ought either to return, Mr. Bolton by a stiff majority or reject him altogether. Mr. S. Davies said that in all questions affecting the interests of ratepayers and working-men Mr. Bolton had always been at the Council to speak out. He moved a resolution in favour of Mr. Bolton's return to the Council.

Mr. H. J. Longton seconded, and spoke in favour of open spaces. being provided in the borough. Councillor Flepherd said he did not think they could find a better candidate than Mr. Bolton if they went all over Warrington for him. Mr. Hampsom denounced the action of the Warrington Temperance Federation with regard to the two questions they had sent out to candidates. The whole business, he said, was onelarge fraud, and he did not think the Rev. Mr. Langham—whose name appeared on the circulars that were sent out, along with that of Mr. W. Roberts— would put his own name there. Mr. Flampson then commented severely on teetotallers in general. The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. Mr. R. Pierpointrecommended Mr. Bolton because he was a man with sa mind of his own, and was not afried to express it. He strongly urged upon the Conservative electors to leave no stone unturned for the return of their candidate.

Mr.Bolton,who was received with applause,said he had opposed in the Councilevery experiment promoted by the Sanitary Committee, and he opposed the planting of the intercepting depots in the ward. Everything the Sank- ary Committee hod done had been a failure. He claimed credit for having promoted the extension of the baths,. and he said if returned he should look upon himself as a representative of the working-men, for it would be by their votes that he would be returned. He condemned the " catch clauses" which were brought before the Town Council by people who called themselves Trades Unionists, or something of that sort, and which, he said, were formulated only as political dodges. If these men wanted to benefit the working classes, they ought to do it straightforwardly and above-board. They ought to come to a man and ask him whether he did or did noc support their scheme. He had. however,answered their questions in the affirmative and would carry them out. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With regard to his position on the Watch Committee he defied anyone to lay a charge against him as to his conduct on that Committee. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor R. Heaton and Councillor Muir also spoke, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meet- ing to a close. MR. C. JACKSON HOLMES'S CANDIDATURE.

MEETING AT BANK QUAY. A meeting in support of Mr. C.Jackson Holmes's candi- dature for St. Austin's Ward was held at the Working- mens Mission, Bask Quay, on Thursday evening. Mr. Julian Winser presided, and there were also present Councillors Flood, Fleming, Plumpton, H. Roberts, Dr. Kisbey, Messrs. T. B. Kiernan, A. Perils. J. Walker, H. Warlow, G. Holford, J. Bonnell, W. Roberts. The CHAIRMAN said he had had great pleasure in in- troducing Mr. C. J. Holmes to the meeting that evening as their candidate for that ward. They could not pos- sibly have a better candidate. Many of them would know the public work that Mr. Helmes had done had been of the very best character, and it would be a recom- mendation, to all voters to support him. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) had been amongst the voters very considerably himself in some districts of,the ward, and he found the reception for Mr. Holmes was extremely good. He thought they had every reason to be satisfied, but what they wanted was plenty of workers on Monday. Victory could only b 3 achieved by the very best work. They had, however, encountered another difficulty. A few years ago they had two polling places in that ward, but now they had only one. The Tories had a committee room in the building, but the Liberals had great difficulty in getting accommoda- tion. One party was therefore placed at an entire dis- advantage. He could not attribute this fault to the Town Clerk, because he could not think for a moment that the Tories would have behaved in the way they have done. They were certain to overcome the difficulty but at present the land all round the polling booth was in the hands of the Tories,and the Liberals were even re- fused permission to put their wooden strulture anywhere near the polling place. They were called upon to elect a member to the Town Council but yet they had not proper facilities for doing the work. It simply showed what the Tories would do on an occasion like that ;it looked as they were getting into a difficult position and wanted to put ev,ery opposition in the way of their op- ponents. (Hear, hear.) Mr. T. B. KIERNAN moved a resolution pledging the meeting to use every legitimate effort to secure the return of Mr. Holmes. He remarked that they needed to put some new blood into the Town Council. (Hear hear.) Mr. J. H. BARLOW seconded and said he supported Mr. Holmes because he had given favourable answers to the questions sent to candidates by the Temperance Federation.

Mr. John WALKER supported the resolution. He thought St. Austin's Ward might congratulate itself upon having such a candidate as Mr. Holmes. As Mr. Kiernan had remarked,they wanted some new blood in the Town Council ; they wanted to tee the young and capable, intelligent and fair-minded men in the town, and of whom Mr. Holmes was one of the best representatives, come forward, to, so to speak, take their fathers' place, when, in the course of time, they retired. During the last few years there had been a little too much govern- ment by the older men, who naturally became Conserva- tive. What they wanted was men who were up to the times in business matters, in improvements necessary for the town, and in that expansiveness of mind which came of comparative youth and energy,and which would lead, he believed, to a greater Warrington. (Applause.) The speaker then referred to the fact that Mr. Holmes was recommended to the electors both by the Temperance Federation and the Trades Council. He pointed out that Mr. Fairclough was one of those who voted against the fair-wages resolution brought forward in July, in the Town Council by Mr. Flood. The answers of Mr. Holmes had been satisfactory to the Trades Council and they earnestly appealed to all workingmen to give him all the support they , could on the election day. (Applause.) Councillor naafis() and Dr. Kpacr also spoke in sup- port of the resolution and warmly recommended Mr. Holmes to the electors.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND THE SALT TRADE A SUCCESSFUL EXPERIMENT.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THE SALT TRADE A SUCCESSFUL EXPERIMENT.

The trade along the lower sections of he Ship Canal which are now opened for traffic has up to the present not been of every extensive dimensions, but an event took place, on Thursday, which may have the effect of most materially increasing the number of vessels that use the artificial waterway. Early in the week the Steamship Sumus of Middles- borough, arrived at Garston with a cargo of salt cake. As the neap tides were on, the vessel could not reach Weston Point by thE., river, and as there was a cargo of salt awaiting it there, the captain, Mr. Hodgson, determined to make the experiment of using the Ship Canal. Piloted by Captain Hill, the well-known pilot of Runcorn, the vessel, which was light, arrived at Delamer° Dock, Weston Point, at ten o'clock on Wednesday , morning, after a quick passage from Garston. With commendable despatch the enterprising firm I of Messrs. Verdin Bros had the holds of the ship filled with salt, and she was .ready to start on her journey next morning. Registered at 141 tons and 133 feet long, the vessel had a cargo of 235 tons causing her to draw llft, aft and 10ft. forward. Again piloted by Captain Hill she left Weston Point at 7 a.m. and slowly steamed up the Weaver Canal. There was some likelihood that the ship having such a deep draught might touch the bottom in one or t wa of the shallow places which are known to ex- but, skilfully handled she avoided any

MAGNETO ELECTRIC MACHINES TOR NERVOUS DISEASES. W. MORTON, ELECTRICIAN, 127. SANKEY - STREET, WARRINGTON.

such mishap, and at 7.45 she had success- fully passed the Marsh Lock and was steam- ing across the Weaver estuary to the ship canal entrance at Frodsham Marsh, and the crew hoisted flags in honour of the occasion, as the Sumus was

div.head: TU 1711.8 T LAWS LOADIM VESSEL.
div.p: TU 1711.8 T LAWS LOADIM VESSEL.

I that had attempted the passagetand was absolutely, the first cargo of salt that had gone down the canal. In order to catch the tide at Eastham, it was neces- sary that the ship, should reach that place by half- past nine, and no fears were entertained of accom- plishing this with considerable time to spare, but unfortunately a thick ground fog sprang up and for some time the banks of the canal were hidden. Proceeding with great caution. Ellesmere Port was passed, and, the fog afterwards lifting, more speed was put on and the ship arrived at Eastham at 9.25, and then proceeded on her voy- age to Swansea, where her cargo was consigned to Messrs. Vivian and CO, The Captain had kindly given a few Runcornians a passage down the canal, and he most hospitably entertained thernon board. They parted from him with the oft repeated wishes for a prosperofas voyage. The Sumus belongs to Messrs. Hogg,Henderson, end Co., of Middlesborough. The importance of the event we are chronicling cannot be over-estimated in its influence on the Ship Canal. The Company recognised that this was so by allowing the vessel to use their waterway tolli free, thus saving the owners about £4 10s. Every year there are millions of tone of salt sent down the Weaver in large barges, which is loaded into large ships at Garston and Liverpool from these craft. Now, in the instance under notice, had the Swims been loaded in Garaton, there would have been a charge of Is. for lighterage and 3d. per ton for dues, making a charge of Is. 3d. on the cargo. At Weston Point the charge is 4d. per ton on the registered tonnage and 2d. per ton on the cargo, making an average of 4411. per ton on the cargo, or a saving of 10,-id. per ton. Captain Hodgson did not hesitate to sound the praises of the canal, which he said was the finest on which he had ever sailed: and ha estimated that being able to use the Ship Canal in his trade with Wes- ton Point would save him £l2 a week. He is to be commended for his enterprise in first making the experiment, and no doubt the shareholders hope that many others will follow the example he has set.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE,/ ?RIR/LT.—nig i a quiet d ay- in- r-I.l' departments, and the riseof the Bank rate iv not calculated nn help matters. Cotton is also tame ; " futures " have nob altered much since the opening, but spot business is covered by the first estimate of 7,000 bales, prices favouring buyers and some Egyptian and Indian qualities reduced. Yasuo are very slow but steady, in part no donbt because so fest buyers are prepared to lead sellers Into temptation Bundles are also tame, and little gets done at quotations. In clotlb dusiness drags all round. There is some inquiry for low Indian shirtings, but the prices offered are too poor, and generally lower thou makers care to accept. MUNICIPAL ELECTION. 'TOTHE ELECTORS OF THE TOWN HALL. WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—The time has arrived for me to again appeal to you for your support. I am no'stranger to you You have had for the past nine years full opportunity of judging of my polfcy in the Council Chamber. The Freeing of the Library. the purchase of the Water Works, and the establishment of Classes for Technical Edu- cation, had my cordial support. and I trust they have' your approval. If you approve of my endeavours to promote the economi- cal and efficient government of the Borough, I hope you will honour me with your vote. As a business man, I claim to know something of the requirements of the town, and will do all in rr y power in the future, as in the past, to further its improvement. Ladies and Gentlemen, I am, yours obediently, WILLIAM PIERPOINT. Latchford, October 15, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION . TOWN HALL WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF TIIE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.-At the repeated requests of a large and influential body of ratepayers of your ward, and after careful consideration, I have consented to offer myself as a candidate to represent you in the Town Council. I have, as most of you know, for many years taken an active part in all movements for the benefit of the people,and whether or not you return me to the Council my serrices in all matters where your welfare is concerned shall be at. your disposal. There are many large and important works under the con- trol of the Corporation which require most careful attention, and should you honour me by returning me as your repre- sentative, I shall devote all my ability to see that they are conducted with efficiency and due economy. I am in favour of the abolition of Meter Rents at the earliest possible moment, and of a reduction in the price of Gas. I have no self-interest to serve by being a member of the Town Council, and if elected shall feel myself free at all times to bring forward and support measures necessary for the comfort and convenience of the Burgesses of the Town Hall Ward. Having consented to serve you, at some sacrifice of my per- sonal interest, I trust ths my friends will rally round me on the 2nd November, and return me as their representative by a large majority. I am Ladies and Gentlemen. Your Obedient Servant. JAMES SMETHURST. 60, Bewsey Street, Warrington, Octobt r 20, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. TO THE BURGESSES OF WHITECROSS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—In June last, you did me the honour of electing me, by a large majority, as one of your representatives to the Town Council The ward has, in my opinion, quite unnecessarily, again been put to the trouble and expense of a contested election. The promises I made to you a few months ago, I am anxious to have the opportunity of fulfilling, and if you renew your con- fidence in me, on the 2nd of November, as I believe you will, no effort shall be wanting on my part to do my duty by all parties conscientiously and faithfully. Your Obedient Servant, GEORGE PLUMPTON.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WHITECROFS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—At the request of a large body of Ratepayers of the Ward. I have consented to become a candidate to represent you in the Town Council. Having been a resident in the Ward for upwards of 36 years, I may fairly claim to be thoroughly conversant with the real wants and requiremeuts of my fellow townsmen, and without promisingto do impossibilities and without seeking to take credit foilanything which has already been settled in the Council, I will at least say that, should you do me the honourto return me as your Representative, my earnest endeavours shall at all times be used to further those mea- sures which are best calculated to promote the comfort and prosperity of the community. The Paving, Lighting and Sewerage of a large portion of the Ward have been much neglected in the past and demand immediate attention. Any improvement in this direction would have my active support. As a Working-man and an employer of labour, I think the whole of my past action is a sufficient guarantee that I believe in a " Fair Day's pay for a Fair Day's Work," and there is no necessity for me to alter my principles in this respect at the present moment simply to gain your votes. As I have been, so shall I consistently continue, a staunch supporter of the working-men. both in and out or the Council. As regards Sanitary and other affairs, I intend to express my view sat a public meeting at an early date, and if the votes of all my friends are accorded to me freely and inde- pendently, I have no fear of the result. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. WILLIAM BELLIAN. 22, Lovely-lane, Warrington, October 14th, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. TO THE ELECTORS OF BEWSEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—My term of Office as your representative in the Town Council having expired, at the request of my friends and supporters, I again offer myself for re-election. My efforts during the past three years have been directed to promoting the interests and welfare of my fellow towns- men. I have guarded their interests by steadfastly opposing any wasteful or extravagant expenditure of the public money. I have taken part in every Educational Movement that has, from time to time, come before the Council, and I have contributed in every way I could to secure a Free Library, which will be a blessing to the present and to future gener- ations. Ihave at all times been most assiduous in attending to questions affecting Sanitary Reform, and should you again honour me by electing me, I shall always be found using my influence in helping to remove the evils of which complaint is made. I have devoted special attention to the Paving and Sewer- ing of your streets, and in that direction I have secured an Improved stateof things compared with what existed previous to my entering the Council. During my term of office, the ratepayers have become the owners of the Water Works ; and with regard to this I take some little credit for early efforts in promoting the agitation which led to this valuable acquisition. As many of you knew, I have, for nearly 30 years been en active Trades Unionist ; and only the other week I had the satisfaction of receiving a u nft,,iinous vote of thanks from the Warrington Trades Counci fc. the successful efforts I made to induce the Town Con-, rc a motion in favour of Fair Wages Clauses being inserted ill Corporation Con- tracts. Under these circumstances, I trust I may count upon a renewed expression of your confidence on the polling day. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant. THOMAS FLOOD. 9, Catherine-street, Warrin gton, October 20, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE BURGESSES OF TIIE BEWSEY WARD. -- LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I have been waited upon by a large body of Ratepayers of the Ward requesting me to con- test it and become your Candidate to represent you in the Town Council. My native town is your borough, and during my years of manhood I have been thoroughly acquainted with the work- ing of the town, and have a good knowledge of its require- ments. The Sanitary matters I know require a great deal of attention. These I promise to attend to, to the uttermost of my ability. Improvements might be made in the bye streets and passages which would be a great boon to the ratepayers, and this shall have my best attention, With regard to the Licensing question, I am of opinion that the men of Bewsey are being unfairly treated, and so far as my influence as your Representative in the Town Council can be of avail, I shall do my utmost to promote the granting of a fully Licensed House in Bewsey Road. As a Working-man and Labour Representative, I scarce need to mention my views. For 20 years I have upheld Trade Unionism, and championed their cause. And I have been at all times to the front when the rights of working-men were challenged. This! shall a ntinue to do both in and out of Council. On other affairs, such as Lighting, Gas, and Water. I shall have the pleasure of expressing my views at an early date. And if my friends accord to me their votes independently, I am sure the result will be victory. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, WILLIAM JAS. SHAW. 89, Dallam-lane, Warrington, October 16th, 1891.

MUNICIPAL BLEGTION, 1891. TO THE BURGESSES OF ORFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, —I have been favoured by receiv- ing a cordial and pressing invitation to offer myself as a can- diate to represent you in the Town Council. In consenting to place my services at your disposal, I think I may describe myself as a friend and neighbour—in fact, one of yourselves—because it has been my good fortune to live In the Ward, and also to be an employer of labour in your midst, for upwards of thirty years. I am, therefore,personally known to a great number of you, and shall if elected, do my utmost to improve the condition of your streets, and if possible, secure better homes for the working classes, It will be known to some of you that many years ago I was the means of introducing and establishing in Warrington the "Saturday afternoon Holiday" for working-men ; and throughout my business career I have always been an ad- vocate of "A Fair Day's Wage for a Fair Day's Work." In conclusion, should you place me at the head of the Poll on theday of election, it will always be my earnest endea- vour to promote every measure which aims at making life happier, brighter, and better, for the deserving poor, and to seek to remove some of the burdens which are so oppressive to the working classes. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Friend and Neighbour, JOHN BONNELL. Folly-lane. October, 1891,

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE BURGESSES OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—My term of office St one of your representatives in the Town Council having expired. I beg to offer myself for re-election. During the time I have had the honour of representing you, it has been my endeavour to serve you to the best of my ability, and, by constant attendance at the various Commit- tees, I have watched your interests very carefully. With reference to tie Intercepting Depots I have, as a property owner in the ward, a great desire to see removed any nuisance which arises from these works, aril will gladly lend my assistance to any movement having this object in view. lam strongly of opinion that the rates of the Borough are excessive, and shall in the future, as in the past, oppose all unnecessary expenditure. Being one of the oldest residents in the neighbourhood, I am personally known to most of you, and shall esteem it a pleasure tc serve you to the best of my ability ; and, if I am honoured by a renewal of your confidence, I shall do what I can to merit the trust reposed in me. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH GARNER. Marshhouse-lane, Warrington, Octobei• 15. 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION.—ST. JOHN'S WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARM LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,-At the reauest of a large and influential body of Burgesses of your Ward. I have much pleasurein offering myself as a Candidate to represent you in the Town Council. I was brought up in your Ward, and have lived amongst you nearly all my life. I may therefore fairly claim that your interests and mine are Identical. My opponent says he has done his best according to'• his ability," but that ability seems to have been merely to sit in the Council and vote as he has been told by the Wire Pullers of a Political Party, without ever saying a word on your be- half. It is may intention, should you honour me by electing me as your repre.entative, to both speak and act on every question brought before the Council in which your interests are concerned. With reference to the Intercepting Depot so cruelly planted and maintained in the heart of your Ward, I am of opinion that it is a public nuisance, incapable of remedy, and that it ought to be entirely done a xay with as soon as possible. My opponent says that in his opinion the Rates of the Borough are excessive. What has he done either to reduce Rates or Rents during the time be has been supposed to repre- sent you in the Council ? I pay a very large sum yearly for rates, ana am personally in favour of their being as low as possible, consistent with the efficient m tnagement of the affairs of the Borough, therefore I shall be careful at all times to secnre economy in that respect, but my first consideration on all occasions shall be your comfort and convenience with- out regard to cost. I shall explain my views on other questions which may in- terest you at a Public Meeting, and in addition shall endeav- our to see each of you personally before the day of election. with a view to ascertain more fully your desires and require- ments. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH DOBSON. Warrington, Oct. 19th, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION.—FAIRFIRLD TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. At the urgent request of many of the Burgssses of this Ward, I have mnch pleasure in again placing my services at your disposal For the past nine years I have been a member of the Town Council, and may,therefore, fairly claim to know all the duties required of your Representative. During the past year I have attended nearly 100 meetings of the Council and the various Committees of which I am a member. You will there- fore see that I have been attentive to my duties, and should you honour me by re-electing me I shall in future as I have done in the past give my earnest and continuous attention to all matters affecting your interests and comfort. lam a native of the Borough, and during the first 24 years of my life resided in your Ward. I have been a manu- facturer and employer of labour in Warrfngton for over 30 years, and am a large Ratepayer, consequently it will always be my desire to keep down the rates as low as possible con- sistent with your necessities. The proper Lighting, Paving, and Sewerage of your Streets shall have my earnest and constant attention. It has already been determined to cover up Howley Brook, and thus, as a death trap, it will soon be a thing of the past. I consider that the Intercepting Depots areon their trial, and If they cannot be worked so as not to be offensive to the Bur- gesses, I shall vote for their entire removal. I feel that I may therefore, with the greatest confidence, appeal to you to return me on the day of election to be your representative by a large majority. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, THOMAS HUTCHINSON. 31. Wilson Fatten-st., Warrington, October 19th, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. T° THE ELECT° t,S OF HOWLEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I have been requested by a large number c,l Electors to allow myself to be nominated as a Candidate for your Ward, and, after giving the matter due consideration, I have consented to place my services at your disposal. I am well known to most of you as a resident in the Ward for thirty years ; and I think I may claim to know something of the needs of this district. If elected as your representative, I shall do what I can in helping to get rid of the nuisance of the Intercepting DepBts. There has been too much delay in dealing effectively with the matter, and lam anxious to see steps taken at once which will either end or mend the DepBts. It is time, too, that something was done to ensure that there shall be no further sacrifice of life at Howley Brook; and that the lower parts of the Ward shall be safeguarded from the flooding of the river. As a joiner and builder, I believe! can be of some service in considering how to remedy these defects, and in helping the working-classes of the Ward to healthier and more comfortable homes by providing them with well-paved streets, yards, and back passages. These and other kindred matters will receive my beet attention, if elected to serve you. Trusting to have your support on the 2nd of November, I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours obediently, JOSEPH MOUNFIELD. 17, Church-at., Warrington, October 20,1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. TO THE ELECTORS OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIEB AND GENTLEMEN.-At the urgent request of an Influential body of ratepayers, I have again decided to offer myself as a Candidate for your sufFrages on the 2nd of November. Since I last addressed you, several of the important mea- sures I then advocated have been adopted. The transfer of the Waterworks to the Corporation has been accomplished; the Library has been made Free; and. the Bathe are being enlarged. Many desirable improvements still remain to be effected before the laws of healthcan thoroughly be complied with in the Borough. In many parts of the town there are "Black Spots" demaneling thoughtful consideration before the rate of mortality can be brought down to its lowest possible paint. I am still of opinion that it Is contrary to the highest in- terests of the Inhabitants that the Liquor Trade should be so strongly represented on the Watch Committee. If you return me to the Council, I shall mgard it as my duty to further your interests, and the interests of the Town generally, by supporting the views which I have here, and have previously, laid before you. Trusting to have your support, / am. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, SAMUEL B. STRINGER. Gordon Villas, Wilderspool-road, October 23,1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. TO THE ELECTORS OF ST. AUSTIN'S WARD LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, —Having been urgently re- quested by a deputation from this Ward to allow myself to be nominated as a candidate for your Ward in the forthcoming Municipal contest. I have consented to do so. I promise, if you return me. to do all in my power to assist in the efficient and economical government of the Borough. I am well known to most of you, having been born in your Ward, and actively engaged in business in the town for a considerable number of years. Hoping I may be favoured with your votes on the day of election, lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, CHARLES JACKSON HOLMES. Market Gate, Oct. 21st, 1891.

MUNICIPAL BLECT_IONS.—ST. AUSTIN'S WARD. The Lord Chancellor, on Monday, received Aldermap Evans, the Lord Mayor-Elect, the Sheriffs-Elect, &c., at the House of Lords. He expressed his pleasure at meet- ing the new Lord May-or, whose appointment had been sanctioned by her Majesty. Alarming anti-Salvationist riots occurred at East- bourne, on Sunday. Many people were injured, and the police for a time were powerless. The Duke of Edinburgh opened a new wing of the Bristol Hospital on Saturday,aad afterwards planted an oak in the grounds of an industrial home.

MEDIATION REFUSED AT SUNDERLAND. The shipowners at Sunderland have declined the Mayor's proffered mediaticn in their dispute with the raen. DROWNED THROUGH THE FOG. During the fog four persons fell into the water at Glasgow on Thursday night. Bridget Quigley was drowned. MEN BURIED IN AN OLD BUILDING. At Liverpool, yesterday, some workmen were dis- mantling an old warehouse, when the building collapsed burying them in the ruins. When rescued, four had to b. taken to the hospital. ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE. The Press Association telegraphs that Reuben Rainbow invited George Brewer, a relative, to ride with him in his trap near Kenilworth, on Thursday night, and shot him in the head. Brewer crawled home, but no hopes are entertained of his recovery. Rainbow drove off im- mediately he had wounded Brewer, and shot himself fatally when near Rugby.
